findings.headline: The draft budget proposes a 4.99% council tax increase for 2027/28, made up of a 2.99% core increase and a 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept.
findings.detail: The provisional Band D figure is £1,939.72, and the increase is subject to consultation starting 2 December 2026.
findings.matters: The council is using the full social care precept alongside its core increase, which is a revenue choice a finance director at another council will compare against their own council tax decisions.
findings.figures: 4.99% total increase; 2.99% core increase; 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept; £1,939.72 provisional Band D
findings.quote: a 4.99% increase on the previous year (2.99% core increase plus a 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept)

findings.headline: Capital resources are 'challenged', with new projects limited to essential or ring-fenced ones, and a potential 2027/28 to 2031/32 funding gap being assessed
findings.detail: The programme is refreshed for revised expenditure profiles and includes rolling 2031/32 programmes based on known or projected ring-fenced funding. The pipeline update assesses a potential funding gap and the choices to be made.
findings.matters: A council restricting its capital programme to essential or fully funded schemes, and naming a pipeline funding gap, is a signal of capital capacity for peers and lenders.
findings.figures: Capital programme 2027/28 to 2031/32; rolling programme for 2031/32
findings.quote: Capital resources are challenged, and this has resulted in only essential projects, or those with ring fenced funding being added to the programme.

findings.headline: The HRA stock condition survey programme has been accelerated, with 90% of stock surveyed within the last 18 months.
findings.detail: The original plan was to survey one-third of properties each year over three years. Results to date have not identified major investment needs, but the paper says the surveys are not yet complete.
findings.matters: A housing authority with non-traditional stock accelerating condition surveys to size investment needs is relevant to any council with similar asset profiles.
findings.figures: 90% of housing stock surveyed within the last 18 months; original approach one-third per year over three years
findings.quote: The stock condition survey programme has been significantly accelerated, with 90% of the housing stock surveyed within the last 18 months

findings.headline: The Housing Revenue Account now has a balanced position over the medium term, and planned borrowing is within the target Interest Cover Ratio threshold.
findings.detail: The HRA business plan was refreshed at the end of quarter 2. The paper says future planned borrowing is within the target Interest Cover Ratio threshold.
findings.matters: A council whose HRA plan shows planned borrowing inside its interest cover target is giving lenders a specific test they can use to judge capacity.
findings.figures: Balanced medium-term HRA position; planned borrowing within target Interest Cover Ratio threshold
findings.quote: The Council now has a balanced position over the medium term and future planned borrowing is within the target Interest Cover Ratio threshold.

findings.headline: The draft budget closes the 2027/28 gap through budget reductions, income proposals and higher Business Rates income, with no reserves used for the base budget.
findings.detail: The paper says pressures and inflation have been offset by services' budget reductions and income proposals. It also says the council is not using reserves to balance the base budget.
findings.matters: A council stating it is not using reserves for day-to-day spending, a commitment in its Council Plan, is one a lender or peer finance director will check against actual outturn.
findings.figures: Council Plan target: balanced 2027/28 budget not relying on reserves for day-to-day spending
findings.quote: Currently we are not using reserves to balance the base budget.

findings.headline: The draft General Fund budget for 2027/28 is balanced, with a forecast base budget gap of £5.547m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: The council says pressures and higher inflation have been offset by budget reductions, income proposals and higher Business Rates income. The February 2026 forecast had a 2027/28 gap of £1.631m.
findings.matters: A council moving from a £1.631m 2027/28 gap to a balanced draft budget, with savings and income offsetting pressures, shows a method other finance directors can compare with their own gap closure.
findings.figures: £5.547m forecast base budget gap by 2030/31; £1.631m February 2026 forecast 2027/28 gap
findings.quote: The 2027/28 Draft General Fund budget is currently balanced, with a forecast base budget gap of £5.547m by 2030/31.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes City Council did not receive High Needs Stability Grant because it held an overall DSG surplus at 31 March 2026, while the national grant total was £5.812bn.
findings.detail: The grant was for councils with an overall DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 and covered 90% of that deficit. The council's surplus status meant it was excluded.
findings.matters: Eligibility depended on the year-end DSG position, so a council in surplus at 31 March received nothing, which matters to peers judging how far the grant offsets deficits.
findings.figures: £5.812bn total national grant; 90% of deficit balance as eligibility basis
findings.quote: Milton Keynes City Council was not eligible for funding as it held an overall DSG surplus balance at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: The council has applied to the DfE to move 0.5% of the Schools Block, approximately £1.515m, to the High Needs Block, after Schools Forum did not support the proposal.
findings.detail: The disapplication request is pending. The final High Needs position, including the outcome of the request and any savings measures, will go to Cabinet with the final budget in February 2027.
findings.matters: It shows a council using a disapplication route, with the local schools forum opposed, to close a High Needs gap, a route other councils with DSG pressures may consider.
findings.figures: 0.5% of Schools Block allocation; approximately £1.515m
findings.quote: seeking approval to transfer 0.5% of the Schools Block allocation (approximately £1.515m) to the High Needs Block

findings.headline: Current forecasts put the 2027/28 High Needs year-end deficit at £2.473m, before confirmation of 2027/28 DSG allocations.
findings.detail: The paper says the position is expected to worsen in 2027/28. DfE has not yet confirmed 2027/28 DSG allocations, and the draft High Needs budget assumes no increase in funding.
findings.matters: A forecast deficit rising from £0.376m to £2.473m on a flat-funding assumption is a pressure finance officers at other councils will be tracking against their own High Needs forecasts.
findings.figures: £2.473m forecast 2027/28 year-end deficit; £0.376m 2026/27 forecast year-end deficit
findings.quote: The financial position is expected to deteriorate further in 2027/28, with current forecasts indicating a forecast year-end deficit of £2.473m

findings.headline: The High Needs Block 2026/27 Period 6 forecast shows an in-year deficit of £1.615m, partly offset by a £1.239m brought-forward surplus, leaving a forecast year-end deficit of £0.376m.
findings.detail: The paper reports that expenditure on the High Needs Block continues to exceed DSG funding. The forecast year-end position is reduced by a surplus carried forward from 2025/26.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a High Needs pressure can compare the in-year gap and the offset from prior-year balances against their own DSG position.
findings.figures: £1.615m in-year deficit; £1.239m surplus brought forward from 2025/26; £0.376m forecast year-end deficit
findings.quote: The latest 2026/27 Period 6 forecast projects an in-year deficit of £1.615m. This will be partially offset by the £1.239m surplus balance brought forward from 2025/26, resulting in a forecast year-end deficit of £0.376m.

findings.headline: Total pressures are shown as £7,407k in 2027/28, £5,237k in 2028/29, £7,793k in 2029/30 and £8,724k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The risk-level table totals the pressures by year. The demand subtotal (£6,451k) and other subtotal (£733k) for 2027/28 add to £7,184k, not the £7,407k total shown in the same paper.
findings.matters: A council's total pressure across the MTFP is the figure a finance director and lender would use to size the gap, so the difference between subtotals and total is worth checking.

findings.headline: Environmental Services contract annual leave alignment is estimated at £310k from 2027/28, subject to a 15 December delegated decision.
findings.detail: The paper says the council is seeking to align annual leave entitlements across TUPE-transferred staff as part of a proposed contract extension. The final amount depends on agreement with the contractor and confirmation of the affected workforce.
findings.matters: A TUPE-driven contract cost decided by delegation within weeks is a decision point other councils with similar contracts may face.
findings.figures: estimated recurring cost £310k from 2027/28; delegated decision date 15 December
findings.quote: The estimated recurring contract cost is £310k from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Local elections move to a base budget from 2028/29, with a £460k cost and a reserve to smooth the four-year cycle.
findings.detail: The paper says a base budget for average election costs will replace one-off funding from 2028/29. In the fallow year the budget is added to a reserve, which is drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.
findings.matters: Moving a cyclical cost into a base budget with a reserve is an approach other councils with four-year election cycles may consider.
findings.figures: 2028/29 base budget £460k
findings.quote: During this fallow year, the budget will be added to the reserve, which can be drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.

findings.headline: A £300k saving from charging for second and third food and garden waste bins is reversed after uptake fell short of assumptions.
findings.detail: The paper says demand has been materially below the level assumed in the budget. The income target is reversed, with a corresponding £300k reduction in the Environmental Services contract budget proposed separately.
findings.matters: A charged garden waste service that has not reached the assumed uptake is a saving other councils have also budgeted, and the paper shows how one council reversed it.
findings.figures: £300k saving reversed; corresponding £300k reduction in Environmental Services contract budget; income line -£380k (gross)
findings.quote: Demand has been materially below the level assumed and there is currently insufficient evidence that uptake will increase to the level required.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract forecast retains the existing £1.9m pressure and adds £500k.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has procured and mobilised a new 10 + 5 year contract for the Waste Recovery Park. The pressure is based on visible operating costs, and any later evidenced efficiency will be reflected in future MTFP updates.
findings.matters: A contract pressure rising by £500k after mobilisation shows how operating costs can move after a re-procurement, which other councils with similar contracts may face.
findings.figures: existing pressure £1.9m; additional £500k; gross budget £19,902k
findings.quote: The current forecast requires the existing £1.9m pressure to be retained and a further £500k added.

findings.headline: Families First reforms must be delivered by March 2027, with a £947k pressure shown for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the government programme requires significant reforms to Children's Services by March 2027, including family help hubs, an edge of care service and enhanced data reporting. The table shows £947k in 2027/28 and -£288k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A statutory reform deadline with a costed pressure attached is one a finance director elsewhere will be tracking for delivery and funding.
findings.figures: deadline March 2027; 2027/28 pressure £947k; 2028/29 -£288k
findings.quote: The government programme requires significant reforms to Children's Services by March 2027.

findings.headline: Educational psychology service is no longer eligible for high needs block funding, creating a £149k 2027/28 pressure.
findings.detail: The paper says a review of high needs block eligibility and terms and conditions removed the service's eligibility for this funding stream. Funding had previously supported a significant share of staffing costs.
findings.matters: A loss of high needs block funding for a statutory service is a funding change that other councils may face when reviewing the same grant conditions.
findings.figures: 2027/28 pressure £149k; gross budget £1,195k
findings.quote: the educational psychology service is no longer eligible to receive this funding stream.

findings.headline: Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub is managing approximately 28% more contacts than in 2024/25, with delays emerging in the system.
findings.detail: The paper links the rise partly to Families First reforms and partly to population growth and housing expansion. It says the service needs additional capacity to meet statutory assessment timescales.
findings.matters: A rise in front-door contacts drives statutory workload and cost in children's services, and a finance director in another area would want to know whether they face the same trend.
findings.figures: approximately 28% more contacts than 2024/25; 2027/28 pressure £64k; gross budget £3,091k
findings.quote: the service now managing approximately 28% more contacts than in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Average weekly cost for care leavers' accommodation rose from £133 in 2023/24 to £389 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says placement numbers have stabilised at 32 care leavers, but costs have risen due to longer stays and more complex need. A fall in the proportion of UASC care leavers has also reduced external funding available to offset costs.
findings.matters: A roughly threefold rise in unit cost, alongside lower external grant, is a cost-per-placement change that other councils may be experiencing.
findings.figures: £133 weekly (2023/24); £389 weekly (2026/27); 2027/28 pressure £535k; gross budget £403k; 32 care leavers (2026/27)
findings.quote: Average weekly costs have risen from £133 in 2023/24 to £389 in 2026/27.

findings.headline: External children's residential placements rose from 26 in 2023/24 to 67 in 2026/27, with the pressure based on 53 placements in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the rise to a significant increase in residential placements over three financial years. The pressure line reduces to 46 placements in 2028/29, with the table showing -£3,089k in that year.
findings.matters: A large and rising count of external residential placements is one of the main cost exposures in children's social care, and the paper's planned reduction depends on an assumption that a finance director can test.
findings.figures: 26 placements (2023/24); 67 placements (2026/27); 53 placements (2027/28 basis); 46 placements (2028/29); gross budget £25,123k; 2027/28 -£643k; 2028/29 -£3,089k
findings.quote: increasing from 26 in 2023/24 to 67 in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities has 339 packages against a budget of 419 in 2026/27, with the pressure reduced by £708k.
findings.detail: The paper says weekly panels now review all new and increased care packages, and that this scrutiny contributed to the forecast 2026/27 underspend. Package numbers are expected to rise to 378 in 2027/28, 389 in 2028/29 and 400 in 2029/30.
findings.matters: A council that has cut a disability package pressure through panel scrutiny is showing a control measure other councils with similar demand may want to compare.
findings.figures: 339 packages; budget of 419 packages; pressure change -£708k in 2027/28; gross budget £4,190k
findings.quote: In 2026/27 there are currently 339 packages against a budget of 419.

findings.headline: Children's Services shows a total of -£71k for 2027/28 and -£2,118k for 2028/29 across its pressure lines.
findings.detail: The total for Children's Services is a net reduction in the first two years of the MTFP, after the individual lines for packages and placements are netted off. The paper attributes the reductions to lower package numbers and lower projected placements.
findings.matters: A net reduction in the service with the largest demand exposure in the paper is the kind of change a finance director would compare against their own children's budget.
findings.quote: Total Children's Services 67,558 -71 -2,118 693 1,552

findings.headline: Older People demand is shown as meetable within current budgets for 2027/28, with the pressure reduced by £325k.
findings.detail: The paper says the Older People pressure has decreased because 2026/27 Homecare and Direct Payments budgets are underspent, following a 2025/26 surge after internal homecare closed. Demand is still forecast to rise by 7% in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere will want to see how a council reversed a demand pressure after it had been built into the budget, and what caused the earlier overshoot.
findings.figures: 2027/28 change -£325k; gross budget £34,767k; OP demand forecast to increase 7% in 2027/28
findings.quote: we have established that this can be met by current budgets for 2027/28, resulting in a decrease in the predicted pressure.

findings.headline: Election Reserves will be replaced by a base budget from 2028-29, which the paper says will eliminate the need for one-off funding
findings.detail: From 2028-29 the paper proposes a base budget for elections based on average cost. The budget is added to the reserve during the fallow year and drawn down when election costs exceed it, with forecast balances moving up and down across the cycle.
findings.matters: A council moving a recurring cost from one-off reserve funding into the base budget is a change in how it funds a regular cost that other councils with four-year election cycles would weigh.
findings.figures: £0.838m drawn (31/03/2028 forecast movement); £0.198m (31/03/2029 forecast movement)
findings.quote: incorporating a base budget for Elections to cover the average cost of elections will eliminate the need for one-off funding.

findings.headline: Corporate Property and Asset Reserve is forecast to fall from £2.222m to nil by 31/03/2029, with allocations added to the capital programme
findings.detail: The reserve funds one-off expenditure on operational buildings. The paper says a Strategic Asset Management Strategy has been developed and that allocations have been added into the capital programme.
findings.matters: Moving a reserve balance into the capital programme shows where operational building investment is being recorded, which affects how peers compare asset renewal plans.

findings.headline: Bereavement Reserve is forecast to rise from £5.413m to £8.039m by 31/03/2031 as a sinking fund for crematorium and cemetery provision
findings.detail: The reserve is to replace and extend crematorium and cemetery provision as the borough grows. The paper describes it as a sinking fund to offset that pressure, and the balance increases in every forecast year.
findings.matters: A sinking fund for future capital provision on a growing population shows how a council is planning for demand-driven capital costs.
findings.quote: This reserve is a sinking fund to offset this pressure.

findings.headline: The HRA Financing & Debt Risk Reserve holds £5.343m in every forecast year to cover unplanned interest rate increases
findings.detail: The reserve gives cover should the council experience unplanned interest rate increases in a particular year. The forecast balance is unchanged across the period from 31/03/2026 to 31/03/2031.
findings.matters: A dedicated reserve against interest-rate exposure on housing debt is a risk measure that lenders and finance directors compare across councils with HRA borrowing.
findings.quote: The purpose of this reserve is to provide cover should we experience unplanned interest rate

findings.headline: Infrastructure Reserve, which funds the borrowing costs of highways investment, is forecast to fall from £11.868m to £4.489m by 31/03/2031
findings.detail: The reserve holds revenue contributions for the prior year, current and future borrowing costs of highways investment. The paper says it will remain in use for the term of the borrowing, and that the current programme of work runs until 2038.
findings.matters: A reserve earmarked for borrowing costs over a long programme is a direct indicator of how a council expects to service its debt, which lenders assess closely.
findings.quote: This reserve will remain in use for the term of the borrowing - Borrowing terms vary

findings.headline: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve is forecast to rise from £11.406m to £30.649m by 31/03/2031 as annual revenue contributions build up for vehicle replacement
findings.detail: The reserve is built up through annual revenue contributions so that replacement waste vehicles can be financed when they reach the end of their useful life. The paper says expenditure will be added to the capital programme once the replacement profile is confirmed.
findings.matters: A reserve set aside to fund vehicle replacement shows how a council is preparing to replace capital assets without borrowing, which other councils with fleet renewal needs will compare.
findings.quote: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve Through annual revenue contributions, the Waste Renewal Fund will be built up to enable the

findings.headline: The General Fund Balance is held at £34.677m in every year to 31/03/2031, with the minimum balance reassessed on a refreshed risk assessment
findings.detail: The paper keeps the General Fund Balance flat across the forecast period. It says the minimum balance has been reassessed using a refreshed risk assessment, which is set out in Annex A8.
findings.matters: A council that holds the general balance flat while reassessing its minimum level shows how it is setting its own floor for unplanned costs.
findings.quote: Minimum Balance has been reassessed based on a refreshed risk assessment (Annex A8).

findings.headline: Schools Balances are forecast to fall from £10.455m to £4.275m from 31/03/2029, which the paper says belong to schools
findings.detail: The balances are net funds held for maintained schools, consolidated into the council accounts. The paper says the policy treats them as belonging to schools and not the council, and that they are fully delegated.
findings.matters: School balances consolidated into a council's reserves can overstate the council's own usable reserves, which matters when peers or lenders compare reported totals.
findings.quote: This is not our money and is fully delegated to schools.

findings.headline: Tariff Reserve is forecast to rise from £15.441m to £28.093m and hold at that level from 31/03/2029, set aside under the Risk Sharing Agreement
findings.detail: The reserve manages the potential financial cost to the council under the Risk Sharing Agreement, including excess costs of delivering infrastructure over the remaining life of the programme, which the paper gives as 2031.
findings.matters: A reserve built against infrastructure cost-sharing risk indicates how much a council expects that risk to cost, which is a point of comparison for other councils with similar agreements.
findings.quote: Funding set aside to manage the potential financial cost to the Council under the Risk Sharing Agreement, excess costs of delivering infrastructure over the remaining life of the programme

findings.headline: MKWRP Risk Reserve is forecast to rise from £10.000m to £17.000m by 31/03/2031, held as a contingency against contractor failure at the Waste Plant
findings.detail: The reserve covers exceptional costs, including landfill, insurance and business rates, if the Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park stops operating because of contractor failure. The forecast balance increases each year from 2028.
findings.matters: Contingency reserves for single-contractor facilities are a risk position that finance officers and lenders assess when a council depends on one operator.
findings.quote: Risk reserve provides a contingency in the event of the Waste Plant no longer being operational as a result of contractor failure.

findings.headline: The Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve is forecast to fall from £19.201m to £10.701m from 31/03/2028, and the paper states it is not available for use
findings.detail: The paper says the reserve is held to manage timing differences between the Collection Fund and the General Fund. It sets out forecast balances that stay flat at £10.701m from 2028 to 2031.
findings.matters: A reserve described as unavailable still counts in the total, so a finance director comparing reported reserves with usable reserves would want to see the distinction.
findings.quote: This reserve is not available as this is held to manage timing differences between the Collection Fund and General Fund.

findings.headline: Capital Reserve - GF is forecast to fall from £51.933m to £16.072m by 31/03/2031 as held revenue contributions finance the capital programme
findings.detail: The reserve holds General Fund revenue contributions to finance the current capital programme. The balance drops in every forecast year, and the paper says the funding is for specific projects in the programme.
findings.matters: A reserve that is drawn down to finance capital spending shows how much of the programme depends on past revenue contributions rather than new borrowing or grant.
findings.quote: Capital Reserve - GF GF revenue contributions held to finance the current capital programme. Active (51.933) (35.317) (30.001) (27.774) (21.923) (16.072)

findings.headline: Total reserves are forecast to fall from £258.238m at 31/03/2026 to £216.926m at 31/03/2028, then rise to £225.980m by 31/03/2031
findings.detail: The total row shows reserves reducing in 2027 and 2028 before recovering in later years. The paper gives the balances in the same parenthesised format as the reserve lines, with no separate commentary on the total.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can compare the forecast reserve trajectory with the council's own risk assessment and its reliance on reserves to balance future budgets.

findings.headline: Environmental Services fleet replacement, a pipeline item of £20,652,359 in 2028/29, is to be financed from a sinking fund set up in the 2023/24 base revenue budget.
findings.detail: The pipeline shows the fleet replacement, funded by a revenue contribution. The paper explains that a sinking fund was created in the 2023/24 base revenue budget to finance the replacement fleet, and the pipeline's unfunded column shows 0.
findings.matters: Using a reserve set aside in the revenue budget to fund a future capital fleet replacement shows how a council is building up cash for large asset renewals.
findings.figures: £20,652,359 fleet replacement in 2028/29; £20,652,359 total for the fleet pipeline item
findings.quote: A sinking fund was created as part of the 23/24 base revenue budget to enable the financing of the replacement fleet

findings.headline: HRA Planned Asset Management Programme changes total £25,540,175 across five years, and the paper says the programme was reviewed to keep funding within debt cap limits.
findings.detail: The HRA planned asset management changes are realigned over the five years, with the 2031/32 figure reflecting the inclusion of new allocations. The explanation says the review was done to ensure the funding stays within the HRA debt cap.
findings.matters: Explicit reference to the HRA debt cap in a capital programme shows how borrowing headroom is shaping which housing investment goes ahead.
findings.figures: £25,540,175 total five-year change to HRA Planned Asset Management Programme; £29,026,373 change in 2031/32
findings.quote: Programme reviewed to ensure funding remains within the debt cap limits

findings.headline: Pipeline schemes totalling £31,081,601 are listed without approved budget business cases.
findings.detail: The paper says the pipeline schemes were highlighted although their budget business cases had not been approved by the Corporate Portfolio Board when the draft was prepared. Several pipeline lines show a cost of TBC, and the unfunded column shows 0.
findings.matters: A large capital pipeline without approved business cases, with some costs still to be set, is what finance officers at peer councils will want to see before relying on the same schemes in their own programmes.
findings.figures: £31,081,601 total 2027/28 capital programme pipeline list; £20,652,359 pipeline fleet item in 2028/29; £10,429,242 pipeline in 2027/28
findings.quote: The following future capital scheme bids have been highlighted, although at the time of preparing the draft, budget business cases had not been approved by the Corporate Portfolio Board.

findings.headline: A £9.000m Milton Keynes Council contribution is requested for Milton Keynes East highways, alongside £50.000m of Homes England Housing Infrastructure Fund money.
findings.detail: The paper asks for additional resource allocation and spend approval of £9.000m as the council's share of the strategic highways infrastructure. The Housing Infrastructure Fund - Highways line also carries £37,616,595 in 2027/28 from prior years.
findings.matters: A council co-funding a grant-backed infrastructure scheme with its own capital, and funding it from capital receipts, shows how the council is committing its own resources to unlock housing growth.
findings.figures: £9.000m MKCC contribution; £50.000m additional Housing Infrastructure Fund offered by Homes England; £37,616,595 Housing Infrastructure Fund - Highways 2027/28 continuation
findings.quote: as an MKCC contribution towards the Milton Keynes East strategic highways infrastructure, supplementing the additional £50.000m Housing Infrastructure Fund (HIF) funding offered by Homes England.

findings.headline: The WEA4 New Primary School project budget is increased from £18m to £24.750m, with the paper citing construction inflation and updated project risks.
findings.detail: The paper requests additional resource allocation of £6,750,000 for this project. It attributes the increase to construction inflation, statutory requirements, labour and material costs, and updated project risks.
findings.matters: A £6.75m rise on an £18m project, attributed to construction costs, is the kind of cost movement other councils with school-place schemes will be tracking.
findings.figures: £18m original project budget; £24.750m revised project budget; £6,750,000 additional draft resource allocation
findings.quote: total project budget from £18m to £24.750m.

findings.headline: Transport's funding line shows a surplus of £1,122,546 in 2027/28 and a deficit of £400,000 in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The transport funding deficit/(surplus) row gives a negative figure for 2027/28, which the paper's brackets show as a surplus, and a positive £400,000 in 2028/29. The cumulative line over five years is a surplus of £722,546.
findings.matters: Year-by-year transport funding that moves between surplus and deficit shows how dependent the programme is on grant timing and borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: (£1,122,546) surplus 2027/28; £400,000 deficit 2028/29; (£722,546) cumulative five-year surplus

findings.headline: The Children and Families 2027/28 programme of £69,412,796 is set against £36,229,712 of total available funding.
findings.detail: The Children and Families summary shows total programme and total available funding for each year. The paper's own summary rows carry the difference as the funding deficit line, which is not clearly labelled in the extracted text.
findings.matters: A gap between capital programme spend and identified funding in the first year is what a lender or finance director would check against borrowing or grant assumptions.
findings.figures: £69,412,796 total programme 2027/28; £36,229,712 total available funding 2027/28; £50,738,394 five-year total in the deficit row
findings.quote: Total Available Funding

findings.headline: The reported draft capital programme totals £570,577,668 over 2027/28 to 2031/32, against £348,954,072 in the Agreed Programme from Feb 26.
findings.detail: The paper's change table lists July Cabinet changes of £31,740,490, slippage and rephasing of £18,360,138, September Cabinet changes of £27,400,000, and December budget changes of £24,661,884. Amendments included in the draft are shown separately.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can see how far a five-year capital programme has grown since the last agreed version and which cabinet decisions drove the change.
findings.figures: £348,954,072 Agreed Programme Feb 26 (five years); £570,577,668 Reported Draft Budget Position (five years); £31,740,490 July Cabinet changes; £18,360,138 slippage and rephasing; £27,400,000 September Cabinet changes; £24,661,884 December budget changes

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Environmental Services contract mobilisation costs end after five years, with a part-year saving of £190k in 2028/29 and a full £320k saving from 2029/30.
findings.detail: The Environmental Services contract started in September 2023 and its mobilisation costs are spread over the first five years. The line is rated Green and is previously approved and unchanged.
findings.matters: A mobilisation cost that is spread over a fixed period ends on a known date, which a finance director can use to forecast the budget effect.
findings.figures: £190k part-year (year 1); £320k full-year saving; £130k in 2029/30 (table)
findings.quote: At the end of the first 5 years, this cost will therefore end.

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Household Waste Recycling Centres saving from the move to two new 'Recycling and Reuse' sites is £0.860M over the full period, including 2026/27.
findings.detail: The move follows a January 2025 Delegated Decision, which covered buying new land and disposing of existing sites. The line is previously approved and unchanged, with the rating Amber.
findings.matters: A saving tied to a site consolidation depends on land and disposal decisions already taken, and a council planning a similar move would compare the full-period figure with the annual profile.
findings.figures: £0.860M over the full period including 2026/27; £345k (2027/28); £300k (2028/29)
findings.quote: The saving being included over the full period is £0.860M

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Landscape and play-area devolution is shown at £100k a year from 2028/29, while the text gives a net benefit of about £40k a year during implementation.
findings.detail: The devolution transfers play areas and landscape responsibilities to parish and town councils, with a fixed-term project officer and legal support costing £60k a year for three years. The paper says delivery depends on parish and town council participation and completion of asset information.
findings.matters: The table and the narrative give different first-year values for the same saving, and a reader would need to see which figure the budget relies on.
findings.figures: £100k a year from 2028/29 (table); net c.£40k a year during implementation; £60k a year for three years (cost); c.£100k a year thereafter
findings.quote: The resulting net benefit is therefore approximately £40k per annum during implementation, rising to £100k per annum thereafter.

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Concessionary EV charger income is shown at £70k in 2028/29, £192k in 2029/30 and £15k in 2030/31, on a line previously approved and now amended.
findings.detail: The income comes from rental and possible revenue share on Council land, with the residential concession procured and further phases commencing later in 2026/27. The paper describes the income stream as a prudent view based on initial market feedback.
findings.matters: Income from a concession whose later procurement phases have not yet begun depends on those phases landing, which a finance director would test against the phasing.
findings.quote: The income stream is a prudent view based on initial feedback from market engagement.

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Children's Social Care legal costs are proposed for a £400k reduction because legal proceedings have fallen over the previous 18 months.
findings.detail: The budget was increased under Child First and is now proposed to be reduced in line with current case numbers. The line is rated Green and is a 2027/28 saving only.
findings.matters: A reduction in legal proceedings reduces cost in a demand-led area, and a finance director would check whether the fall in proceedings is sustained before taking the saving.
findings.quote: the number of legal proceedings has significantly reduced over the previous 18 months

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards referrals fell after a June 2026 Attorney General for Northern Ireland ruling, and the paper expects assessment demand to fall by around two-thirds, giving a £304k saving.
findings.detail: The paper says current data indicates lower demand, and proposes reviewing agency staffing and service delivery arrangements. The line is rated Green and is a 2027/28 saving only.
findings.matters: A court ruling that changes statutory assessment demand is an external driver a finance director elsewhere would need to check against their own DoLS referral data.
findings.figures: £304k (2027/28); demand expected to fall by around two-thirds
findings.quote: Current data indicates that demand for DoLS assessments is likely to reduce by around two-thirds

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation proposals are shown at £1,740k in 2027/28 and £500k in 2028/29, rated Amber, with the saving linked to reducing the number of households placed in temporary accommodation.
findings.detail: The proposal covers more homelessness prevention, faster move-on to permanent homes, shorter placements and less use of nightly-paid accommodation, hotels and B&Bs. The saving depends on changes in household numbers and placement durations.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led cost, so a saving that depends on household numbers is exposed to how demand actually moves.
findings.quote: reducing the number of households placed in temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Linford Wood Place saving of £299k in 2027/28 is tied to a reduction of 12.62 FTE, as teams move to one site.
findings.detail: The saving is listed as previously approved and unchanged, with the rating Amber and consultation required. The paper says teams will deliver efficiencies by being based on one site.
findings.matters: A staffing reduction of 12.62 FTE with consultation still required is a delivery risk that finance directors track alongside the saving itself.
findings.quote: saving is due to a reduction of 12.62 FTE within the establishment

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Adult Services proposes a £1,000k saving from the remaining budget of its Internal Homecare service, which the paper says has now closed.
findings.detail: The line takes the surplus budget left after the service closed as a 2027/28 reduction. The item is rated Green and is classed as new this year, with no FTE change recorded.
findings.matters: A closed in-house service releasing its leftover budget as a saving is a specific step a council takes when it exits direct provision, and a peer council reviewing its own homecare would look at how the surplus was measured.
findings.quote: Internal Homecare - service has now closed, this is the remaining surplus budget

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Corporate savings lines total £1,450k in 2027/28, £1,850k in 2028/29 and £1,200k in 2029/30, with four of the five lines rated Amber.
findings.detail: The corporate block covers HP1 to HP4 and OD2 and is not attached to a single service. Corporate HP1 and HP2 show FTE impact as TBC, and HP1 is shown at £200k, £600k and £1,200k across the three years.
findings.matters: Corporate savings not tied to a service budget are harder to track to delivery, and a finance director at another council would check how the FTE impact is being measured.

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Draft budget reduction and income proposals total £8,918k in 2027/28, £3,403k in 2028/29, £1,798k in 2029/30 and £65k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The grand total row sets out the combined reductions and income proposals across all portfolios and corporate savings, with a potential FTE reduction of 19.82. The figures are shown as negative values in the table, denoting reductions.
findings.matters: This is the scale of the savings programme the council is relying on to balance its 2027/28 budget, and the profile shows how much of it falls in later years.

findings.headline: Transfers from reserves include £3,900k from the waste infrastructure reserve in 2027/28, and the MKWRP risk reserve shows £1,000k in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper's reserves lines show a £3,900k waste infrastructure transfer in 2027/28 followed by £969k in 2028/29. The MKWRP risk reserve line shows £1,000k in each of the first two years, and the change reserve shows a £1,546k release in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Using one-off reserves to fund pressures in the first two years means the underlying gap is smaller than the recurring position, and a finance director would check when those reserves are depleted.
findings.quote: - Waste  - Infrastructure 3,900 969 0 0

findings.headline: Council tax is modelled at 2.99% in 2027/28 and 2028/29 and 1.99% in 2029/30 and 2030/31, with the adult social care precept at 2% then 1%.
findings.detail: The paper's local funding choices assume the general council tax increase is cut from 2.99% to 1.99% from 2029/30, and the adult social care precept is cut from 2% to 1% over the same period. Council tax base growth is shown separately.
findings.matters: Council tax rates and precept levels are the main local revenue levers, and the planned reduction from 2029/30 directly affects how much future gaps must be closed by other means.
findings.figures: Council tax yield: (£5,694k), (£6,061k), (£4,336k), (£4,570k). Adult social care precept yield: (£3,808k), (£4,054k), (£2,182k), (£2,297k). Council tax base uplift: (£2,283k), (£2,787k), (£5,091k), (£5,244k).

findings.headline: Children's social care placements and emergency beds move from a £2,272k reduction in 2028/29 to a £1,113k pressure in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The paper shows children's social care placements and emergency beds as a reduction in 2027/28 and 2028/29, then as pressures in 2029/30 and 2030/31. The forecast reverses direction over the period.
findings.matters: A forecast that swings from a saving to a growing pressure in children's placements is one a finance director would test against placement numbers and unit costs.
findings.quote: Children's Social Care (Placements/emergency beds) (71) (2,272) 401 1,113

findings.headline: Adult social care demographic and cost pressures are modelled at £6,005k in 2027/28, rising to £6,175k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The paper lists adult social care demographic and cost pressures from Annex A4 in every year of the forecast. The amount increases slightly each year.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically the largest demand-led pressure in a council budget, and a steady multi-year pressure of this size is what peers and lenders would compare against their own forecasts.
findings.quote: Adult Social Care - Demographic/Cost pressures 6,005 6,022 6,097 6,175

findings.headline: Reductions & income growth are scheduled at £8,918k in 2027/28, falling to £65k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The paper's reductions and income growth schedule, drawn from Annex A5, is largest in the first year and then declines each year. The 2030/31 figure is £65k.
findings.matters: A savings profile that falls away this sharply after year one means later budget years depend on new savings not yet identified in this model.
findings.quote: Reductions & Income Growth (Annex A5) (8,918) (3,403) (1,798) (65)

findings.headline: The 2027/28 sum required to balance the budget is £10,078k, met by £8,918k of reductions and income growth and £1,160k of one-off funding, leaving a draft budget gap of 0.
findings.detail: The paper shows a draft budget gap of 0 for 2027/28. For 2028/29 the gap is shown in brackets, which the paper's sign convention reads as a surplus, followed by gaps of £3,458k in 2029/30 and £5,481k in 2030/31. The row has five values for four years, and the last appears to be a cumulative total, but the paper does not label it.
findings.matters: A balanced first year depends on front-loaded savings and one-off funding, and the later gaps show what remains to be found once those are used up.
findings.figures: Sum required to balance budget: £10,078k (2027/28), £183k (2028/29), £5,416k (2029/30), £5,646k (2030/31). Reductions & income growth: £8,918k, £3,403k, £1,798k, £65k. One-off funding: £1,160k, £172k, £160k, £100k. Draft budget gap: 0, (£3,392k), £3,458k, £5,481k; final row value £5,547k.
findings.quote: Budget Gap Draft Budget 0 (3,392) 3,458 5,481 5,547

findings.headline: Emissions Trading Scheme cost delayed to 2031.
findings.detail: The paper reports that confirmation has been received that the Emissions Trading Scheme has been delayed to 2031. It is listed among the budget risks, which the paper describes as largely outside the Council's direct control.
findings.matters: A deferred cost with a confirmed date changes the timing of a council exposure, which is relevant to finance officers planning for the same scheme.
findings.figures: Delayed to 2031
findings.quote: confirmation has been received that this has now been delayed to 2031

findings.headline: Contingency provision of £6.6m included in the 2027/28 General Fund draft budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the contingency is intended to manage in-year financial risks and reduce the potential need to draw on reserves. It notes that the provision is about 1% of net General Fund expenditure and 10% of the Children's External Residential Placements budget.
findings.matters: The size of the contingency relative to the children's residential budget shows how the council is buffering its highest-volatility demand line, which peers would compare with their own provisions.
findings.figures: £6.6m contingency; roughly 1% of net General Fund expenditure; 10% of Children's External Residential Placements budget
findings.quote: A contingency provision of £6.6m has been included within the 2027/28 General Fund draft budget

findings.headline: High Needs Block expected to go into deficit in 2026/27, with the General Fund impact unclear pending Government announcements.
findings.detail: The paper states that the High Needs Block is expected to move into deficit and that the impact on the General Fund is unknown until Government confirms whether financial support will be provided.
findings.matters: A high-needs deficit with no confirmed funding route is a contingent liability that a finance director, here or at another council, would need to track against the General Fund.
findings.figures: Deficit expected in 2026/27; General Fund impact not quantified
findings.quote: High Needs Block - is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27 - Impact on GF Budget is currently unclear as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support.

findings.headline: General Fund working balance stands at £34.677m, which is £3.707m above the minimum recommended level.
findings.detail: The paper reports the General Fund working balance as part of the robustness and reserves assessment under Section 25 of the Local Government Act 2003. It states that the balance adequately meets the Council's needs for 2027/28.
findings.matters: A working balance above the minimum recommended level is a buffer that a finance director and lenders would look at when judging the ability to absorb in-year pressures.
findings.figures: £34.677m General Fund working balance; £3.707m above the minimum recommended level
findings.quote: the General Fund working balance stands at £34.677m, which is £3.707m above than the minimum recommended level.

findings.headline: Risk reserves forecast to fall in the short term as some are drawn on.
findings.detail: The paper says the draft budget does not include the planned use of earmarked reserves for non-recurrent expenditure. It also notes that further provision will be needed over the MTFO to keep risk reserves at an appropriate level.
findings.matters: A forecast fall in risk reserves, with further top-ups required later, is a reserve position a finance director would need to monitor against the risks it covers.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: In the short term, we are forecasting the level of risk reserves to fall, due to the need to draw on some of these reserves.

findings.headline: Council Tax income forecast reduced by £0.576m following lower tax base growth.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 Council Tax base was agreed at Delegated Decision on 3 November 2026, reflecting lower growth than previously forecast. It also reports a Band D tax base of 103,062.64, an increase of 1,235.77 from 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lower tax base growth assumption reduces the recurring income available to fund services, which lenders and peers would want to see alongside the wider gap.
findings.figures: £0.576m reduction in Council Tax income since September 2026; 103,062.64 Band D equivalent properties; increase of 1,235.77
findings.quote: leading to a reduction in Council Tax income of £0.576m since September 2026

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract adds £2.400m base budget pressure from 2027/28.
findings.detail: The new contract started on 1 October 2026. The paper states that the one-off £1.900m allowance in 2026/27 was based on a desktop estimate and has now been replaced by a base budget pressure following the procurement.
findings.matters: Moving a one-off allowance into the base budget after procurement shows a recurring cost that peers with similar waste contracts would want to benchmark.
findings.figures: £2.400m base budget pressure from 2027/28; £1.900m one-off allowance in 2026/27
findings.quote: we have now included £2.400m as a base budget pressure from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities pressure reduced by £0.989m following a review of package demand and costs.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction followed a review of packages and that the latest forecast assumes 378 packages in 2027/28, compared with 451 previously assumed. Growth is described as having stabilised.
findings.matters: A reduction in the budget requirement from a package review is a measurable change in demand forecasting that peers could compare against their own review outcomes.
findings.figures: £0.989m pressure reduction since February 2026; 378 packages in 2027/28; 451 previously assumed
findings.quote: The pressure has reduced by £0.989m since February 2026 following a review of package demand and costs.

findings.headline: Looked After Children numbers at 438 in October 2026, against an average of 489 during 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports a fall in the Looked After Children population, while noting that the residential placement count rose over the same period. It attributes the contrast to the complexity of need and a lack of sufficiency in the placement market.
findings.matters: A falling cohort alongside rising residential placements means total volume and cost do not move together, which a finance director would want to track when comparing children's services budgets.
findings.figures: 438 Looked After Children (October 2026); 489 average in 2025/26; 10% decrease
findings.quote: In October 2026, our Looked After Children (LAC) numbers were 438, which is a reduction from the average of 489 during 2025/26 (10% decrease).

findings.headline: Children in residential placements at 74 in October 2026, against an average of 66 in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the number of children in residential placements has grown over several years, from 26 in 2023/24 to 47 in 2024/25 and 66 in 2025/26. It gives an average cost of £0.427m per child per year and describes the placement cost as volatile.
findings.matters: High-cost residential placements carry a large per-child cost, and the paper says the budget assumes their share will fall, which makes the outturn sensitive to a small number of placements.
findings.figures: 74 children in residential placement (October 2026); 66 average in 2025/26; 47 in 2024/25; 26 in 2023/24; £0.427m average cost per child per year
findings.quote: As of October 2026, there were 74 children in a residential placement, which is a substantial increase from an average of 66 in 2025/26

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation saving raised from £1.296m to £1.740m.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to reduced use of high-cost nightly lets, greater use of Harben House and other lower-cost accommodation, and more move-on into private rented accommodation.
findings.matters: A saving that has been increased in the draft budget shows a service-level plan reported as moving ahead of its earlier estimate, a pattern peers facing similar homelessness costs would want to compare.
findings.figures: £1.296m previous saving; £1.740m revised saving; £0.444m increase
findings.quote: saving increased from £1.296m to £1.740m

findings.headline: Draft 2027/28 budget balanced through service budget reductions and income proposals of £7.399m.
findings.detail: The paper states that the increase in budget reductions and income proposals since February 2026 is the main lever used to balance 2027/28. Total reductions for 2027/28 are £8.918m, with the Changing Because We Have To programme contributing £1.450m.
findings.matters: Balancing a budget through savings and income proposals of this size depends on delivery, and peers tracking the same reductions would want to compare the scale and timing.
findings.figures: £7.399m movement in reductions since February 2026; £8.918m total 2027/28 reductions and income proposals; £1.450m from the CBWHT programme in 2027/28
findings.quote: the draft budget has been balanced by a series of budget reductions and income proposals from services (£7.399m)

findings.headline: Cumulative four-year funding gap stated at £5.547m, up from £3.840m in September 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2027/28 budget is balanced, but the cumulative gap over the four-year period has risen since the September outlook. It attributes the change to pressures, higher inflation, a lower Council Tax base and a revised Fair Funding assumption, partly offset by savings and Business Rates income.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to see how a widening medium-term gap is being closed, since the 2028/29 to 2030/31 years are not yet balanced.
findings.figures: £5.547m cumulative gap over four years; £3.840m in September 2026; 2027/28 gap of £0.000m
findings.quote: the cumulative funding gap over the four-year period has increased from £3.840m in September to £5.547m

findings.headline: Pension Fund reserve forecast to fall by £0.852m in-year to £3.709m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The Pension Fund reserve opens at £4.561m and reduces by £0.852m during the year, leaving a closing balance of £3.709m.
findings.matters: Drawing on a pension fund reserve is a specific exposure for councils with pension liabilities, and peers will compare the scale of use against their own.
findings.figures: Opening £4.561m; in-year movement £0.852m; closing £3.709m

findings.headline: One-off & Political Priority reserves forecast to fall by £5.520m in-year to £3.776m, with £1.470m transferred to Election Reserves
findings.detail: The One-off & Political Priority reserves open at £10.766m. A £1.470m transfer out is shown in the Election Reserves row as a matching movement, and a £5.520m in-year reduction takes the balance to £3.776m.
findings.matters: A large planned reduction in discretionary one-off funding shows how much of the council's flexibility for political priorities is being committed during the year.
findings.figures: Opening £10.766m; transfer £1.470m; in-year movement £5.520m; closing £3.776m
findings.quote: One-off & Political Priority reserves (10.766) 1.470 5.520 (3.776)

findings.headline: Schools Balances forecast to fall by £2.211m in-year to £8.243m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: Schools Balances open at £10.455m and reduce by £2.211m during the year. The summary table records the same £2.211m as a key movement.
findings.matters: A fall in schools balances is a measure of how much schools are drawing on their own cushion, which finance officers at other councils track alongside school budget pressures.
findings.figures: Opening £10.455m; in-year movement £2.211m; closing £8.243m

findings.headline: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve forecast to increase by £3.571m in-year to £14.977m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The Waste Asset Renewals Reserve opens at £11.406m and rises by £3.571m, shown as a bracketed movement, and the summary table lists it as the Waste asset renewal fund. The Waste Market Risk Reserve also rises by £1.000m, to £3.063m, in the same table.
findings.matters: Building a reserve for future waste asset renewal shows the council setting aside funds ahead of replacement costs rather than relying on borrowing when those costs fall due.
findings.figures: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve: opening £11.406m, in-year movement £3.571m, closing £14.977m; Waste Market Risk Reserve: in-year movement £1.000m, closing £3.063m
findings.quote: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve (11.406) 0.000 (3.571) (14.977)

findings.headline: Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve forecast to fall by £3.710m in-year to £15.491m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve opens at £19.201m and is forecast to reduce by £3.710m during the year. The summary table records the same £3.710m as a key movement.
findings.matters: Using a collection fund cashflow reserve shows how the council is bridging timing differences in council tax and business rates receipts, which is relevant to peers managing similar cashflow pressures.
findings.figures: Opening £19.201m; in-year movement £3.710m; closing £15.491m
findings.quote: Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve (19.201) 0.000 3.710 (15.491)

findings.headline: Tariff Reserve forecast to increase by £4.156m in-year to £19.596m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The Tariff Reserve opens at £15.441m and rises by £4.156m, shown as a bracketed movement. The summary table labels the same reserve as the Tariff Risk reserve.
findings.matters: A growing risk reserve set aside against tariff exposure shows the council building cover against a specific income risk rather than spending it.
findings.figures: Opening £15.441m; in-year movement £4.156m; closing £19.596m

findings.headline: Capital Reserve - GF forecast to fall by £16.878m in-year to £35.317m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: The General Fund Capital Reserve opens at £51.933m, with a £0.262m transfer shown in the movement column and a £16.878m in-year reduction. It is the largest single reduction in the earmarked non-distributable reserves in the table.
findings.matters: Capital reserves funding a programme that is being drawn down quickly shows how much of the capital plan depends on reserve cash rather than new borrowing.
findings.figures: Opening £51.933m; in-year movement £16.878m; closing £35.317m

findings.headline: Total reserves forecast to fall from £258.238m to £229.987m by 31 March 2027, with £28.250m of in-year movements
findings.detail: The table shows total reserves opening at £258.238m and closing at £229.987m, with in-year movements of £28.250m. The summary table sets out the key movements, including a £21.093m addition to the Delivering the Capital Programme line.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can compare the scale of planned reserve use against the council's own risk and capital commitments over the year.
findings.figures: Opening total reserves £258.238m; closing £229.987m; in-year movement £28.250m; Delivering the Capital Programme £21.093m

findings.headline: Agora land development forecasts £21,932,611 for 2026/27 against a £24,000,000 current-year budget, with £2,067,389 slipping to future years
findings.detail: The paper states that the contractor is progressing with works on site, with car parking to St George's complete and foundations ongoing to Phase 2, with Block C due to start in November. The slippage reflects the contractor's recent forecast. The RAG status is Amber.
findings.matters: A large town-centre development with a total scheme value of £74,400,781 and a forecast slipping in-year is a delivery pressure that lenders to the council and peer councils with similar regeneration schemes would track.
findings.figures: Total expenditure £74,400,781; current-year budget £24,000,000; current-year actuals £4,648,573; current forecast 2026/27 £21,932,611; forecast slippage to future years £2,067,389
findings.quote: Contractor progressing with works on site.

findings.headline: MK East Primary School New Build forecasts £400,000 over its £28,931,467 budget, with tariff funding identified for the overspend
findings.detail: The paper states that recommissioning is partly complete, with a new permanent power meter installed and awaiting a recommissioning date. The forecast includes assumed final account contract costs, and tariff funding has been identified for the overspend.
findings.matters: A finance director will want to see how an overspend on a school build is being funded and whether the funding is secured or assumed.
findings.figures: Total scheme forecast £29,331,467; capital budget £28,931,467; forecast variance to capital budget £400,000
findings.quote: Tariff funding identified for overspend.

findings.headline: Whitehouse 12FE Secondary School reported as completed, with £39,243,238 actuals to date against a £39,261,952 total scheme forecast
findings.detail: The paper records that the project is completed and that the final retention will be paid at the end of the defects period. The variance to capital budget is -£18,714.
findings.matters: A completed large school build reporting spend below the approved budget is the kind of delivery outcome a finance director at another council will compare against their own school-build cost experience.
findings.figures: Total scheme forecast £39,261,952; total actuals to date £39,243,238; forecast variance to capital budget -£18,714
findings.quote: Project completed, final retention to be paid at end of defects period.

findings.headline: Reema buybacks on hold, with the next phase due to start from April 2027 against a £3,705,006 total budget
findings.detail: The paper states that the buybacks are on hold and that the next phase will start from April 2027 as per the phasing plan. It records £532,109 of current-year actuals and £511,891 forecast to slip to future years. Initial conversations with owners have taken place.
findings.matters: A deferral of a buyback programme into the following financial year is a delivery and timing decision that affects how much council-housing stock the council brings back in-house in 2026/27.
findings.figures: Total budget £3,705,006; prior-year actuals £2,350,253; current-year budget £1,044,000; current-year actuals £532,109; forecast slippage to future years £511,891
findings.quote: Reema buy backs on hold. Good progress was made and the next phase of buybacks will start again from April 2027 as per phasing plan.

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant (R&M) allocation reduced by £1,403,132 against a £15,973,542 total budget, with £1,120,777 forecast to slip to future years
findings.detail: The paper describes a reduced allocation of £1.121m, reflecting prior-year slippage and contractor capacity constraints in delivering backlog works. Task is alongside the current year's programme of works.
findings.matters: Contractor capacity constraints delaying a statutory grant-funded programme is a pressure other councils with similar adaptation backlogs will recognise.
findings.figures: Total budget £15,973,542; forecast variance to capital budget -£1,403,132; forecast slippage to future years £1,120,777; current-year budget £2,157,348 forecast
findings.quote: Reduced allocation of £1.121m, reflecting prior-year slippage and contractor capacity constraints

findings.headline: Housing Infrastructure Fund highways scheme (£129,556,689 total) shows £0 actuals in 2026/27 against a £21,950,000 current-year budget, with funding drawdown expected by Spring 2028
findings.detail: The paper states that the highway procurement is led by Berkeley Group using HIF funding, that Phase 2 onsite works commenced in Summer 2026, and that funding drawdown is expected by Spring 2028. The scheme's forecast for 2026/27 matches its current-year budget with no slippage reported.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance officers track how quickly externally-funded infrastructure, and the drawdown of the grant that finances it, converts into spend.
findings.figures: Total £129,556,689; total scheme forecast £129,556,689; current-year budget £21,950,000; current-year actuals £0; current forecast 2026/27 £21,950,000
findings.quote: Highway procurement led by Berkeley Group utilising HIF.Phase2 onsite works commenced Summer 2026, funding drawdown by Spring 2028.

findings.headline: Total scheme forecast of £1,075,195,649 against a £1,088,221,859 capital budget, a forecast variance of -£13,026,210 across the programme, with £34,033,964 forecast to slip to future years
findings.detail: The grand total row shows £44,328,489 spent against a current-year capital budget of £242,922,675, and a 2026/27 forecast of £198,790,145. The forecast variance to the current-year budget is -£10,098,566, and the paper attributes the difference between the current-year budget and the current forecast largely to slippage.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the scale of in-year slippage and the total forecast underspend against their own capital programme delivery rate.
findings.figures: Total scheme forecast £1,075,195,649; capital budget £1,088,221,859; forecast variance to capital budget -£13,026,210; current-year capital budget £242,922,675; current-year actuals £44,328,489; 2026/27 forecast £198,790,145; forecast slippage to future years £34,033,964; forecast variance to current-year budget -£10,098,566

findings.headline: Tariff 2a is expected to bring in £240m including indexation until 2049, with £9.9m and £14.5m already allocated to two schemes.
findings.detail: Tariff 2a covers Milton Keynes East and contributions have started. The paper names the Health Hub and the H10 Bletcham way connection to Church Farm as the first allocations.
findings.matters: Early allocations against a long-running developer income stream show how a council commits future contributions to named schemes.
findings.figures: £240m total contributions including indexation to 2049; £9.9m allocated to Health Hub; £14.5m allocated to H10 connection
findings.quote: The Council has allocated £9.9m of Tariff 2a funding towards the social infrastructure Health Hub facility and £14.5m for the H10 Bletcham way connection to Church Farm.

findings.headline: Tariff 1 is expected to collect over £311m in developer contributions over its lifetime, with £97.280m of Council-project allocations in the capital programme.
findings.detail: The Tariff funds 18 portfolios, 11 of them delivered by the council. Allocations to council projects are in the capital programme, and new requests are considered project by project.
findings.matters: The scale of Tariff income and how much of it is already committed to the programme show how much developer funding is locked in.
findings.figures: over £311m developer contributions; £97.280m Tariff allocations to council projects in the capital programme
findings.quote: Tariff allocations to the Council’s projects totalling £97.280m are included within the Capital Programme.

findings.headline: The Tariff's current long stop date is 2031, with a further five years for the Western Expansion Area after its planning permission was extended.
findings.detail: The Western Expansion Area is around a third of the Tariff by value. The council says it has until five years beyond 2031 to invest those contributions, and it holds a Tariff Risk Reserve for shortfalls.
findings.matters: Tariff deadlines and the scale of the risk reserve determine how much developer money the council must spend and by when.
findings.figures: Long stop date 2031; further 5 years beyond 2031 for Western Expansion Area; over £311m expected in developer contributions over the Tariff's lifetime
findings.quote: In respect of the Western Expansion Area, which accounts for around a third of the Tariff by value, and where the life of the planning permission has recently been extended the Council has a further 5 years beyond 2031 to invest the contributions.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 School Condition Allocation has not been confirmed, and the programme uses a prudent estimate based on previous years.
findings.detail: Basic Need funding for 2027/28 is confirmed, but the School Condition Allocation is still pending. The programme assumes a figure based on prior allocations.
findings.matters: Education capital grant assumptions that are not yet confirmed are a common funding risk for councils in the same position.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: The 2027/28 School Condition Allocation has not yet been confirmed and a prudent estimate, based on previous years’ allocations, has therefore been assumed in the programme.

findings.headline: The paper says some projects not in the capital programme will add to the overall funding shortfall, with no figure given.
findings.detail: Projects that still need work or funding are kept in a pipeline outside the main programme. The paper does not quantify the shortfall.
findings.matters: An unquantified shortfall that the council expects to grow is a funding gap a finance director would want sized.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: There are a number of projects which are not currently included within the capital programme and will require funding in the future, therefore increasing the overall funding shortfall.

findings.headline: Investment income above the draft budget will be used to contribute to financing the capital programme, with release decided by the s151 Officer.
findings.detail: Any short-term investment gains above the budgeted level will be used as a buffer against delayed receipts. The s151 Officer decides when funding is released once available funding is confirmed.
findings.matters: Using interest gains as a financing buffer is a specific mechanism that other councils and lenders can compare against their own treasury-driven funding.
findings.figures: none stated
findings.quote: any short-term gains on investment income, achieved by current interest rates, over and above, that built into the draft budget will be used to contribute to the financing of the programme.

findings.headline: The draft 2026/27 capital programme assumes £50.3m of capital receipts, and the paper says the timing of land sales is not certain.
findings.detail: Receipts depend on completing land sales. The paper says delays or lower receipts could mean new projects need further scrutiny or existing schemes are delayed.
findings.matters: A large assumed receipt that depends on land-sale completion is a timing risk for the council and for lenders assessing its funding.
findings.figures: £50.3m of receipts assumed
findings.quote: A total of £50.3m of receipts are assumed within the financing of the draft 2026/27 capital programme.

findings.headline: The paper states there is no unallocated funding for new capital projects outside the ring-fenced surplus within the current programme.
findings.detail: The £36.663m surplus is tied to Education, Highways and Local Transport, so it cannot fund other new capital projects. Only ring-fenced projects have been added to the budget proposals.
findings.matters: It shows a council with a reported surplus that still cannot fund new general capital schemes, which is a pattern other finance officers will recognise.
findings.figures: £36.663m ring-fenced surplus
findings.quote: meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects outside of this funding within the current Programme.

findings.headline: Table 1 shows a cumulative capital surplus of £36.663m by 2031/32, with the 2028/29 net position a deficit of £2.556m.
findings.detail: Forecast capital resources exceed capital expenditure over the period, but the net position is a deficit in 2028/29. The cumulative position stays in surplus in every year shown.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see how much headroom the programme has and which single year is out of balance on a net basis.
findings.quote: Whilst Table 1 shows an excess of resources over planned expenditure, all £36.663m of this funding is either Education , Highways or Local Transport fund specific

findings.headline: HRA PWLB borrowing is set 40 bps below the certainty rate until the end of March 2027, if not further extended
findings.detail: The paper notes the certainty rate is the standard rate minus 20 bps. HRA PWLB borrowing is a further 40 bps lower until March 2027, with the note that this may be extended.
findings.matters: A time-limited PWLB discount for HRA borrowing creates a deadline for councils that plan to borrow for housing, and it bears on the replacement funding cost of any repaid loans.
findings.figures: 40 bps HRA PWLB discount below the certainty rate; 20 bps certainty rate discount to standard rate; end of March 2027
findings.quote: Note that Housing Revenue Account (HRA) PWLB borrowing is currently a further 40 bps lower than the certainty rate until the end of March 2027 (if not further extended).

findings.headline: HRA borrowing limits were amended to allow shorter-period borrowing at current elevated market rates until longer-term rates fall
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA's maturity structure boundaries were changed this year to add capacity for shorter-period borrowing. The 2 to 5 year band is forecast to rise from 14.1% at Q2 to 31.7% at outturn.
findings.matters: A council changing its maturity limits to borrow shorter at elevated rates is a refinancing-risk choice that finance directors and lenders across the sector will read as a signal of how they expect rates to move.
findings.figures: 14.1% of HRA loans in the 2 to 5 year band (Q2); 31.7% forecast outturn; 5.7% HRA under-12-month band forecast outturn
findings.quote: HRA boundaries were amended this year to allow additional capacity to fund HRA borrowing commitments over shorter periods at current elevated market rates until longer-term rates reduce to more sustainable target levels.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes finalised a loan facility of up to £15.0m over 10 years to its wholly owned subsidiary MKDP in September 2026
findings.detail: The facility lets MKDP draw funds up to the maximum or repay principal in part or full on a monthly option. The paper says loan rates are set with reference to subsidy regulations and prevailing market rates.
findings.matters: A council lending to its own development company on a monthly drawdown basis is a funding arrangement that other councils and lenders will want to understand in terms of exposure and subsidy control.
findings.figures: £15.0m maximum facility; 10 years term
findings.quote: In September 2026, we finalised a new long term loan facility with our wholly owned subsidiary company Milton Keynes Development Partnership (MKDP) for a maximum of £15.0m over the next 10 years.

findings.headline: CCLA property fund holding stood at £13.754m at 30 September 2026 against a £15.0m cash deposit, with an unrealised loss of -£1.246m
findings.detail: The fund's fair value fell by £0.232m over the half-year from an opening balance of £13.986m. The paper says there are no immediate plans to liquidate the investment and that it has yielded 4.67% average gross return so far this year.
findings.matters: A council holding a long-standing property fund within its treasury portfolio is showing a loss against cost, which other councils with similar holdings will want to track against their own valuations.
findings.figures: £13.754m holdings at 30/09/2026; £13.986m opening balance; £0.232m fair value loss; -£1.246m unrealised loss; £15.0m total cash deposit; 4.67% average gross return
findings.quote: On 30th September 2026, our holdings stood at £13.754m against an opening balance of £13.986m on 1st April 2026, representing a fair value loss of £0.232m and an overall unrealised loss of -£1.246m against the £15.0m total cash deposit.

findings.headline: HRA ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast at 34.74%, against 40.64% in the February 2026 indicator
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to delayed new borrowing, which saves interest, and reduced voluntary MRP. Both follow from 2025/26 capital programme slippage and refinancing.
findings.matters: Slipped capital spend lowers the HRA's financing cost ratio in the short term, and the paper links the same slippage to the timing of the future borrowing requirement.
findings.figures: 40.64% HRA ratio (Feb 2026 indicator); 34.74% HRA ratio (Q2 / forecast outturn)
findings.quote: The HRA ratio has decreased due to delaying new borrowing (saving in interest costs) and reduced voluntary minimum revenue provision because of 2025/26 capital programme slippage and refinancing.

findings.headline: HRA forecast outturn assumes £70m funded by new external loans this year, with further internal loans possible
findings.detail: The officer commentary says the HRA is approaching a point of needing extra funding for its business plan capital objectives, subject to slippage. The HRA external loans forecast is £260.860m against £196.360m at Q2.
findings.matters: The council expects to enter the external market for the first time this year, which is a new funding requirement for any lender or treasury team watching HRA borrowing.
