findings.figures: £70m new external HRA loans (forecast); £196.360m HRA external loans (Q2); £260.860m HRA external loans (forecast outturn); 4.48% internal loan rate from March 2026
findings.quote: The HRA forecast outturn figures shown above assumes £70m funded by new external loans, but further internal loans may be considered.

findings.headline: Average rate of investment return for the first half is 4.34%, 0.59% above the SONIA 3-month benchmark of 3.75%
findings.detail: The paper reports the mid-year average of 4.34% against the 3.75% benchmark, and that there were no counterparty credit issues or principal losses. Investments were tactically laddered to lock in higher rates for longer durations.
findings.matters: Outperforming the benchmark on deposits is the reason the General Fund ratio falls, and other councils can compare their own returns against the same SONIA measure.
findings.figures: 4.34% average return; 3.75% SONIA benchmark; +0.59% difference; £333.484m investments at 30/09/2026
findings.quote: The average rate of investment return was 4.34%, which was 0.59% above the benchmark.

findings.headline: General Fund ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast at 3.40%, against 4.43% in the February 2026 indicator
findings.detail: The officer commentary attributes the fall to expected investment income above budget. Net financing costs are gross interest and MRP less treasury investment income, so the ratio moves with investment performance.
findings.matters: It shows a council's investment income offsetting capital financing costs in the general fund, which is a lever other councils can measure against their own budgets.
findings.figures: 4.43% GF ratio (Feb 2026 indicator); 3.40% GF ratio (Q2 / forecast outturn)
findings.quote: The GF ratio has decreased which reflects the positive impact upon net revenue of expecting to outperform our budget for investment income.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing is £422.299m, the gap between the underlying borrowing CFR and aggregate external borrowing
findings.detail: The paper describes this gap as the strategic temporary use of cash-backed balances and reserves to suppress external debt. The Q2 gross debt against CFR table shows the General Fund and HRA both below their CFR, and the officer commentary says the internal approach 'remains a prudent choice'.
findings.matters: Using reserves and working capital in place of external loans is a choice that another council's finance director can benchmark, and it carries a future replacement cost when those balances are spent.
findings.figures: £422.299m internal borrowing; £799.908m forecast outturn CFR; £785.543m underlying borrowing requirement excluding leases
findings.quote: The £422.299m difference between the underlying borrowing CFR and aggregate external borrowing is known as internal borrowing

findings.headline: No new external loans were drawn in April to September 2026, with £1.781m of General Fund loan principal repaid
findings.detail: Table 1 records no new loan principal raised and -£1.781m of existing General Fund principal repaid in the first half. The summary at paragraph 3.1.3 gives the repayment as £1.716m, a different figure from the table. The HRA external loan balance was unchanged at £196.360m.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this with their own first-half draw and repayment position, and a lender can see that the council is not adding external debt while it repays General Fund principal.
findings.figures: £0.000m new loan principal raised; -£1.781m existing loan principal repaid (Table 1); £1.716m loan principal repayment (paragraph 3.1.3); £196.360m HRA external loans
findings.quote: No new loans have been drawn during the first half of the year. £1.716m loan principal repayment have been made so far this year against General Fund loans.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The plan assumes an average of 20 HRA units are decommissioned each year, and the paper says this assumption needs review.
findings.detail: The paper says the 20-unit annual stock loss must be checked against the age and profile of the stock, and that a material difference could significantly alter the business plan position.
findings.matters: Stock loss assumptions drive rental income and debt capacity, so a review could change the plan's headroom materially.
findings.figures: Stock loss assumption 20 units per year; stock rationalisation scenario 40 units per year.
findings.quote: This assumption will need to be reviewed, given the age and profile of the stock to ensure it is realistic, as a material difference could significantly alter the business plan position.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The HRA reserve, the Prudent Minimum Balance, is estimated at £8.8m for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the Prudent Minimum Balance is a statutory reserve for unexpected expenditure or income shortfalls, and that the required level has been reviewed as part of the annual risk assessment.
findings.matters: The minimum balance sets the floor below which the council must not draw reserves, which bears on the headroom available for new investment.
findings.figures: Prudent Minimum Balance £8.8m (2027/28); £8.340m (2026/27) in the core assumptions table.
findings.quote: is estimated at £8.8m for 2027/28, as detailed in Annex B3.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The 2027/28 rent increase is 4.5% plus £1.00, an average of £5.93 per week for tenants and £5.07 per week for shared owners.
findings.detail: The paper states the rent increase is within the government's maximum of CPI plus 1% plus £1.00. Shared owners' increase is 4.8% and lags one year behind tenant rents.
findings.matters: The rent increase drives the largest income line in the HRA, and the paper says the plan's income depends on government rent policy.
findings.figures: Rent increase 4.5% + £1.00; average £5.93 per week (tenants); £5.07 per week (shared owners); shared owner increase 4.8%.
findings.quote: This is an average increase of £5.93 per week for tenants and £5.07 per week for shared owners.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Council Tax on Serpentine Court and Reema Phase 1 has been removed through the Valuation Office, a £0.910m saving in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the team has taken these properties off Council Tax, some of which carried 200% or 300% premiums. The remaining budget for operational voids and out-of-management stock is £0.414m.
findings.matters: Removing Council Tax liability on void stock is a saving that peer councils with similar stock may be able to replicate.
findings.figures: Saving £0.910m; remaining budget £0.414m.
findings.quote: The team have been successful in getting Serpentine Court and the Reema Phase 1 taken off the Council Tax through the Valuation Office

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The HRA disrepair budget falls by £0.292m to £1m, and the paper reports fewer new disrepair cases and costs than the 2024/25 peak.
findings.detail: The paper says the disrepair budget covers legal costs, compensation and repairs. It notes that claims take several years to work through, with an average of 467 days per claim.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims are a known pressure for social landlords, and a falling caseload against a reduced budget is a figure peers can benchmark.
findings.figures: Disrepair saving £0.292m; remaining budget £1m; average 467 days per claim.
findings.quote: but the number of new cases and costs is lower than the peak in 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The Acres Lodge development (66 units) is planned at £27m, funded from Right to Buy receipts.
findings.detail: The paper says the business plan commits receipts to Acres Lodge and an £8m acquisition allocation, using all receipts up to 2031/32. From 2036/37 receipts are assumed to fund acquisitions.
findings.matters: Committing receipts to a named scheme up to 2031/32 shows how an HRA allocates limited receipts, which peers facing similar Right to Buy use will compare.
findings.figures: Acres Lodge £27m (66 units); acquisition allocation £8m; receipts committed to 2031/32.
findings.quote: The business plan utilises receipts for the Acres Lodge development scheme (66 units) at £27m and an acquisition allocation £8m, committing all receipts up until 2031/32.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts can now be held for 10 years, rather than five, and will fund 100% of spend on acquisitions or new builds.
findings.detail: From 2027/28 the council can hold Right to Buy receipts for 10 years and combine them with section 106 contributions. The business plan commits receipts to the Acres Lodge scheme of 66 units and to an acquisition allocation up to 2031/32.
findings.matters: A longer holding period changes how Right to Buy receipts are used and committed, which affects other councils' planning for the same receipts.
findings.figures: Holding period 10 years (from 2027/28, previously five); Acres Lodge development £27m (66 units); acquisition allocation £8m.
findings.quote: Current receipts can be held for up to five years but from 2027/28 they can be held for 10 years

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The council has set no significant additional investment until the full impact of the stock condition surveys is known.
findings.detail: The paper states that no significant new investment will be agreed until the survey results are known and there is certainty that there is headroom to manage the risks. It also says overspends on projects would require reductions in other schemes.
findings.matters: Deferring new capital commitments until stock condition is confirmed is a governance decision that affects the pace of capital delivery and the council's borrowing needs.
findings.figures: No figure given.
findings.quote: no significant additional investment can be agreed until the full impact of the stock condition surveys is known and there is certainty that there is sufficient headroom to manage these risks.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The council has completed over 90% of dwelling condition surveys in 18 months, against a planned three-year programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the survey programme was accelerated to review all stock and that this has improved the certainty of the business plan. It also notes that the related savings reflect the compressed programme.
findings.matters: A stock condition programme delivered ahead of schedule reduces uncertainty in the plan's capital needs, which is the main open risk in the paper.
findings.figures: Over 90% of dwellings surveyed; 18 months completed against three years planned.
findings.quote: we have completed over 90% of dwellings in 18 months rather than taking three years.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Stock rationalisation at 40 units a year rather than 20 would leave £72.244m of borrowing outstanding at year 40, with reserves at £0.707m.
findings.detail: The third scenario doubles the assumed annual stock loss. The paper describes this as the worst of the three scenarios and shows the most borrowing outstanding at year 40 and the lowest reserves.
findings.matters: Stock loss rates affect rental income and debt capacity, and a finance director comparing peer plans can test their own stock-loss assumption against this scenario.
findings.figures: Borrowing outstanding at year 40 £72.244m; reserves at year 40 £0.707m (against £222.508m in the draft budget); stock loss 40 units a year rather than 20.
findings.quote: This is the worst of the scenarios, with borrowing outstanding at Year 40 of £72.244m and reserves reduced to £0.707m.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: A rent increase limited to CPI from 2030/31 would leave loans outstanding and a reserve of £2.333m at year 40.
findings.detail: The second scenario tests a change in government rent policy limiting increases to CPI from 2030/31. The paper says this would leave loans outstanding at year 40 and a much smaller reserve than the draft budget, and that the rent policy has been overridden by government before.
findings.matters: Rent policy is the largest single sensitivity in the paper, and the council's own statement that earlier caps were overridden is relevant to any landlord relying on the Rent Standard.
findings.figures: Reserve at year 40 £2.333m (CPI-only rent from 2030/31) against £222.508m (draft budget); loans outstanding at year 40 £57.084m.
findings.quote: At Year 40, there would be loans outstanding and a reserve balance of £2.333m.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: A 0.5% rise in interest rates through the plan would repay all loans by 2061/62, leaving a reserve balance at year 40 of £181.883m.
findings.detail: The paper's first stress test raises interest rates by 0.5% across the plan. It reports that the reserve is £181.883m at year 40 against £222.508m in the draft budget, and shows peak debt rising.
findings.matters: The paper itself says higher rates raise peak borrowing but have a modest long-term effect on reserves, which is a useful benchmark for a lender or finance director stress-testing a similar HRA.
findings.figures: Reserve at year 40 £181.883m (rates +0.5%) against £222.508m (draft budget); all loans repaid by 2061/62.
findings.quote: if rates increased by 0.5% through the business plan, this would see all the loans repaid by 2061/62, with the reserve balance at year 40 £181.883m.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The business plan assumes new HRA loans at 5.75% for three years, falling to 5.00% from year six.
findings.detail: The paper sets out the baseline rate for new loans and says it is informed by advice from the council's treasury advisers and market commentators, and could change with economic conditions. New HRA loans would most likely be fixed-rate, with interest-only and full principal repaid at final maturity.
findings.matters: The assumed cost of new HRA debt is a key input to the plan's interest cover, and comparing it with peers' assumptions shows how each council is pricing refinancing.
findings.figures: New loan rate 5.75% (years 1 to 3), 5.50% (year 4), 5.25% (year 5), 5.00% (year 6 onwards).
findings.quote: The business plan baseline assumption is for new loans to be drawn 5.75% over the next 3 years, 5.50% in year 4, 5.25% in year 5, then 5.00% from year 6 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The HRA can borrow from the PWLB at 40 basis points below the General Fund rate, a discount that runs until March 2028.
findings.detail: The paper states that the housing-specific PWLB discount ends in March 2028. The business plan's borrowing assumptions are set against this date.
findings.matters: A time-limited rate discount affects when the HRA should draw new debt, which is relevant to peers planning similar refinancing windows.
findings.figures: 40 basis points below General Fund rate; discount runs until March 2028.
findings.quote: The HRA is currently able to borrow from the PWLB at 40 basis points less than the GF. This housing-specific discount runs until March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The council reports carrying a significant amount of short-dated debt, including internal borrowing, which it will need to refinance.
findings.detail: The paper says treasury advisers expect long-term rates to fall, but that this has been pushed back by global factors, and it lists refinancing as a key risk. Work on the remaining stock condition surveys could also identify further investment.
findings.matters: Short-dated debt that must be refinanced in a high-rate environment creates exposure to rate timing, which lenders and finance directors track closely.
findings.figures: No figure given for the amount of short-dated debt.
findings.quote: The council is carrying a significant amount of short-dated debt (including internal borrowing) which it will need to refinance.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The HRA plans £47.00m of scheduled loan repayments in 2026/27, with £35.00m of refinancing new loans and £51.07m of new capital loans.
findings.detail: The paper says maturing loans are being repaid and will need to be refinanced because of recent investment. The borrowing summary table sets out scheduled repayments, refinancing loans and new capital loans for each year of the plan.
findings.matters: Replacing maturing HRA debt at the rates assumed is a central funding requirement, and the council's refinancing cost determines how far the plan's headroom holds.
findings.figures: Scheduled repayments £47.00m (2026/27); new loans for refinancing £35.00m (2026/27); new loans for capital £51.07m (2026/27); average borrowing rate 3.90% (2026/27) rising to 4.30% (2029/30).
findings.quote: Whilst maturing loans are being repaid these will need to be refinanced given the significant investment that has been made in recent years.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: The draft HRA budget shows a balanced budget across the MTFP, with the interest cover ratio rising from 1.80 in 2026/27 to 2.27 in 2031/32.
findings.detail: The paper reports a balanced HRA budget across the medium-term financial plan and states that the council is within its Treasury Management Strategy borrowing limit. The business plan table shows the interest cover ratio rising each year and available new borrowing growing from £100.36m to £214.37m.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see the headroom the council is reporting against its own minimum interest cover ratio of 1.25 for new borrowing.
findings.figures: Balanced budget across the MTFP; ICR 1.80 (2026/27) to 2.27 (2031/32); available new borrowing £100.36m (2026/27) to £214.37m (2031/32); minimum ICR 1.25.
findings.quote: The draft HRA budget shows a balanced budget across the MTFP, and we are within the borrowing limit set as part of our Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Families First grant conditions have a £1.1m pressure included in the MTFP while requirements are reviewed
findings.detail: The additional Families First Partnership grant is subject to conditions and delivery requirements. The council says it is reviewing what additional resources compliance will need, and has included a £1.1m pressure in the medium term financial plan in the meantime.
findings.matters: A new grant with delivery conditions that are not yet costed, and a £1.1m MTFP pressure held pending review, is an item other councils taking on the same grant will be assessing.
findings.figures: £1.1m pressure in MTFP
findings.quote: Whilst this is being reviewed, we have included a pressure of £1.1m in the MTFP.

findings.headline: General Fund working balance is £34.677m
findings.detail: The paper reports the working balance at the current date. The reported headroom above the minimum recommended level is £3.707m, which the paper describes as a buffer for unplanned expenditure.
findings.matters: A working balance and headroom figure is what a lender or peer council would use to judge the council's capacity to absorb an unplanned overspend such as the MKWRP pressure.
findings.figures: General Fund working balance £34.677m; headroom £3.707m above the minimum recommended level
findings.quote: The current General Fund working balance is £34.677m

findings.headline: External residential placements for children are at 66 against a budget of 56
findings.detail: Children We Care For have fallen from 486 in 2025/26 to 438 in September 2026, but placement complexity keeps costs above budget. Regulated Supported Accommodation spot placements are also running above plan, and the forecast assumes planned step-downs will happen. The paper flags placement sufficiency in the market as a risk to those step-downs.
findings.matters: Placements running above budget despite a falling child population is a demand-cost pattern that other children's services budgets are facing.
findings.figures: 66 external residential placements against budget of 56; 438 Children We Care For in September 2026 against 486 in 2025/26; placements overspend £0.696m; Children with Disabilities underspend (£1.167m)
findings.quote: External Residential placements remain above budget at 66, compared with a budgeted 56.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation forecasts a £1.736m underspend, with 1,080 households in temporary accommodation in September
findings.detail: The underspend is driven by use of Harben House, lower-cost accommodation, more move-ons into private rental and swift evictions where the council has no duty. The movement since Period 3 of £0.922m follows removal of a £1.000m contingency.
findings.matters: A large temporary accommodation underspend, set against a rising household count elsewhere, shows how a council is managing one of the most volatile demand-led costs.
findings.figures: £1.736m underspend; £0.922m movement since P3; £1.000m contingency removed; 1,080 households in September
findings.quote: In September there were 1,080 of homeless households being supported in temporary accommodation

findings.headline: Interest rates are higher than assumed in the budget, with extra investment income moved to capital for MKWRP
findings.detail: The Treasury Management forecast shows higher interest rates than budgeted, generating additional investment income. The paper says this will be transferred to capital to support future capital pressures, particularly the Waste Recovery Park. The HRA note also flags that rates could rise further later in the year, increasing borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Using treasury gains to fund a capital pressure, while flagging rate risk on future borrowing, is a trade-off that lenders and finance directors will want to see tracked.
findings.figures: Corporate Codes & Debt Financing variance (£2.418m); one-off saving £0.418m from annual leave purchases; £2m contingency release
findings.quote: The Treasury Management forecast is reflecting that interest rates are now higher than at the time of setting the budget.

findings.headline: Public Health reserve forecast to fall from £3.379m to £2.330m through a £1.049m drawdown in 2026/27
findings.detail: The drawdown funds one-off initiatives approved in the budget, partly offset by a planned contribution of £0.094m. Public Health is forecasting a small underspend of £0.025m at Period 6.
findings.matters: A drawdown of a third of a ring-fenced reserve in one year is a number a finance director would weigh against the sustainability of one-off funding.
findings.figures: £3.379m at 31 March 2026; £2.330m at 31 March 2027; £1.049m drawdown; £1.168m one-off funding; £0.094m planned contribution
findings.quote: reducing the reserve balance from £3.379m at 31 March 2026 to £2.330m at 31 March 2027

findings.headline: HRA forecasts a £1.796m underspend, with the saving transferred to revenue contribution to capital
findings.detail: The HRA underspend is up £1.316m since Period 3. The council says the underspend will be offset by a higher revenue contribution to capital to fund future investment and debt repayment. Asset Management is £1.026m under budget, mainly from lower responsive repairs spend.
findings.matters: Redirecting an HRA underspend into capital and debt repayment rather than reserves is a choice other councils with ring-fenced HRAs will compare against their own business plans.
findings.figures: HRA underspend £1.796m; movement of £1.316m since P3; Asset Management £1.026m underspend; revenue contribution to capital budget £6.201m rising to £9.660m forecast
findings.quote: an improvement of (£1.316m) since P3, which will be offset by an increase in the planned level of Revenue Contribution to Capital (RCCO)

findings.headline: Capital programme forecasts £44.133m underspend against a £242.923m budget, with £34.034m slipping to later years
findings.detail: After slippage, the in-year capital underspend is £10.099m. The largest slippage items include HRA asset management (£4.521m), Agora (£2.067m) and Lakes Estate Health Facility (£2.204m). The HRA asset management programme underspend of £11.509m is to be reinvested in other HRA Business Plan projects.
findings.matters: Slippage of this scale against a budget of this size shows how much of the capital programme is being delayed rather than cancelled, which affects borrowing timing and future delivery risk.
findings.figures: £44.133m underspend; £242.923m budget; £34.034m slippage; £10.099m in-year underspend; HRA asset management £11.509m underspend; slippage across 2027/28 to 2030/31 of £15.102m, £3.436m, £10.260m and £5.236m
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is forecasting underspend of (£44.133m), of which £34.034m is planned to slip to later years

findings.headline: High Needs block forecasts a year-end deficit of £0.376m, with the DSG surplus carry forward falling to £1.623m
findings.detail: The paper says the High Needs block remains under pressure, with an in-year overspend of £1.6m partly offset by reserves of £1.2m. The overall DSG surplus carry forward is £1.623m against a budgeted £2.514m, an adverse movement of £0.891m, driven mainly by the Early Years block. The SEND Reform Plan is awaiting DfE approval expected in November.
findings.matters: A ring-fenced DSG deficit on High Needs with a pending DfE plan approval is a position other councils with SEND pressures will be tracking closely.
findings.figures: High Needs deficit £0.376m; in-year overspend £1.6m; reserves £1.2m; DSG carry forward £1.623m against £2.514m budgeted; adverse movement £0.891m; independent placements 87 against budget of 80
findings.quote: The High Needs block remains under significant pressure; the current forecast shows a deficit is expected at year end of £0.376m.

findings.headline: £9.476m of £9.982m savings target forecast to be achieved in 2026/27, with £0.059m undeliverable
findings.detail: The paper reports that 95% of the 2026/27 savings target is forecast in year, including £1.020m carried forward from 2025/26. £0.447m will be delivered next year and £0.059m is undeliverable and is being reviewed as part of the 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: A near-complete savings delivery rate, with the shortfall explicitly moved into 2027/28 planning, is the measure peer finance officers use to judge how far a budget relies on unproven savings.
findings.figures: £9.476m (95%) forecast in year; £0.447m (4%) next year; £0.059m (1%) undeliverable; total target £9.982m; £5.761m achieved to date
findings.quote: £9.476m (95%) are forecast to be achieved in year, £0.447m (4%) will be delivered next year and £0.059m (1%) is undeliverable and is being reviewed as part of the 2027/28 budget.

findings.headline: General Fund forecasts an underspend of £4.813m against budget at Period 6
findings.detail: The paper reports the General Fund forecast underspend of £4.813m, a £0.019m decrease since Period 3. The largest underspends are Adult Social Care (£4.665m), Corporate Codes and Debt Financing (£2.418m) and Children's Services (£1.627m), offset by the Environment & Property overspend of £4.948m.
findings.matters: The headline underspend depends on a £2m contingency release and one-off items, which a finance director would need to test against the rest of the year.
findings.figures: £4.813m underspend; £0.019m decrease since P3; Adult Social Care (£4.665m); Corporate Codes & Debt Financing (£2.418m)
findings.quote: The General Fund Services are currently forecasting an underspend of (£4.813m).

findings.headline: Waste Recovery Park forecast at £6m financial pressure in 2026/27, of which £2m is met from contingency
findings.detail: The paper reports reduced performance at the Waste Recovery Park, with the council now responsible for running costs and repairs since April 2026. SUEZ took over operation on 1 October and has begun improvement works. The £6m pressure is offset in part by releasing £2m from contingency, and the paper lists the facility as a significant risk to the General Fund.
findings.matters: A single waste facility moving in-house on operating and repair costs is producing a pressure of this size in one year, and the paper says it remains reliant on plant availability and market prices.
findings.figures: £6m pressure; £2m released from contingency; Environment & Property variance £4.948m overspend
findings.quote: The Waste Recovery Park has experienced reduced performance, resulting in financial pressure forecast at £6m.

findings.headline: The draft names five specific risk provisions outside the operational calculation, with £1,475k for insurable events above the Insurance Fund and £1,200k for abnormal weather.
findings.detail: The specific risks are listed separately from the operational provision and include cyber attack, in-year legislative pressures and civil emergency or disaster, each at £1,000k.
findings.matters: Named provisions for cyber and legislative risk show how the council has sized those exposures, which peer councils and lenders can compare with their own.
findings.figures: £1,475k insurable events in excess of Insurance Fund provision; £1,200k abnormal weather conditions; £1,000k cyber attack; £1,000k in-year legislative pressures; £1,000k civil emergency/disaster
findings.quote: Insurable events in excess of Insurance Fund provision 1,475

findings.headline: Dwelling rents of £74,147k carry a £556k provision for decreases in rents chargeable, the largest income-side provision in the draft.
findings.detail: The provision is for a fall in rents chargeable. The low-level scenario has a 3% impact and a 20% likelihood, and the high-level scenario has a 7% impact and a 10% likelihood.
findings.matters: Rent is the main HRA income stream, so the level of provision set against it shows how much income shortfall the council is planning for.
findings.figures: £74,147k dwelling rents budget; £556k provision; high-level impact 7%, likelihood 10%
findings.quote: Dwelling Rents Decrease in rents chargeable 74,147 3% 20% 5% 15% 7% 10% 556

findings.headline: The draft carries a £687k provision for unforeseen cost increases on the housing capital programme, which has a 5-year average of £34,358k over 2027/28 to 2031/32.
findings.detail: The capital programme provision is shown against the 5-year average capital expenditure. The high-level scenario has a 30% impact and a 5% likelihood.
findings.matters: Capital cost overruns feed directly into HRA borrowing and reserve needs, and a lender or finance director would want to see how much headroom the plan holds against them.
findings.figures: £34,358k 5-year average housing capital programme (2027/28 to 2031/32); £687k provision
findings.quote: Total Housing Capital Programme #Unforeseen cost increases (Capex 5 yr average 2027/28-2031/32) 34,358 10% 20% 20% 10% 30% 5% 687

findings.headline: Repairs and maintenance has the largest operational risk provision in the draft, at £812k against a £16,233k budget.
findings.detail: The provision covers increases in responsive and void repair costs. The row shows a high-level scenario with a 35% impact and a 10% likelihood, alongside lower-level and medium-level scenarios.
findings.matters: Repairs is the largest operational cost risk on the HRA, so a peer council or lender would see it as the line most exposed to cost pressure on the stock.
findings.figures: £16,233k repairs and maintenance budget; £812k provision; high-level impact 35%, likelihood 10%
findings.quote: Repairs & Maintenance Increases on responsive/void costs 16,233 15% 25% 25% 20% 35% 10% 812

findings.headline: The draft 2027/28 Total HRA Minimum Revenue Balance is £8,807k, made up of a £3,132k total housing operational provision and five named specific risk items.
findings.detail: The table totals the operational risk provisions across income, expenditure and the housing capital programme to £3,132k. It then adds specific provisions for insurable events above the Insurance Fund, cyber attack, in-year legislative pressures, civil emergency and abnormal weather to reach the total minimum balance.
findings.matters: A finance director, or a peer council comparing HRA reserve policy, needs the minimum balance figure and how it is built up to judge whether the reserve is adequate for the risks identified.
findings.figures: £8,807k total HRA minimum revenue balance; £3,132k total housing operational provision; £1,475k insurable events provision; £1,000k cyber attack; £1,000k in-year legislative pressures; £1,000k civil emergency/disaster; £1,200k abnormal weather conditions
findings.quote: Total HRA Minimum Revenue Balance 8,807

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: The council reports a CQC inspection in February 2026 judged it 'good' and the council's risk provision for this area is £500,000.
findings.detail: The annex records the February 2026 CQC inspection rating and notes the council ranks among the top-performing councils nationally. The provision covers the cost of improvements if an 'Inadequate' rating were given.
findings.matters: A recent inspection rating reduces the likelihood of the improvement costs assumed in this provision.
findings.figures: Provision £500,000
findings.quote: In February 2026 the Council was judged 'good' and

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Fair funding review for 2029/30 is listed as 'yet to be assessed', with a possible reduction in funding linked to the business rates reset.
findings.detail: The annex notes a new local government settlement from 2029/30, including the business rates reset, could reduce the council's funding. No amount has yet been assessed and no provision is held.
findings.matters: The 2029/30 settlement and business rates reset will affect many councils' medium-term funding, and this shows one council has not yet quantified its exposure.
findings.figures: Provision 0; amount yet to be assessed
findings.quote: A new settlement deal for Local Government in 2029/30 including potential impact of the business rates reset, could result in a reduction to our funding

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park is rated High risk, with the council liable for unplanned shutdowns lasting more than 5 days and for costs before insurance takes effect after 90 days.
findings.detail: The annex makes the council responsible for additional costs from unplanned plant shutdowns, and states the risk is managed through the MKWRP Risk Reserve rather than a provision in this assessment.
findings.matters: Contract and plant-availability risk sits with the council in this arrangement, so a finance director at another council with a similar waste contract would compare the shutdown and insurance terms.
findings.figures: Shutdown threshold more than 5 days; insurance effective after 90 days; provision 0 (managed through MKWRP Risk Reserve)
findings.quote: The Council is responsible for all additional costs in the event of unplanned shutdowns of the plant lasting more than 5 days, and prior to insurance taking effect after 90 days.

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Children's social care placements carry a £53,358,260 exposure rated High, with a 10.00% risk factor giving a provision of £5,335,826.
findings.detail: The annex attributes the exposure to increasing demand for specialist placements for children with complex needs, and to a lack of fostering sufficiency in the market pushing up costs.
findings.matters: Children's placement costs are a demand pressure that many councils report, and this shows how one council sizes its contingency against it.
findings.figures: Exposure £53,358,260; risk factor 10.00%; provision £5,335,826
findings.quote: Increasing demand for specialist placements due to complex needs of children coming into care.

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Investment risk provision is £3,005,000, set at 1% of a £300,500,000 base.
findings.detail: The annex sets the investment risk provision at 1% of the cash balance, covering loss of principal from credit default or market losses.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors compare the provision rate and base against the council's treasury exposure to judge how much cover is held for principal loss.
findings.quote: Risk provision of 1% on average cash balance.

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Government has extended the IFRS 9 statutory override for pooled investment fund valuation losses until April 2029, so no provision is held for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The annex states that unrealised annual valuation gains and losses on pooled investment funds are exempt from being charged to revenue budgets until April 2029. A £15,000,000 maximum exposure is shown with no provision required for 2027/28.
findings.matters: Councils holding pooled fund investments depend on the override to keep valuation losses off revenue, and the date it runs to determines when that protection ends.
findings.figures: Maximum exposure £15,000,000; provision 0 for 2027/28
findings.quote: budgets until April 2029. No provision is therefore required in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: High Needs Funding (DSG) deficit has a maximum exposure of £64,721,535, with a £1,000,000 risk provision, and the council anticipates going into deficit in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The council states it is liable for any high needs shortfall against national funding. It expects the deficit to start in 2026/27 and grow in 2027/28, and is seeking to reduce it through budget reductions, reform and a transfer from the schools block, which needs DfE approval.
findings.matters: High needs deficits held against general fund balances are a live pressure at many councils, and this shows one council's exposure and the mitigations it depends on.
findings.figures: Maximum exposure £64,721,535; risk provision £1,000,000
findings.quote: anticipating that it will go into deficit in 2026/27 and that this will increase further in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Annex A8 - Reserves Risk Assessment 27-28 Draft Budget
findings.headline: Total minimum working balance required for 2027/28 is £31,639,840, after a 25% reduction for probability of multiple events from an assessed £42,186,453.
findings.detail: The annex totals the risk provisions across the demand, income, contract, service performance, government funding, balance sheet and major events categories. It then applies a 25% reduction for the probability of multiple events, giving the required minimum working balance.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can compare this figure with the general fund balance to see how much headroom the council expects to hold against its identified risks.
findings.figures: Total assessed minimum working balance £42,186,453; percentage reduction (25%) £10,546,613; total minimum working balance required £31,639,840
findings.quote: Total Minimum Working Balance Required 31,639,840

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: Council tax, including parish precepts, is the largest funding line at £213,857k in the 2027/28 draft.
findings.detail: The paper shows council tax of £213,857k against revenue support grant of £73,363k and retained business rates of £71,166k. Parish precepts paid of £14,145k sit alongside the council tax line.
findings.matters: The mix of council tax, business rates and grant shows how much of the council's funding depends on local tax, which a lender or peer will want to compare.
findings.figures: Council tax (including parish precepts) £213,857k; revenue support grant £73,363k; retained business rates £71,166k; parish precepts paid £14,145k
findings.quote: Council Tax (including parish precepts) (213,857)

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: The draft budget includes a corporate contingency of £6,614k for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper shows the corporate contingency rising from £5,919k by £695k to £6,614k in the 2027/28 draft. A separate corporate pay inflation line shows a net negative of £1,881k.
findings.matters: A contingency sized at £6,614k indicates the amount the council holds against unbudgeted pressures, which a peer can compare with its own contingency.
findings.figures: Contingency £5,919k (2026/27) to £6,614k (2027/28), a movement of £695k; pay inflation and other line (£1,881k)
findings.quote: Corporate Items (Contingency) 5,919 695 6,614 0.000 0.000 0.000 6,614

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: Debt financing gross expenditure rises by £948k to £6,266k, with a net budget of (£1,926k) in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper shows the debt financing line moving from £5,318k to £6,266k in gross expenditure, with gross income rising by £1,070k to £8,192k. The net budget for the line is a credit of £1,926k.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors look at the cost of debt financing, and this line shows the net position the council expects on borrowing in 2027/28.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £5,318k (2026/27) to £6,266k (2027/28), a movement of £948k; gross income £8,192k; net budget (£1,926k)

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: Children's Services gross expenditure rises by £1,044k to £338,132k, with a net budget of £103,946k in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper shows Children's Services gross expenditure increasing from £337,088k by £1,044k and gross income broadly flat, at £234,186k after a £16k movement. The net budget for the service is £103,946k.
findings.matters: Children's Services is the largest gross spend line in the draft, so a finance officer elsewhere can compare how the same demand pressures are set against a near-flat income line.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £337,088k (2026/27) to £338,132k (2027/28), a movement of £1,044k; gross income £234,186k; net budget £103,946k

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: Adult Services gross expenditure rises by £9,105k to £229,774k, with a net budget of £155,218k in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper shows Adult Services gross expenditure increasing from £220,669k in 2026/27 by £9,105k, with gross income increasing by £7,325k to £74,556k. The net budget for the service is £155,218k.
findings.matters: Adult social care is the largest net service line in the draft, and the rise in gross spend is the kind of movement a peer council can compare against its own demand pressures.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £220,669k (2026/27) to £229,774k (2027/28), a movement of £9,105k; gross income £74,556k; net budget £155,218k

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: The draft budget includes a contribution to reserves of £7,653k.
findings.detail: The paper shows a positive contribution to reserves in the 2027/28 draft, shown as a contribution to rather than a draw from. This is the only reserves movement in the summary.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the scale of the reserves contribution against peers, and a lender can see that the draft adds to reserves rather than drawing them down.
findings.figures: Contribution to reserves £7,653k
findings.quote: Contribution to/(from) Reserves 7,653

findings.paper_title: Annex A1 - 2027_28 General Fund Draft Budget Summary
findings.headline: The draft 2027/28 general fund budget shows a budget gap of £0 against total expenditure and funding of £344,241k.
findings.detail: The paper reports total expenditure of £344,241k after a £7,653k contribution to reserves, a £683k levies line and a £26,030k asset management credit. Funding of £344,241k comes from revenue support grant, retained business rates, council tax and parish precepts.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a balanced draft is reached, and a lender can see that the council projects no gap for 2027/28 on these figures.
findings.figures: Total expenditure £344,241k; total funding £344,241k; budget gap £0
findings.quote: Budget Gap 0

findings.headline: The paper states it is possible that further budget measures will be needed before the 2027/28 budget is set.
findings.detail: The paper links this to risks around demand and inflation which will be reviewed further before the budget is finalised. It also says the council will need to make some difficult choices in some service areas.
findings.matters: A stated possibility of further measures before the budget is set signals that the draft position may change at final budget, which is relevant to anyone reading the draft.
findings.quote: It is possible that further budget measures will be needed before the budget is set.

findings.headline: About £1.1m of Families First Partnership Grant was absorbed into the Children's base budget, with a £0.947m pressure if the grant funds programme activity.
findings.detail: The paper says Department for Education guidance has clarified programme expectations, including workforce, IT and multi-agency working. The paper says the financial impact is included within Children's Services based on an assessment of the grant conditions, with the balance held in contingency.
findings.matters: A grant that was used to fund core budget and may now need to fund programme activity is a grant-conditions risk that other councils using similar funding should review.
findings.figures: approximately £1.1m (assumed budget contribution); £0.947m (pressure)
findings.quote: Should the Council be required to utilise this funding to deliver specific grant-related activities rather than supporting existing budgeted expenditure, an equivalent pressure would arise within the General Fund.

findings.headline: The paper reports that the Emissions Trading Scheme has been delayed to 2031.
findings.detail: The paper lists this as a confirmed change in the risks section. The Extended Producer Responsibility allowance is also unconfirmed for 2027/28, with the council hoping the change will not be significant given its high recycling rate.
findings.matters: A confirmed deferral of a cost exposure to 2031 removes it from the medium-term plan for councils with a similar waste and carbon position.
findings.figures: 2031 (revised start date)
findings.quote: confirmation has been received that this has now been delayed to 2031.

findings.headline: The General Fund has no new external borrowing planned for 2027/28, with existing external debt set to be repaid at maturity.
findings.detail: The paper says the General Fund has sufficient cash-backed reserves and balances to avoid new external debt. It adds that if new capital funding proposals come forward, borrowing may be considered and presented to Cabinet and Council.
findings.matters: A council planning to fund from reserves rather than new borrowing is a position a lender will want to read against its own exposure.
findings.figures: No new external debt assumed in 2027/28 budget proposals (no value given)
findings.quote: The General Fund has sufficient cash-backed reserves and balances to negate drawing any new external debt,

findings.headline: Risk reserves are forecast to fall in the short term, as some are drawn on to meet specific risks.
findings.detail: The paper says the current budget includes new contributions to some risk reserves, but further provision will be needed over the life of the MTFO to keep them at an appropriate level.
findings.matters: Falling risk reserves, with a commitment to rebuild them later, is a reserve position other councils and lenders will compare against their own.
findings.quote: we are forecasting the level of risk reserves to fall, due to the need to draw on some of these reserves.

findings.headline: The General Fund working balance stands at £34.677m, which is £3.707m above the minimum recommended level.
findings.detail: The paper says the Chief Finance Officer has reviewed the risk assessment and estimate of the General Fund balance and considers it adequate for 2027/28. The draft budget also includes a £6.6m contingency provision.
findings.matters: The headroom above the minimum recommended working balance is the figure a finance director uses to judge how much in-year risk the council can absorb.
findings.figures: £34.677m working balance; £3.707m above minimum recommended level; £6.6m contingency provision (2027/28)
findings.quote: Currently, the General Fund working balance stands at £34.677m, which is £3.707m above than the minimum recommended level.

findings.headline: The High Needs Block is expected to go into deficit in 2026/27, with the impact on the General Fund unclear pending government announcements on support.
findings.detail: The paper says the General Fund impact is currently unclear as the council awaits government announcements on whether there will be any financial support.
findings.matters: A high needs deficit with no confirmed funding route is a contingent General Fund exposure that finance directors and lenders across the sector are tracking.
findings.figures: Deficit expected in 2026/27 (no value given in this paper)
findings.quote: is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27 - Impact on GF Budget is currently unclear as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support.

findings.headline: The latest forecast for children with disabilities assumes 378 packages in 2027/28, against 451 previously assumed.
findings.detail: The paper says weekly panels now review new and increased care packages, and that this has strengthened control of expenditure. Packages are forecast at 339 in P6 against a 2026/27 budget of 419. The paper quotes the pressure reduction as £0.708m in one place and £0.989m in another.
findings.matters: A large cut in forecast package numbers, achieved through panel scrutiny, is a demand-control result other councils can compare with their own disability spend.
findings.figures: 378 packages (2027/28, latest forecast); 451 (previously assumed); 339 (P6 forecast, 2026/27); 419 (2026/27 budget); £0.708m and £0.989m (pressure reductions as stated in the paper)
findings.quote: latest forecast assumes 378 packages in 2027/28 compared with 451 previously assumed

findings.headline: The budget assumes the share of looked after children in external residential settings falls from 17% at September 2026 to an average of 14% in 2027/28 and 12% thereafter.
findings.detail: The paper says the reduction depends on work to step down children who can be placed in another setting. It also says the external IFA placements budget is realigned to 131 placements for 2027/28, from 160 in 2026/27. It describes a failure of these plans to materialise as a significant financial risk.
findings.matters: A forecast that depends on a step-down in residential share is a budget assumption a reader can test against their own placement data.
findings.figures: 17% of looked after children in external residential (September 2026); 14% average (2027/28); 12% (remainder of MTFP); IFA placements 160 (2026/27) to 131 (2027/28)
findings.quote: The MTFP assumes that this percentage will reduce to an average of 14% in 2027/28 and 12% for the remainder of the MTFP

findings.headline: Children in external residential placements stood at 74 in October 2026, against an average of 66 in 2025/26, 47 in 2024/25 and 26 in 2023/24.
findings.detail: The paper says the number of looked after children fell to 438 in October 2026, against an average of 489 in 2025/26, but the residential cohort has risen. The current average cost is £0.427m per child per year, which the paper describes as demonstrating volatility.
findings.matters: Residential placement cost per child is one of the largest single demand exposures in children's services budgets, and a rising count at this unit cost is a number other finance directors will want to compare.
findings.figures: 74 children (October 2026); 66 (2025/26 average); 47 (2024/25); 26 (2023/24); £0.427m average cost per child per year; 438 looked after children (October 2026) against 489 (2025/26 average)
findings.quote: As of October 2026, there were 74 children in a residential placement, which is a substantial increase from

findings.headline: The Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract, which started on 1 October 2026, adds £2.400m to the base budget from 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2026/27 budget carried a one-off £1.900m allowance funded from the waste reserve, based on a desktop estimate. Following the procurement, the base pressure is £2.400m, and the net cost depends on plant operation, supply chain and market factors.
findings.matters: A waste contract moving from a desktop estimate to a base pressure shows a one-off reserve-funded allowance becoming recurring cost.
findings.figures: £2.400m base pressure from 2027/28; £1.900m one-off allowance in 2026/27
findings.quote: now included £2.400m as a base budget pressure from 2027/28.

findings.headline: A £0.300m green bin charging income saving, included in the 2025/26 budget, has proved unachievable and is carried as a 2027/28 budget pressure.
findings.detail: The paper says take-up of the additional green bin charges has been lower than planned. The Table 10 line 'Undelivered Saving' carries £0.300m into 2027/28.
findings.matters: A failed income saving, carried forward rather than replaced, shows how a planned income line can become a permanent budget gap.
findings.quote: The take up of this service has been lower than planned and income levels have not proved achievable.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation saving raised from £1.296m to £1.740m, reflecting reduced reliance on high-cost nightly lets.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to greater use of Harben House and other lower-cost accommodation, and more move-on into private rented accommodation. It also lists court backlogs of Section 21 cases and the Renters Rights Act as risks to this assumption.
findings.matters: A saving raised on evidence of lower-cost delivery is a concrete example of a demand-side saving that other councils running similar temporary accommodation pressures can compare.
findings.figures: £1.296m increased to £1.740m; (£0.444m) movement
findings.quote: saving increased from £1.296m to £1.740m, reflecting reduced reliance on high-cost nightly lets

findings.headline: Budget reduction and income proposals total £8.918m in 2027/28, after a net increase of £11.291m in total budget reductions since February 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the Medium Term Financial Outlook already incorporated savings of £14.357m between 2027/28 and 2030/31, and that a further £5.547m in savings will be needed to bridge the gap. The Changing Because We Have To programme is named as the main strategy.
findings.matters: The size of the savings programme needed to balance the budget is a delivery risk that other councils and lenders can measure against their own plans.
findings.figures: £8.918m (2027/28 reductions); £11.291m net increase since February 2026; £14.357m (2027/28 to 2030/31 savings already in MTFO)
findings.quote: budget reductions since February 2026 is £11.291m.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 General Fund budget is now balanced, with the cumulative four-year funding gap risen from £3.840m in September to £5.547m.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the change to demand and inflation pressures and a Council Tax Base revised for lower growth, partly offset by savings, Business Rates and corporate changes. The paper says further budget measures may be needed before the budget is set.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how a balanced year-one budget sits alongside a growing four-year gap.
findings.figures: 2027/28 balanced; cumulative gap £5.547m (four years to 2030/31); £3.840m in September 2026
findings.quote: the budget for 2027/28 is now balanced, although the

findings.headline: Families First reforms require significant changes to Children's Services by March 2027, with £947k of additional investment in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the government programme requires reforms including family help hubs, an edge of care service and enhanced data reporting. The reforms are also expected to increase demand at the front door. A £288k reduction is shown in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A statutory reform with a fixed deadline and a funded cost is one that finance directors nationally are tracking against grant allocations.
findings.quote: The government programme requires significant reforms to Children's Services by March 2027.

findings.headline: Local elections base budget of £460k from 2028/29 would replace one-off funding, with unused amounts added to a reserve in fallow years.
findings.detail: The four-year election cycle includes a fallow year. In that year, the budget is added to a reserve, which is drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.
findings.matters: The mechanism moves one-off election funding into a base budget plus a reserve, which other councils with cyclical costs could compare against their own approaches.
findings.figures: £460k in 2027/28 column; four-year election cycle
findings.quote: During this fallow year, the budget will be added to the reserve, which can be drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.

findings.headline: Multi-Agency Safeguarding Hub is managing approximately 28% more contacts than in 2024/25, with delays beginning to emerge.
findings.detail: The paper says contacts have increased for two consecutive years and remain significantly above previous levels. It attributes this partly to Families First reforms and partly to population growth and housing expansion. Additional capacity of £64k is requested for 2027/28.
findings.matters: Front-door demand growth and emerging delays against statutory timescales are pressures that other councils running safeguarding hubs will be tracking.
findings.figures: approximately 28% more contacts than in 2024/25; £64k in 2027/28; £3,091k gross budget
findings.quote: the service now managing approximately 28% more contacts than in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Care leavers accommodation budget rises as average weekly costs increase from £133 in 2023/24 to £389 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the number of care leavers requiring accommodation has increased from 22 to 32, while costs have risen due to longer stays and more complex need. A reduction in UASC care leavers has also reduced external funding that offsets these costs.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs combined with lower external grant offset is a pressure other councils with similar care leaver populations would recognise.
findings.figures: £133 average weekly cost in 2023/24; £389 in 2026/27; 22 care leavers in 2023/24; 32 in 2026/27; £535k in 2027/28; £403k gross budget
findings.quote: Average weekly costs have risen from £133 in 2023/24 to £389 in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Supported accommodation re-procurement for 16+ provision is planned for implementation in March 2028, with demand expected to fit within the existing budget from 2028/29.
findings.detail: The 2027/28 budget rises by 7 placements to 54 and includes higher average costs for more complex needs. The paper says the revised arrangements are expected to absorb future demand within budget from 2028/29.
findings.matters: The budget depends on a re-procurement hitting a specific implementation date, which is a deadline other councils could compare against their own supported accommodation plans.
findings.figures: 54 placements in 2027/28 (up 7); 47 placements in 2026/27; £117k in 2027/28; £2,267k gross budget
findings.quote: The revised arrangements are expected to enable future demand to be accommodated within the existing budget from 2028/29.

findings.headline: Continuing Health Care income reduced by £200k as service user numbers fall, mainly in Short Breaks.
findings.detail: The paper says CHC income has decreased because of fewer service users, predominantly in Short Breaks. The pressure is classified as a policy choice in the risk column.
findings.matters: A health income stream falling with service numbers is a funding gap that councils with similar CHC arrangements would want to track.
findings.figures: £200k in 2027/28; £1,391k gross budget
findings.quote: CHC income has decreased due to the decrease in service users predominately in Short Breaks.

findings.headline: Education software contract expires in March 2028 and cannot be extended, with a replacement to be procured at current market rates.
findings.detail: The paper says a one-off pressure is expected in 2028/29 for implementation and transition costs. It also says an ongoing pressure is anticipated because the replacement contract will be priced at higher current market rates than existing costs.
findings.matters: A non-extendable contract expiry with an expected step-up in ongoing cost is a common replacement-cost pattern that other councils will be planning for.
findings.quote: the current software contract will expire in March 2028 and cannot be extended.

findings.headline: Educational Psychology team loses high needs block funding, creating a £149k budget pressure in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Following a review of high needs block funding eligibility and terms, the paper says the educational psychology service is no longer eligible for this funding stream. This funding previously supported a significant proportion of staffing costs.
findings.matters: Loss of a grant-funded stream that supported statutory staffing is a funding change that other councils with high needs block pressures may also face.
findings.figures: £149k in 2027/28; £1,195k gross budget
findings.quote: the educational psychology service is no longer eligible to receive this funding stream.

findings.headline: £300k green bin charge saving to be reversed because demand is "materially below the level assumed".
findings.detail: The saving came from charging £55 for second and third food and garden waste bins. The paper says insufficient evidence exists that uptake will rise to the required level. A corresponding £300k reduction in the Environmental Services contract budget is proposed separately, producing a neutral net effect.
findings.matters: An undelivered income saving is being reversed, and the offsetting contract reduction is the mechanism to watch for other councils that have set similar charges.
findings.figures: £300k income target reversed; £300k reduction in Environmental Services contract budget; -£380k in 2026/27 column
findings.quote: Demand has been materially below the level assumed and there is currently insufficient evidence that uptake will increase to the level required.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract pressure of £1.9m is retained and a further £500k is added following mobilisation of the new 10+5 year contract.
findings.detail: The paper says the council has procured and mobilised a new contract to operate and maintain the Waste Recovery Park. The updated pressure reflects visibility of operating costs. The paper says any evidenced efficiency reduction will be reflected in future MTFP updates.
findings.matters: A large, long-term waste contract is now carrying a higher pressure than before, and the efficiency mechanism is an open question for other councils with similar PFI-style or long-term operating contracts.
findings.figures: £1.9m retained pressure; £500k added; £19,902k gross budget; 10 + 5 year term
findings.quote: The current forecast requires the existing £1.9m pressure to be retained and a further £500k added.

findings.headline: Older People adult services pressure reduced, with the paper stating that 2027/28 demand can be met by current budgets.
findings.detail: The paper says an underspend in Homecare and Direct Payments in 2026/27 followed a surge in packages in 2025/26. That surge was linked to the closure of internal homecare and service users moving to a provider no longer commissioned directly. The paper still allows for 7% demand growth across Older People in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A pressure is being removed because a prior-year forecast overstated growth, which shows how demand forecasts are being corrected in-year.
findings.figures: -£325k in 2027/28; 7% forecast demand increase in 2027/28; £34,767k gross budget
findings.quote: we have established that this can be met by current budgets for 2027/28, resulting in a decrease in the predicted pressure.

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities pressure reduced by £708k after a review of package demand and cost, with 339 packages against a budget of 419 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the reduction to weekly panels scrutinising new and increased care packages. It says this has contributed to a forecast underspend in 2026/27. Package numbers are expected to rise to 378 in 2027/28, 389 in 2028/29 and 400 in 2029/30.
findings.matters: This is a reduction in a demand-led budget attributed to a specific control mechanism, which other councils running similar panels could compare against.
findings.figures: -£708k pressure reduction; 339 packages in 2026/27; 419 budgeted packages; 378 packages in 2027/28; 389 in 2028/29; 400 in 2029/30; £4,190k gross budget
findings.quote: There is a pressure reduction of £708k due to a review of package demand and cost.

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements are forecast to fall from 67 in 2026/27 to 53 in 2027/28 and 46 in 2028/29, after rising from 26 in 2023/24.
findings.detail: The paper reports a significant rise in residential placements over three financial years. The 2027/28 pressure is based on 53 placements, falling by 7 to 46 in 2028/29. The pressure is shown as a reduction of £643k in 2027/28 and £3,089k in 2028/29.
findings.matters: A large, high-cost statutory demand line is being reduced in the budget, and a finance director at another council would want to see the placement assumptions behind that reduction.
findings.figures: 26 placements in 2023/24; 67 placements in 2026/27; 53 placements in 2027/28; 46 placements in 2028/29; -£643k in 2027/28; -£3,089k in 2028/29; £25,123k gross budget
findings.quote: The pressure is based on an expectation of 53 placements being in a residential in 2027/28, reducing by 7 to 46 in 2028/29.

findings.headline: The Tariff Reserve rises from £15.441m to £19.596m, with £4.156m added in the year.
findings.detail: The reserve is added to during the year. The summary table lists the £4.156m movement as a key movement in reserves.
findings.matters: A reserve built from tariff income is a risk reserve for future obligations, and finance directors comparing how councils set aside funds for similar risks will want to see the scale.
findings.figures: £15.441m opening; £4.156m in-year addition; £19.596m outturn at 31 March 2027 (£m, as read from the paper's tables)

findings.headline: Schools Balances fall from £10.455m to £8.243m, with £2.211m applied in the year.
findings.detail: The reserve is drawn down during the year. The summary table records the movement as a key movement in schools balances.
findings.matters: Schools balances are a ring-fenced reserve that finance officers at other councils track as a sign of pressure on school budgets.
findings.figures: £10.455m opening; £2.211m in-year drawdown; £8.243m outturn at 31 March 2027 (£m, as read from the paper's tables)

findings.headline: The Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve falls from £19.201m to £15.491m, with £3.710m applied in the year.
findings.detail: The reserve is drawn down during the year to cover collection fund cashflow. It is one of the reserves the summary table lists as a key movement.
findings.matters: Collection fund cashflow reserves are used to manage timing differences in council tax and business rates income, a pressure many councils face.
findings.figures: £19.201m opening; £3.710m in-year drawdown; £15.491m outturn at 31 March 2027 (£m, as read from the paper's tables)
findings.quote: Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve (19.201) 0.000 3.710 (15.491)

findings.headline: One-off and Political Priority reserves fall from £10.766m to £3.776m, with £5.520m applied in the year.
findings.detail: The table shows a £1.470m movement out of this reserve to the Election Reserves. The summary table records the £5.520m 'Political Priorities Reserve' movement as a key movement.
findings.matters: A large drawdown from a discretionary reserve shows the council using one-off funds for priorities, which other councils budgeting for similar pressures will compare against their own.
findings.figures: £10.766m opening; £1.470m transferred to Election Reserves; £5.520m in-year drawdown; £3.776m outturn at 31 March 2027 (£m, as read from the paper's tables)
findings.quote: One-off & Political Priority reserves (10.766) 1.470 5.520 (3.776)

findings.headline: Capital Reserve - GF falls from £51.933m to £35.317m, with £16.878m applied in the year.
findings.detail: The General Fund capital reserve is the largest single reserve movement in the table. The summary table shows £21.093m applied under 'Delivering the Capital Programme' in key movements. The table also shows a £0.262m movement in the opening position.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund the capital programme is a funding choice that finance directors and lenders track closely, because it reduces the cushion available for future schemes.
findings.figures: £51.933m opening; £16.878m in-year drawdown; £35.317m outturn at 31 March 2027; £21.093m 'Delivering the Capital Programme' in key movements (£m, as read from the paper's tables)

findings.headline: The General Fund Balance is shown at £34.677m at 31 March 2027, with no movement in the year.
findings.detail: The unearmarked General Fund Balance is held at its opening level. No in-year contribution or drawdown is shown against it.
findings.matters: The unearmarked General Fund is the council's general buffer, so a finance director elsewhere will look at whether it is held or moved.
findings.figures: £34.677m General Fund Balance, opening and outturn; £0.000m in-year movement
findings.quote: General Fund Balance (34.677) 0.000 0.000 (34.677)

findings.headline: Total reserves are shown moving from £258.238m to £229.987m across the year to 31 March 2027, an in-year movement of £28.250m.
findings.detail: The total line gives the opening balance, the in-year movement and the outturn balance at 31 March 2027. Separately, the summary table shows a £23.525m net movement in key reserves, with a further £4.725m movement in other reserves.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how fast total reserves are being drawn against their own reserve strategy.
findings.figures: £258.238m opening total; £28.250m in-year movement; £229.987m outturn at 31 March 2027 (£m, as read from the paper's tables)

findings.headline: The General Fund minimum balance has been reassessed and is held at £34.677m across all years to 31/03/2031, based on a refreshed risk assessment
findings.detail: The General Fund Balance is the statutory reserve for unexpected or unplanned expenditure. The paper refers to a refreshed risk assessment at Annex A8, and the minimum balance is shown unchanged in every year.
findings.matters: The minimum balance and the method used to set it are a key reference point for finance directors and lenders assessing a council's resilience.
findings.figures: £34.677m at 31/03/2026 and in each forecast year to 31/03/2031
findings.quote: Minimum Balance has been reassessed based on a refreshed risk assessment (Annex A8).

findings.headline: The Legal Fees Reserve is forecast to fall from £1.653m at 31/03/2026 to £0.403m at 31/03/2031, with no current plans for new contributions
findings.detail: The reserve funds unexpected or exceptional legal costs not in the base budget. The paper says the funding level will be reviewed each year.
findings.matters: A reserve for reactive legal costs running down with no planned top-up leaves less cover for litigation, which lenders and finance directors track across councils.
findings.quote: There are no current plans to make new contributions to this reserve but the funding level will be reviewed each year.

findings.headline: The Elections reserve is set to end its reliance on one-off funding from 2028-29, when a base budget for elections is introduced
findings.detail: The paper says a base budget for the average cost of elections will remove the need for one-off funding from 2028-29. In fallow years the budget goes into the reserve, which is drawn down when election costs exceed the base budget.
findings.matters: Moving a recurring cost from one-off reserve funding into the base budget is a structural budget change that finance officers at other councils with four-year election cycles can compare with their own arrangements.
findings.quote: incorporating a base budget for Elections to cover the average cost of elections will eliminate the need for one-off funding.

findings.headline: MKWRP Risk Reserve forecast to rise from £10.000m at 31/03/2026 to £17.000m at 31/03/2031 as contingency against Waste Plant closure from contractor failure
findings.detail: The reserve is shown rising each year from 2028, with the commentary listing landfill, insurance and business rates as the exceptional costs it would fund.
findings.matters: A contractor-failure contingency on a waste facility is a specific exposure that other councils with PFI or long-term waste contracts can benchmark against.
findings.quote: Risk reserve provides a contingency in the event of the Waste Plant no longer being operational as a result of contractor failure.

findings.headline: The Highways and E&W transformation reserve is being closed by 31/03/2027, after the paper says the highways programme did not start in 19/20 as expected
findings.detail: The reserve was set aside for major highways and environment and waste commissioning. The funding is now to be drawn down over the next couple of years, and the reserve closes by 31/03/2027.
findings.matters: A delayed commissioning programme that leaves ring-fenced funding waiting for years is a delivery signal that peers and lenders can check against their own programmes.
findings.figures: £0.012m balance; to be closed by 31/3/2027
findings.quote: There highways programme did not start in 19/20 as expected and the funding has been set aside to fund the works as required over the next couple of years.

findings.headline: The Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve is forecast to fall from £19.201m at 31/03/2026 to £10.701m from 31/03/2029, and the paper says it is not available for general use
findings.detail: The reserve is held for timing differences between the Collection Fund and General Fund, and is shown as flat at £10.701m from 2029 to 2031. The reserve covers business rates volatility from appeals, unbudgeted levy costs and government changes.
findings.matters: A reserve described as unavailable for general use changes how total reserves should be read, and the business rates volatility it covers is common across councils.
findings.quote: This reserve is not available as this is held to manage timing differences between the Collection Fund and General Fund.

findings.headline: The GF Capital Reserve, which holds revenue contributions for the current capital programme, is forecast to fall from £51.933m at 31/03/2026 to £35.317m at 31/03/2027
findings.detail: The reserve is shown drawing down each year to £16.072m by 31/03/2031. The commentary says the funding is for specific projects allocated within the current capital programme.
findings.matters: Drawdown of revenue-funded capital reserves is a direct measure of how much of the capital programme is being paid from cash held in reserve rather than borrowing.
findings.quote: Capital Reserve - GF GF revenue contributions held to finance the current capital programme. Active (51.933) (35.317)

findings.headline: Total reserves are forecast at £229.987m at 31/03/2027, down from £258.238m at 31/03/2026, rising to £225.980m by 31/03/2031
findings.detail: The total reserves line shows balances in brackets for the actual 2026 position and each forecast year to 2031. The largest single movement in the table is in the GF capital and collection fund reserves, which fall across the period.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can compare the scale of planned reserve drawdown against their own forecast balances over the same period.

findings.detail: The paper says the budget was increased under Child First and can now be reduced in line with latest numbers. The saving is rated Green and is new this year.
findings.matters: A fall in court proceedings reducing a legal cost line is a demand-side change a finance officer elsewhere could check against their own care proceedings numbers.

findings.headline: Adult Services cites a DoLS referral fall after the June 2026 AGNI ruling, with demand for assessments expected to reduce by around two-thirds, and a £304k saving proposed.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall in referrals to the AGNI (Attorney General for Northern Ireland) ruling in June 2026 and proposes reviewing agency staffing and service delivery arrangements on that basis. The saving is rated Green.
findings.matters: A legal ruling changing statutory assessment demand is a driver other councils with DoLS pressures would need to track, and the paper ties a budget reduction directly to it.

findings.headline: Adult Services removes a £1,000k surplus budget after the internal homecare service closed.
findings.detail: The paper says the service has now closed and that the reduction is the remaining surplus budget. The item is rated Green and is a new proposal this year with no FTE effect recorded.
findings.matters: Closing a service and removing its residual budget is a concrete change to the council's cost base, and peers running similar in-house provision may want to compare how the surplus was carried.
