findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Corporate savings of £1,450k in 2027/28 and £1,850k in 2028/29 are rated Amber, with the paper stating consultation is required and FTE effect TBC on the HP1 and HP2 items.
findings.detail: Four 'CBWHT HP' corporate proposals and one OD2 social care review sit under Corporate savings. Each HP line is rated Amber, marked as requiring consultation, and shows 'Y' in the sensitive column for the HP items.
findings.matters: A large share of the 2028/29 reduction sits in corporate proposals that are not yet confirmed and need consultation, which is the kind of delivery risk a peer council or lender would test.

findings.paper_title: Annex A5 - 2027_28 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Proposed budget reductions and income growth total £8,918k in 2027/28, falling to £3,403k in 2028/29, £1,798k in 2029/30 and £65k in 2030/31, with a 19.82 FTE reduction.
findings.detail: The grand total across Adult Services, Children's Services, Customer and Community, Planning, Environment and Property, and Corporate savings is shown in the paper's summary row. Corporate savings carry the largest unconfirmed element, with FTE effect 'TBC' on two items.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the scale and phasing of a single authority's savings programme against its own gap, and a lender can see how much of the 2027/28 position depends on reductions not yet delivered.

findings.headline: The paper states that funding for the Disabled Facilities Grant is 'assumed to be funded at the same level as confirmed for 27/28 subject to future review' for the years after 2027/28.
findings.detail: The R&M Disabled Grant Facilities line carries £1,629,585 in each of 2028/29 to 2031/32 against £2,806,833 in 2027/28. The paper records that these years are not yet confirmed, and the grant is ring-fenced Better Care Fund money.
findings.matters: Capital grant funding that is assumed rather than confirmed over four years is a planning risk for any council relying on it for adaptations.
findings.quote: Funding has not yet been confirmed for these years, assumed to be funded at the same level as confirmed for 27/28 subject to future review.

findings.headline: £31,081,601 of pipeline schemes appear in a list where the paper states the budget business cases had not been approved by the Corporate Portfolio Board.
findings.detail: The pipeline list covers the Doing the Essentials Well and Building Better Communities categories, including the £20,652,359 Environmental Services fleet replacement in 2028/29 funded by RCCO. The paper records the unfunded column as £0 for the total pipeline, with several lines marked TBC.
findings.matters: Schemes presented as pipeline without approved business cases carry cost and funding risk that a finance director will want to see flagged before they enter the programme.
findings.figures: £31,081,601 total pipeline; £10,429,242 in 2027/28; £20,652,359 in 2028/29; £5,100,000 Building Better Communities total
findings.quote: budget business cases had not been approved by the Corporate Portfolio Board

findings.headline: The HRA Planned Asset Management Programme is realigned, with the paper stating that the programme was reviewed to keep funding within debt cap limits.
findings.detail: The HRA Planned Asset Management line moves by £160,997 in 2027/28 and by negative amounts in 2028/29 to 2030/31, then adds £29,026,373 in 2031/32 for new allocations, for a net change of £25,540,175. The change is attributed to the current business plan.
findings.matters: A HRA capital programme reshaped to stay inside a debt cap is a direct borrowing constraint that finance directors and lenders watch closely.
findings.quote: Programme reviewed to ensure funding remains within the debt cap limits

findings.headline: The Transport section shows 2027/28 funding available of £94,027,384 against starts of £92,904,838, a surplus of £1,122,546, moving to a deficit of £400,000 in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The funding deficit/(surplus) row shows a bracketed surplus in 2027/28 and a £400,000 deficit in 2028/29, leaving a cumulative surplus of £722,546 from 2028/29 onward. The paper does not explain how the 2028/29 gap will be met.
findings.matters: A transport programme that is funded in its first year and has a stated but unexplained gap in its second is the kind of profile a lender or finance director will want to check against grant assumptions.
findings.figures: £94,027,384 funding available 2027/28; £92,904,838 total 2027/28 starts; £(1,122,546) surplus 2027/28; £400,000 deficit 2028/29; £(722,546) cumulative surplus

findings.headline: A £9.000m MKCC contribution to Milton Keynes East strategic highways infrastructure is requested, alongside £50.000m of Housing Infrastructure Fund money offered by Homes England.
findings.detail: The paper asks for additional resource allocation and spend approval of £9.000m, funded from capital receipts, to supplement the Homes England HIF offer. The 2027/28 Housing Infrastructure Fund highways line stands at £37,616,595.
findings.matters: The council is committing its own capital receipts to a housing-enabling highway scheme alongside external grant, which is a funding structure other councils with HIF schemes will recognise.
findings.figures: £9.000m MKCC contribution; £50.000m HIF funding offered by Homes England; £37,616,595 Housing Infrastructure Fund - Highways in 2027/28 (total programme)
findings.quote: Additional Resource Allocation and Spend Approval of £9.000m is requested as an MKCC contribution towards the Milton Keynes East strategic highways infrastructure

findings.headline: WEA4 - New Primary School project budget is increased from £18m to £24.750m, citing construction inflation, statutory requirements, labour and material costs and updated project risks.
findings.detail: The paper requests additional resource allocation for the WEA4 primary school, adding £4,286,813 in 2027/28 and £2,463,187 in 2028/29. The school is to provide a 630-place primary school, 39-place nursery and 24 specialist SEND places.
findings.matters: A £6.75m uplift on a single primary school, attributed to inflation and risk, is a concrete example of a school scheme's cost moving after approval.
findings.figures: £18m original total project budget; £24.750m revised total project budget; £6,750,000 increase (£4,286,813 in 2027/28, £2,463,187 in 2028/29)
findings.quote: total project budget from £18m to £24.750m

findings.headline: The draft capital programme totals £570,577,668 over 2027/28 to 2031/32, against £348,954,072 in the programme agreed in February 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reconciles the February 2026 agreed programme to the reported draft through July and September Cabinet changes, slippage and rephasing, December budget changes, and draft amendments. The reconciliation rows show increases in each category, with the 2027/28 year carrying the largest share.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can see how far the five-year capital envelope has moved since the last approved programme, and which changes drove it.
findings.figures: £348,954,072 agreed Feb 26 total; £570,577,668 reported draft budget position total; £236,961,329 in 2027/28; £31,740,490 July Cabinet changes; £18,360,138 slippage and rephasing; £27,400,000 September Cabinet changes; £24,661,884 December budget changes

findings.headline: The paper gives General Fund loan principal repaid in the first half as £1.716m in the summary, while Table 1 shows -£1.781m.
findings.detail: The summary says £1.716m was repaid against General Fund loans this year. Table 1 records existing loan principal repaid of -£1.781m, which matches the fall from the £168.665m opening balance to the £166.884m closing balance. The paper does not explain the difference.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing the summary with the portfolio table will need the correct repayment figure to reconcile the General Fund debt position.
findings.figures: £1.716m (summary); -£1.781m (Table 1); £168.665m opening General Fund balance; £166.884m closing balance
findings.quote: £1.716m loan principal repayment have been made so far this year against General Fund loans.

findings.headline: In September 2026 the council finalised a loan facility of up to £15.0m over 10 years with its wholly owned subsidiary Milton Keynes Development Partnership (MKDP).
findings.detail: The paper says MKDP can draw funds up to the maximum or repay principal in part or in full, with options exercisable monthly. Loan rates are set with reference to subsidy regulations and prevailing market rates. The paper reports this under investments made for policy reasons outside normal treasury management.
findings.matters: Council lending to a wholly owned company is an investment outside normal treasury management, and finance officers elsewhere will want to see how the terms and subsidy controls are set.
findings.figures: £15.0m maximum facility; 10-year term; monthly draw and repayment options
findings.quote: In September 2026, we finalised a new long term loan facility with our wholly owned subsidiary company Milton Keynes Development Partnership (MKDP) for a maximum of £15.0m over the next 10 years.

findings.headline: In March 2026 the General Fund agreed a new £30m internal loan to the HRA at 4.48%, maturing 19/03/2027.
findings.detail: The paper lists the new loan alongside four older General Fund to HRA loans at rates between 1.75% and 1.91%. Total internal loans outstanding are £80.0m at an average 2.82%. The paper notes that further internal loans may be agreed if mutually beneficial.
findings.matters: Internal lending at a rate well above the older internal loans shows how a council prices cash-backed reserves against new borrowing, and it sets a repayment date in March 2027.
findings.figures: £30.0m loan at 4.48%, maturing 19/03/2027; £80.0m total internal loans at 2.82% average; older loans at 1.75%-1.91%
findings.quote: In March 2026 a new £30m loan was agreed.

findings.headline: The HRA ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast at 34.74%, against a 40.64% indicator, because of delayed new borrowing and 2025/26 capital slippage.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the fall to two causes: delaying new HRA borrowing, which saves interest, and reduced voluntary minimum revenue provision because of 2025/26 capital programme slippage and refinancing.
findings.matters: Capital slippage lowering financing costs is a pattern finance directors see when delivery lags budget, and it shows the timing trade-off between delay and future borrowing need.
findings.figures: 40.64% HRA indicator (Feb 2026); 34.74% HRA actual Q2 / forecast outturn
findings.quote: The HRA ratio has decreased due to delaying new borrowing (saving in interest costs) and reduced voluntary minimum revenue provision because of 2025/26 capital programme slippage and refinancing.

findings.headline: The paper says the HRA is approaching a point of needing additional funding for its business plan capital objectives, and the forecast outturn assumes £70m of new external loans.
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA forecast outturn assumes £70m funded by new external loans, and that further internal loans may be considered. HRA maturity limits were amended to allow more borrowing over 2-5 years at current elevated rates until longer-term rates fall. The paper notes HRA PWLB borrowing is 40 bps below the certainty rate until the end of March 2027, if not extended.
findings.matters: A council whose HRA needs new external borrowing will face replacement funding costs and maturity-structure decisions that other housing authorities also face.
findings.figures: £70m assumed new external HRA loans in forecast outturn; £196.360m HRA external loans on 30/09/2026; £276.360m total HRA borrowing including internal loans; 40 bps discount to certainty rate until end March 2027
findings.quote: The HRA is approaching a point of requiring additional funding to meet its business plan capital objectives (subject to slippage).

findings.headline: The CCLA property fund holding is valued at £13.754m on 30/09/2026 against £15.0m invested, an unrealised loss of £1.246m.
findings.detail: The council has no immediate plans to sell the holding, which yielded 4.67% average gross return so far this year. The officer commentary forecasts a slight recovery towards year end but flags the risk of further market devaluation.
findings.matters: Property fund valuations are a known risk on local authority balance sheets, and other councils holding similar funds will be watching how the unrealised loss is being handled.
findings.figures: £13.754m holding on 30/09/2026; £13.986m opening balance 01/04/2026; £0.232m fair value loss; -£1.246m unrealised loss; £15.0m total cash deposit; 4.67% average gross return
findings.quote: representing a fair value loss of £0.232m and an overall unrealised loss of -£1.246m against the £15.0m total cash deposit.

findings.headline: The General Fund ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast at 3.40%, against a 4.43% indicator set in February 2026.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the lower General Fund ratio to expected investment income outperformance feeding into net revenue. The indicator was set when the Treasury Management Strategy and Budget were approved in February 2026.
findings.matters: A lower financing cost ratio means more of the General Fund's net revenue is free of capital financing costs, which is directly comparable across councils.
findings.figures: 4.43% indicator (Feb 2026); 3.40% actual Q2 / forecast outturn
findings.quote: The GF ratio has decreased which reflects the positive impact upon net revenue of expecting to outperform our budget for investment income.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes reports an average investment return of 4.34% in the first half of 2026/27, 0.59% above the SONIA 3-month benchmark of 3.75%.
findings.detail: The paper says the council's investment performance beat the benchmark over the first half. Cash balances averaged £348.828m, and the paper reports no counterparty credit risk issues or principal losses. The paper links the outperformance to the General Fund financing cost forecast.
findings.matters: Investment income above benchmark offsets capital financing costs, and a finance director at another council will want to compare that return with their own treasury performance.
findings.figures: 4.34% average return; 3.75% benchmark; +0.59% difference; £348.828m average cash balance; £333.484m investments on 30/09/2026
findings.quote: The average rate of investment return was 4.34%, which was 0.59% above the benchmark.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Disrepair budget cut by £0.292m to £1m, with new cases and costs lower than the 2024/25 peak
findings.detail: The paper reduces the disrepair budget by £0.292m, leaving £1m for legal costs, compensation and repairs. It says new cases and costs are lower than the 2024/25 peak but the area remains volatile, with an average of 467 days per claim.
findings.matters: Disrepair claims are a common cost pressure for social landlords, and the paper ties the budget reduction to falling case numbers.
findings.figures: Disrepairs (£0.292m); budget of £1m; average days per claim 467
findings.quote: Disrepairs (£0.292m) – This will leave a budget of £1m to cover legal costs, compensation and repair work.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: No significant additional HRA investment to be agreed until stock condition survey impact is known and headroom is certain
findings.detail: The paper says no significant additional investment can be agreed until the full impact of the stock condition surveys is known and headroom is confirmed. If projects overspend, other schemes will need to be reduced.
findings.matters: A stated limit on new investment until survey results are known is a constraint on the capital programme that finance directors and lenders would need to model.
findings.figures: £155m planned maintenance and investment and £17m regeneration and acquisitions across five years
findings.quote: no significant additional investment can be agreed until the full impact of the stock condition surveys is known and there is certainty that there is sufficient headroom to manage these risks.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Acres Lodge development (66 units, £27m) and an £8m acquisition allocation are funded from Right to Buy receipts up to 2031/32
findings.detail: The business plan commits all Right to Buy receipts to the Acres Lodge development scheme and an acquisition allocation up to 2031/32. From 2036/37 the paper assumes all receipts fund acquisitions.
findings.matters: Committing all receipts to a named scheme shows how the council is using its receipts, which peers and lenders will compare against their own programmes.
findings.figures: 66 units; £27m for Acres Lodge development; £8m acquisition allocation; committed up until 2031/32
findings.quote: The business plan utilises receipts for the Acres Lodge development scheme (66 units) at £27m and an acquisition allocation £8m, committing all receipts up until 2031/32.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipts can be held for 10 years from 2027/28, up from five
findings.detail: The paper says Right to Buy receipts can be held for 10 years from 2027/28 rather than five, and can fund 100% of expenditure when combined with section 106 contributions to deliver additional stock.
findings.matters: A longer holding period changes how councils can time and fund acquisitions and new build, and reduces the risk of receipts being returned to government with interest.
findings.figures: up to five years (current); 10 years from 2027/28; 100% of expenditure
findings.quote: Current receipts can be held for up to five years but from 2027/28 they can be held for 10 years and fund 100% of the expenditure

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Proposed 2027/28 rent increase for existing tenants is 4.5% + £1.00, an average £5.93 per week
findings.detail: The paper proposes a rent increase at the maximum permitted under the Rent Standard, which allows September CPI plus 1% plus £1.00. Shared owners' increase is 4.8%, lagging a year as set by their leases.
findings.matters: Rent setting under the Rent Standard is the largest single driver of HRA income, and the paper notes the projected income cannot be regarded as certain.
findings.figures: 4.5% + £1.00 for existing tenants; 4.8% for shared owners; average £5.93 per week for tenants and £5.07 per week for shared owners; dwelling rents £74.288m (2027/28)
findings.quote: we propose to increase rents by 4.5% + £1.00 for existing tenants in 2027/28 and for shared owners there will be an increase of 4.8%

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Stock rationalisation at 40 units a year, the paper's worst scenario, leaves £72.244m of borrowing and £0.707m of reserves at Year 40
findings.detail: The paper models three stress scenarios. The stock rationalisation scenario doubles stock loss from 20 to 40 units a year, leaving borrowing outstanding at year 40 and reserves much lower than the draft budget.
findings.matters: It shows how sensitive a 40-year HRA plan is to stock loss, which matters to councils with ageing, non-traditional stock.
findings.figures: borrowing outstanding at Year 40 £72.244m; reserves £0.707m; stock loss 40 units a year; draft budget year-40 surplus £222.508m
findings.quote: This is the worst of the scenarios, with borrowing outstanding at Year 40 of £72.244m and reserves reduced to £0.707m.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: HRA can borrow from the PWLB at 40 basis points below the General Fund rate until March 2028
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA's housing-specific PWLB discount is 40 basis points below the General Fund rate and runs until March 2028. The paper does not say what follows that date.
findings.matters: The discount lowers the HRA's cost of new borrowing, and its expiry in March 2028 affects the timing of borrowing decisions for councils with similar arrangements.
findings.figures: 40 basis points less than the GF; runs until March 2028
findings.quote: The HRA is currently able to borrow from the PWLB at 40 basis points less than the GF. This housing-specific discount runs until March 2028.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Business plan assumes new HRA loans at 5.75% for three years, falling to 5.00% from year 6
findings.detail: The paper sets out the baseline rate for new HRA loans, which steps down over the plan. The paper says this is informed by treasury advisers and market commentators and could change with economic conditions.
findings.matters: The new-loan rate assumption drives the plan's interest costs and headroom, and lenders can compare it with current PWLB pricing.
findings.figures: 5.75% for the next 3 years; 5.50% in year 4; 5.25% in year 5; 5.00% from year 6; average interest rate on all borrowing 3.90% (2026/27) rising to 4.30% (2029/30)
findings.quote: The business plan baseline assumption is for new loans to be drawn 5.75% over the next 3 years, 5.50% in year 4, 5.25% in year 5, then 5.00% from year 6 onwards.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: HRA borrowing table shows £47.00m of scheduled repayments and £35.00m of refinancing loans in 2026/27
findings.detail: The council states that maturing loans are being repaid and will need to be refinanced. It also says it is carrying a significant amount of short-dated debt, including internal borrowing, which it will need to refinance.
findings.matters: Refinancing a large short-dated HRA debt stack at elevated rates is the main borrowing exposure the paper identifies, and the same pressure applies to other councils holding short-dated HRA debt.
findings.figures: Scheduled Repayments £47.00m (2026/27), £17.00m (2027/28); New Loans: Refinancing £35.00m (2026/27), £11.50m (2027/28); New Loans: Capital £51.07m (2026/27)
findings.quote: The council is carrying a significant amount of short-dated debt (including internal borrowing) which it will need to refinance.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Available HRA borrowing against the February 2026 position changes by £30.82m in 2026/27 and -£11.56m in 2028/29
findings.detail: The headroom table shows the change in available borrowing since the February 2026 budget. The change is positive in 2026/27, negative in 2027/28 to 2029/30, and positive again from 2030/31.
findings.matters: A change in available HRA borrowing headroom directly limits how much the council can borrow for stock and new build, which lenders and peers will track.
findings.quote: Changes since Council Feb 2026: Available Borrowing 30.82 -3.59 -11.56 -2.26 4.36 9.95

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Serpentine Court and Reema Phase 1 removed from Council Tax through the Valuation Office, with a £0.910m budget saving
findings.detail: The council says its team has had Serpentine Court and Reema Phase 1 taken off Council Tax, some of which carried 200% or 300% premiums. The Council Tax line is reduced by £0.910m, leaving £0.414m for operational voids and other out-of-management stock.
findings.matters: Council Tax liability on empty or out-of-management stock is a recurring cost that other councils with void or regeneration stock may face, and the paper shows a specific route to reducing it.
findings.figures: Council Tax (£0.910m); leaves a budget of £0.414m; 200%/300% premiums
findings.quote: The team have been successful in getting Serpentine Court and the Reema Phase 1 taken off the Council Tax through the Valuation Office, some of these had 200%/300% premiums.

findings.paper_title: Annex B - 2027-28 Draft Housing Revenue Account
findings.headline: Condition survey programme has completed over 90% of dwellings in 18 months rather than taking three years
findings.detail: The council says its accelerated condition survey programme has covered over 90% of dwellings in 18 months. The 2027/28 budget reduces condition surveys by £0.257m because the programme is compressed, within a £0.424m compliance contracts saving.
findings.matters: A stock survey delivered well ahead of schedule brings forward the data the council says it needs before committing further HRA investment, and the budget saving is reflected in the draft.
findings.figures: over 90% of dwellings; 18 months rather than three years; Compliance Contracts (£0.424m); Condition Surveys reduced by £0.257m
findings.quote: we have completed over 90% of dwellings in 18 months rather than taking three years.

findings.headline: The Disabled Facilities Grant (GF) reports a £1,403,132 reduction in allocation, with the paper attributing it to prior-year slippage and contractor capacity constraints.
findings.detail: The R&M Disabled Grant Facilities project has a total scheme budget of £3,802,270 and a forecast variance of -£1,403,132. The paper links the reduction to contractor capacity constraints in delivering backlog works, alongside the current year's programme.
findings.matters: Contractor capacity constraints delaying statutory adaptations spending is a service pressure that peer councils managing demand for adaptations would want to compare against their own delivery.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £3,802,270; forecast variance -£1,403,132; slippage £1,120,777; current-year forecast £2,157,348
findings.quote: Reduced allocation of £1.121m, reflecting prior-year slippage and contractor capacity constraints in delivering backlog works

findings.headline: The Tickford Park Developments project reports a £30,000 overspend, which the paper says will be cleared when a capital receipt is received, following exchange of the development agreement with Vistry.
findings.detail: The paper states that the development agreement has been exchanged and that work continues to maintain the land until the agreement completes and final legal points are resolved. The overspend is expected to be cleared once the capital receipt is received.
findings.matters: A land disposal that will offset a capital overspend is a funding mechanism that finance directors and lenders would track through to completion.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £1,467,221; total scheme forecast £1,497,221; forecast variance £30,000
findings.quote: Development Agreement has been exchanged with Vistry.

findings.headline: The Highway Infrastructure Fund (HIF) highways project shows a £21,950,000 current-year slippage, with funding drawdown now expected by Spring 2028.
findings.detail: The project has a capital budget of £129,556,689 and a current-year budget of £21,950,000, with the full amount slipping to future years. The paper states that phase 2 onsite works commenced in Summer 2026 and rates the project Amber.
findings.matters: Slippage of this scale on a grant-funded highways programme, with drawdown pushed out two years, affects the timing of cash flows and funding that lenders and finance directors would want to assess.
findings.figures: Capital budget £129,556,689; current-year budget £21,950,000; slippage £21,950,000; funding drawdown by Spring 2028
findings.quote: Highway procurement led by Berkeley Group utilising HIF.Phase2 onsite works commenced Summer 2026, funding drawdown by Spring 2028.

findings.headline: The Harrier Court project forecasts a £500,000 underspend, which the paper attributes to a reduction in the scope and costs of the finishing grounds work.
findings.detail: The project has a total scheme budget of £2,233,405 and a forecast of £1,733,405, a variance of -£500,000. The paper notes that the cost of reletting individual flats was charged to the voids budget.
findings.matters: A scheme delivered under budget through reduced scope is a useful benchmark for peer councils managing similar estate refurbishment works.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £2,233,405; total scheme forecast £1,733,405; forecast variance -£500,000
findings.quote: Underspend relates to a reduction in the scope and costs of the finishing grounds work.

findings.headline: The MK East Primary New Build (HIF Social Infrastructure) project forecasts a £400,000 overspend, with the paper stating that tariff funding has been identified to cover it.
findings.detail: The project has a total scheme forecast of £29,331,467 against a capital budget of £28,931,467. The paper states that the forecast includes assumed final account contract costs and that the project is rated Amber due to recommissioning being partly complete.
findings.matters: An overspend on a Housing Infrastructure Fund-linked school with tariff funding identified is an example of how councils are covering scheme cost increases from developer contributions, which peers and lenders would want to compare.
findings.figures: Total scheme forecast £29,331,467; capital budget £28,931,467; forecast variance £400,000
findings.quote: Tariff funding identified for overspend.

findings.headline: The Lakes Estate Heath Facility project reports £2,204,000 of slippage, with the programme affected by NHS governance requirements under negotiation.
findings.detail: The project has a total scheme budget of £2,504,000 and a current-year budget of £300,000, with £2,204,000 slipping to future years. The paper states that the slippage reflects the anticipated programme based on the outstanding NHS governance.
findings.matters: A project whose critical path depends on an external partner's governance is a delivery risk a lender or peer authority would want to track, particularly where the council is funding a facility in partnership with the NHS.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £2,504,000; current-year budget £300,000; slippage £2,204,000; forecast variance £-2,502,968 against actuals to date
findings.quote: NHS governance requirements in negotiation, this affects programme critical path.

findings.headline: The Reema Demolition project forecasts a £255,041 overspend, attributed to asbestos removal across all seven blocks and site security costs.
findings.detail: The R&M Reema Demolition project has a total scheme budget of £2,730,294 and a forecast variance of £255,041. Phase 1 (four blocks) has been demolished and the first three blocks of Phase 2(a) are being soft stripped.
findings.matters: Asbestos and site-security costs on large demolition projects are a recurring cost pressure, and a peer council planning similar works would benefit from knowing this overspend has occurred.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £2,730,294; forecast variance £255,041; current-year budget £1,325,134; current forecast 2026/27 £1,580,175
findings.quote: Overspend due to asbestos removal required (all 7 blocks) and arrangements for leaving sites secure once the contractor has left.

findings.headline: The Voids - Structure project records that 'current costs are in revenue which need to be moved', with a £4,000,000 forecast underspend.
findings.detail: The paper says the voids structure costs are currently charged to revenue and will need to be moved to capital. The project records a forecast variance of -£4,000,000 against a total scheme budget of £8,313,540.
findings.matters: Costs sitting in revenue that should be capitalised is a classification issue a finance director or auditor would expect to see corrected, and it affects both the revenue and capital position.
findings.figures: Total scheme budget £8,313,540; forecast variance -£4,000,000; current-year forecast £4,259,111
findings.quote: Demand led, current costs are in revenue which need to be moved.

findings.headline: The Fire Safety Works programme forecasts a £3,809,332 underspend, with the Fire Door Renewal and Communal Fire Doors projects reporting variances of -£3,000,000 and -£809,352.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Fire Door Renewal underspend to a delay in starting replacements and the survey contract, with spend expected to increase in Q3 and Q4. The Communal Fire Doors project records a delay in contract mobilisation and survey contracts, with a £500K WIP and a further £500K to be in progress before end of Q4.
findings.matters: Fire safety is a regulatory obligation for social landlords, so a council forecasting a multi-million underspend in this programme while the work is delayed is a point a lender or peer authority would want to see addressed.
findings.figures: Fire Safety Works total scheme budget £16,003,053; forecast variance -£3,809,332; Fire Door Renewal variance -£3,000,000; Communal Fire Doors variance -£809,352; current-year forecast £6,364,041
findings.quote: Delay in start of replacements and survey contract. Survey programme commenced with spend expected to increase Q3 & Q4.

findings.headline: Housing & Regeneration HRA shows a total scheme forecast of £351,179,132 against a £362,299,693 capital budget, a forecast variance of -£11,120,561.
findings.detail: The HRA line forecasts £66,846,053 for 2026/27 against a current-year budget of £87,597,325, with £10,074,973 slipping to future years. The paper records a forecast variance of -£10,676,299 on the current-year outturn.
findings.matters: A large HRA underspend and slippage set against a £362m programme is a signal of delivery capacity that lenders and peer finance teams track for housing investment plans.
findings.figures: Total capital budget £362,299,693; total scheme forecast £351,179,132; forecast variance -£11,120,561; current-year budget £87,597,325; current forecast 2026/27 £66,846,053; slippage £10,074,973; current-year outturn variance -£10,676,299

findings.headline: The capital programme forecasts £198,790,145 for 2026/27 against a current-year budget of £242,922,675, with £34,033,964 forecast to slip to future years.
findings.detail: The grand total line shows total scheme forecasts of £1,075,195,649 against a £1,088,221,859 capital budget, a forecast variance of -£13,026,210. The current-year figures show £44,328,489 spent to date and £-198,594,186 variance on the current-year outturn.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, can compare how much of the in-year programme is slipping and how much total scheme cost is coming in under budget.
findings.figures: Current-year budget £242,922,675; current forecast 2026/27 £198,790,145; slippage to future years £34,033,964; total scheme forecast £1,075,195,649 against budget £1,088,221,859; forecast variance -£13,026,210; forecast variance on total outturn -£10,098,566

findings.headline: Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund lodgements: about 1,100 submitted, 117 outstanding, with grant return to be settled with DESNZ
findings.detail: Mears has submitted circa 1,100 lodgements with just over 117 still outstanding. The report says discussions with DESNZ on the final account and outstanding lodgements will determine how much grant must be returned.
findings.matters: Grant clawback on a government-funded retrofit programme with unresolved lodgements is a risk other councils running similar schemes may face.
findings.figures: circa 1,100 lodgements submitted; just over 117 outstanding
findings.quote: will impact the amount of grant that is required to be returned

findings.headline: 31 procurements approved by Directors as officer decisions under the Light Touch Regime
findings.detail: All 31 contracts relate to Adult and Children's services and were awarded under emergency procedures, with no requirement to follow the standard routes under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015.
findings.matters: A count of emergency-route awards under the Light Touch Regime is a governance indicator finance and procurement teams at other councils may compare against their own records.
findings.figures: 31 procurements; Adult and Children's services; Light Touch Regime
findings.quote: Annex A reports 31 procurements that were approved by Directors as officer decisions.

findings.headline: Three council tax debts above £50,000 written off after company insolvency
findings.detail: Three company debts exceeded the £50,000 write-off threshold, and the Cabinet is asked to note them. The debts were written off because the companies entered administration or liquidation between March 2025 and April 2026.
findings.matters: Write-offs of this size against insolvent business ratepayers show the council's exposure to company insolvency on council tax debt.
findings.figures: £236,112.22 (Meg Trading 2 Limited); £81,669.68 (Nhd Bletchley Ltd); £102,630.57 (Hornbeam Court Ltd); threshold £50,000
findings.quote: There has been Three Council Tax debts which exceeded the £50,000 threshold

findings.headline: General Fund working balance at £34.677m, £3.707m above the minimum recommended level
findings.detail: The working balance provides headroom above the minimum recommended level for unplanned expenditure. The report describes this as a buffer, though the headroom is set against forecast pressures on the Waste Recovery Park and children's placements.
findings.matters: The headroom above the minimum working balance is the figure a finance director or lender would use to judge the council's capacity to absorb unplanned pressures.
findings.figures: £34.677m working balance; £3.707m headroom above minimum
findings.quote: The current General Fund working balance is £34.677m, which provides headroom of £3.707m above than the minimum recommended level

findings.headline: Public Health Reserve forecast to fall from £3.379m to £2.330m over 2026/27
findings.detail: The Public Health drawdown of £1.049m funds one-off initiatives approved in the budget, partly offset by a planned £0.094m contribution to the reserve. The service is forecasting a £0.025m underspend.
findings.matters: A reserve being drawn down for one-off initiatives reduces the cushion available for future public health spending.
findings.figures: £3.379m reserve at 31 March 2026; £2.330m forecast at 31 March 2027; £1.049m drawdown; £1.168m one-off use
findings.quote: reducing the reserve balance from £3.379m at 31 March 2026 to £2.330m at 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: HRA forecasts a £1.796m underspend, with the surplus moved to revenue contribution to capital
findings.detail: The HRA underspend is up £1.316m since period 3, mainly from lower responsive repairs spending and vacancy savings in Asset Management. The report says the underspend will increase the revenue contribution to capital reserves, and separately flags a £1.026m Asset Management underspend.
findings.matters: Redirecting HRA surplus into capital reserves rather than holding it as an in-year saving is a choice other HRA finance teams may compare against their own business plans.
findings.figures: £1.796m HRA underspend; £1.316m improvement since P3; £1.026m Asset Management underspend
findings.quote: The underspend will be offset by an increase in the revenue contribution to capital reserves.

findings.headline: External residential children's placements at 66, against a budgeted 56
findings.detail: The average number of Children We Care For has fallen from 486 in 2025/26 to 438 in September 2026. External residential and regulated supported accommodation placements remain above budget, and the report says delivery of planned step-downs is critical to the forecast.
findings.matters: A fall in the care population is accompanied by a rise in placement complexity and cost, which is a dynamic peers with children's services budgets are likely to watch.
findings.figures: 66 external residential placements against 56 budgeted; 438 Children We Care For in September 2026, down from 486 in 2025/26
findings.quote: External Residential placements remain above budget at 66

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation forecasts a £1.736m underspend, after a £1.000m contingency was removed
findings.detail: The service is supporting 1,080 homeless households in temporary accommodation as of September, including those in HRA properties. The report attributes the underspend to Harben House, lower-cost accommodation, move-ons to private rental and swift evictions, and says the year-on-year movement reflects reduced reliance on high-cost nightly lets.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand and cost is a pressure many councils track, and the report flags the Renters' Right Act and court backlogs as risks to this forecast.
findings.figures: £1.736m underspend; £1.000m contingency removed; 1,080 households in temporary accommodation
findings.quote: The favourable movement of (£0.922m) is due to the removal of £1.000m contingency

findings.headline: Treasury forecast reports higher interest rates than budgeted, with the extra investment income moved to capital
findings.detail: The Corporate Codes and Debt Financing variance of £2.418m includes a £2m contingency release for the Waste Recovery Park and a £0.418m one-off saving. The report says extra investment income will be transferred to capital to support future pressures, particularly the Waste Recovery Park.
findings.matters: The council is directing treasury gains into capital funding, and the report flags that interest rates could rise further later in the year, which would increase borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £2.418m Corporate Codes and Debt Financing underspend; £2m contingency release; £0.418m one-off saving
findings.quote: interest rates are now higher than at the time of setting the budget

findings.headline: MK East HIF Social Infrastructure forecast £0.400m over project budget, with funding still to be identified
findings.detail: The project's overspend is £1.100m in total, of which £0.700m was incurred by the end of 2025/26 and £0.400m is now forecast in 2026/27. The overspend is attributed to temporary power, water and drainage arrangements. The report says additional funding will need to come from future tariff receipts.
findings.matters: An overspend on an infrastructure scheme with no identified funding source, to be met from tariff receipts, is a pressure other councils running similar housing infrastructure projects may face.
findings.figures: £1.100m total project overspend; £0.700m incurred by end of 2025/26; £0.400m forecast in 2026/27
findings.quote: Additional funding will need to be identified from future tariff receipts, and the necessary approvals sought.

findings.headline: Capital Programme forecasts a £44.133m underspend, of which £34.034m slips to later years
findings.detail: Against a £242.923m budget, the forecast underspend leaves a £10.099m in-year underspend after slippage. The report lists HRA asset management, Serpentine Demolition, Agora and Lakes Estate Health Facility among the slipped schemes.
findings.matters: A slippage figure this large, against a capital budget of this size, shows how far the in-year capital programme is being rephased into later years.
findings.figures: £44.133m underspend; £242.923m budget; £34.034m slippage; £10.099m in-year underspend
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is forecasting underspend of (£44.133m), of which £34.034m is planned to slip to later years

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant carry-forward forecast at £1.623m against £2.514m budgeted, with a High Needs deficit of £0.376m
findings.detail: The DSG carry-forward is forecast to fall by £0.891m against budget, mainly from an Early Years DfE adjustment and additional provider payments. The High Needs block is forecast to overspend by £1.6m in year, partly offset by £1.2m of reserves, leaving a year-end deficit of £0.376m.
findings.matters: A High Needs deficit that is partly covered by reserves is a pattern finance officers at other councils will recognise, and the SEND Reform Plan approval is still pending.
findings.figures: £2.514m budgeted carry-forward; £1.623m forecast carry-forward; £0.891m adverse movement; £0.376m High Needs deficit; £1.6m in-year overspend; £1.2m reserves
findings.quote: a deficit is expected at year end of £0.376m

findings.headline: £9.476m of a £9.982m savings target is forecast to be achieved in 2026/27
findings.detail: The report shows 95% of the in-year savings target is forecast to be delivered this year, with a further 4% delivered next year and 1% judged undeliverable and under review for the 2027/28 budget.
findings.matters: The split between in-year, slipped and undeliverable savings indicates how far the MTFP savings programme is holding up under delivery.
findings.figures: £9.476m (95%) forecast in year; £0.447m (4%) next year; £0.059m (1%) undeliverable; £9.982m total target
findings.quote: £9.476m (95%) are forecast to be achieved in year, £0.447m (4%) will be delivered next year

findings.headline: Environment & Property forecasts a £4.948m overspend, with the Waste Recovery Park pressure at £6m
findings.detail: The Waste Recovery Park has reduced performance and is forecast at £6m of financial pressure, of which £2m is met by releasing contingency. SUEZ took over operation of the facility on 1 October, and the report describes the pressure as a significant risk to the General Fund.
findings.matters: Council-run waste infrastructure whose operating costs have transferred in-house is a pressure other councils with similar contracts may face, and the report ties the forecast to plant availability and waste and electricity prices.
findings.figures: £6m Waste Recovery Park pressure; £2m met from contingency; £4.948m Environment & Property overspend
findings.quote: The Waste Recovery Park has experienced reduced performance, resulting in financial pressure forecast at £6m.

findings.headline: General Fund forecasts a £4.813m underspend against its £332.797m budget at period 6
findings.detail: The Cabinet report states the General Fund is forecasting a net underspend, with the largest variances in Adult Social Care, Children's Services and Corporate Codes and Debt Financing, offset by an Environment & Property overspend.
findings.matters: A forecast net underspend of this size, set against a service overspend in the same period, shows how the council is currently balancing its budget across services.
findings.figures: £4.813m underspend; £332.797m budget; Environment & Property £4.948m overspend
findings.quote: The General Fund Services are currently forecasting an underspend of (£4.813m).

findings.headline: Capital Strategy is being reviewed and will return to Cabinet in February 2027, with a focus on schemes that deliver financial returns or reduce asset lifecycle costs.
findings.detail: The paper says expected pressures on the revenue budget over the medium term mean prioritisation will favour schemes with financial returns or that reduce lifecycle costs. The updated strategy will set out significant future infrastructure investment requirements.
findings.matters: A stated shift in capital prioritisation toward income-generating or cost-reducing schemes is a policy direction that finance directors and lenders would track.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: The Capital Strategy is currently being reviewed and will be presented to Cabinet in February 2027.

findings.headline: Projects not yet in the capital programme are described as increasing the overall funding shortfall, and a pipeline has been developed for them.
findings.detail: The paper says several projects will need funding in future but are not yet included. Some still need further work, and others require funding before they can be considered for the main programme.
findings.matters: A council that has a named funding shortfall with an unfunded pipeline signals future borrowing or grant pressure, which is relevant to lenders and to peers planning their own capital programmes.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: There are a number of projects which are not currently included within the capital programme and will require funding in the future, therefore increasing the overall funding shortfall.

findings.headline: Tariff 2a is expected to generate £240m including indexation until 2049, and Tariff 2b around £103m excluding indexation until 2044.
findings.detail: Tariff 2a funding has been allocated to the Health Hub (£9.9m) and the H10 Bletcham Way connection to Church Farm (£14.5m). Tariff 2b covers around 3,000 homes in South East Milton Keynes, with contributions from Woburn Sands starting to arrive and infrastructure works progressing.
findings.matters: Long-running developer-contribution programmes with indexation shape a council's future capital capacity and the timing of infrastructure delivery.
findings.figures: Tariff 2a total £240m including indexation, to 2049; Tariff 2a allocations £9.9m and £14.5m; Tariff 2b approximately £103m excluding indexation, to 2044; approximately 3,000 homes
findings.quote: Total contributions over the life of the programme are expected to be £240m, including indexation, with the programme running until 2049.

findings.headline: Tariff 1 long stop date is 2031, with a further five years to 2036 for the Western Expansion Area, which accounts for around a third of the Tariff by value.
findings.detail: The paper says most of the delivery programme must be completed by 2031. It notes that the Western Expansion Area's planning permission has recently been extended, giving the Council five years beyond 2031 to invest those contributions. A Tariff Risk Reserve is held for shortfalls in contributions or cost overruns.
findings.matters: Deadlines for spending developer contributions create a risk of forfeiture or cost pressure, and holding a risk reserve is a specific mitigation other councils with similar tariff arrangements would compare.
findings.figures: long stop date 2031; a further 5 years beyond 2031 for the Western Expansion Area, around a third of the Tariff by value
findings.quote: The current long stop date of the Tariff is 2031 for the majority of the delivery programme to be completed.

findings.headline: Tariff 1 is forecast to collect over £311m in developer contributions over its lifetime, with £97.280m of Tariff allocations to Council projects included in the capital programme.
findings.detail: The Tariff covers the expansion areas of the former Urban Development Area and funds 18 portfolios, 11 of which the Council delivers. Allocations include cash and works in kind, and new requests are considered project by project.
findings.matters: A large developer-contribution stream that is committed to specific infrastructure shows how a council's capital programme depends on S106 and Tariff income rather than its own borrowing.
findings.figures: over £311m in developer contributions over the Tariff's lifetime; £97.280m Tariff allocations to Council projects; 18 portfolios, 11 Council-delivered
findings.quote: the Council will collect over £311m in developer contributions over its lifetime, which will be re-invested in a Programme of strategic and local infrastructure covering a total of 18 ‘portfolios’, 11 of which are delivered through the Council.

findings.headline: Short-term investment income above the draft budget will be used to contribute to financing the capital programme, to cover possible delays in receipts.
findings.detail: The paper says that investment gains from current interest rates above the level in the draft budget will support programme financing. The section 151 Officer will decide when funding is released once funding is confirmed.
findings.matters: Using interest income above budget to bridge capital financing is a mechanism other finance teams could compare against their own treasury-to-capital arrangements.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper
findings.quote: any short-term gains on investment income, achieved by current interest rates, over and above, that built into the draft budget will be used to contribute to the financing of the programme.

findings.headline: Draft 2026/27 capital programme assumes £50.3m of capital receipts from land sales, with timing not certain.
findings.detail: The paper says receipts are forecast from latest data but depend on completing land sales. It states that delays or lower receipts may require new projects to be scrutinised or existing schemes to be delayed.
findings.matters: Reliance on land-sale receipts for financing creates timing risk that other councils with similar disposal programmes would also need to manage.
findings.figures: £50.3m of receipts assumed in the draft 2026/27 capital programme
findings.quote: A total of £50.3m of receipts are assumed within the financing of the draft 2026/27 capital programme.

findings.headline: Capital programme shows a cumulative £36.663m surplus of resources over 2027/28 to 2031/32, all of it ring-fenced to Education, Highways or Local Transport.
findings.detail: Table 1 shows resources exceeding planned expenditure across the period. The paper states that none of the surplus is unallocated, so there is no funding for new capital projects outside the ring-fenced streams within the current programme.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, would want to know that an apparent surplus in the capital position may not be available to fund new schemes or cover shortfalls elsewhere.
findings.figures: £36.663m cumulative surplus (Table 1, 2031/32); £37.352m surplus in 2027/28; £2.556m deficit in 2028/29
findings.quote: all £36.663m of this funding is either Education , Highways or Local Transport fund specific, meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects outside of this funding within the current Programme.

findings.headline: Two equality impact assessment areas are rated Amber: Children’s Social Care placement and care budget reductions, and School Travel.
findings.detail: The paper says no areas are rated Red. The two Amber areas need further assessment and mitigation before final decisions are taken.
findings.matters: Budget reductions in children's care that remain Amber before final decisions carry delivery risk for other councils making similar reductions.
findings.figures: 34 proposals grouped into 12 assessment areas; 3 Green, 7 Green-Amber, 2 Amber, 0 Red
findings.quote: The Amber areas relate to Children’s Social Care placement and care budget reductions and School Travel

findings.headline: Funding for 2027/28 and 2028/29 was announced in the three-year settlement and is unchanged from the February 2026 figures; funding from 2029/30 is uncertain.
findings.detail: The paper assumes Revenue Support Grant rises 2% in each of the two following years. A further three-year settlement is expected from 2029/30, but its position is uncertain.
findings.matters: The 2029/30 funding position is unknown, and a lender or finance officer needs to see how much of the medium term rests on it.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant assumed +2% in each of the two following years
findings.quote: Funding for 2027/28 and 2028/29 was announced as part of the three-year settlement and remains unchanged from the figures presented in February 26.

findings.headline: Capital programme refreshed to add essential projects and those with ring-fenced funding, with a potential funding gap assessed for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.detail: Capital resources are described as challenged. The Pipeline programme was updated to show the potential funding gap and the choices to be made. The paper gives no figure for the gap.
findings.matters: A council stating that it has limited its capital programme to secured or essential schemes is a signal other finance officers will compare with their own choices.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: Capital resources are challenged, and this has resulted in only essential projects, or those with ring fenced funding being added to the programme.

findings.headline: 90% of housing stock surveyed within the last 18 months, with results to date not highlighting any major investment requirements.
findings.detail: The stock condition survey was accelerated from a three-year plan of one-third a year. Surveys are not complete, so additional investment needs could still be identified, and the capital programme would be revised in the final budget if material issues are found.
findings.matters: Stock condition on a non-traditional build stock is a material capital risk for any housing borrower, and the survey result is a relevant data point.
findings.figures: 90% of housing stock surveyed within the last 18 months
findings.quote: Results to date have not highlighted any major investment requirements.

findings.headline: HRA business plan refreshed to a balanced position over the medium term, with future planned borrowing within the target Interest Cover Ratio threshold.
findings.detail: The HRA business plan was refreshed at the end of quarter 2. The paper also proposes a 4.5% + £1.00 rent increase for tenants and a 3.5% garage rent increase, with garage rents frozen since 2024.
findings.matters: Interest cover against a target threshold is a core test for lenders to a HRA borrower.
findings.figures: rent increase 4.5% + £1.00; garage rent increase 3.5%
findings.quote: The Council now has a balanced position over the medium term and future planned borrowing is within the target Interest Cover Ratio threshold.

findings.headline: Provisional Band D Council Tax of £1,939.72, a 4.99% increase (2.99% core plus 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept), for consultation.
findings.detail: The provisional Band D figure is for the Milton Keynes element and is subject to consultation and the final settlement.
findings.matters: The 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept is a specific lever that finance directors elsewhere will compare against their own precept choices.
findings.figures: Band D £1,939.72; increase 4.99% (2.99% core + 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept)
findings.quote: a 4.99% increase on the previous year (2.99% core increase plus a 2.00% Adult Social Care Precept)

findings.headline: Council is not using reserves to balance the base budget.
findings.detail: The paper states that reserves have been reviewed as part of the 2027/28 draft budget. Council Plan item 65 commits to a balanced 2027/28 budget that does not rely on reserves for day-to-day spending.
findings.matters: Reserves-free balancing is a stated commitment, and other councils and lenders assess reserve dependence in the same way.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: Currently we are not using reserves to balance the base budget

findings.headline: A 2027/28 budget gap of £1.631m forecast in February 2026 has been offset by budget reductions, income proposals and higher Business Rates income.
findings.detail: The paper says pressures and higher than anticipated inflation have been offset by services' budget reductions and income proposals and an increase in Business Rates income.
findings.matters: A finance director will want to see how a February gap was closed, including the reliance on Business Rates income.
findings.figures: February 2026 forecast 2027/28 gap £1.631m
findings.quote: In February 2026 we had forecasted that the budget gap for 2027/28 was £1.631m

findings.headline: Delegated authority is requested for final 2027/28 school funding arrangements because the DfE's APT deadline in January 2027 falls before the council's budget is formally ratified.
findings.detail: The Director of Children's Services would approve the funding formula, high needs and early years arrangements in consultation with the Cabinet Member and the Director of Finance and Resources. Schools Forum has a decision-making role at its meeting on 14 January 2027.
findings.matters: A deadline that falls before budget ratification is a timing mismatch other councils submitting APT returns may have to manage the same way.
findings.figures: APT submission deadline January 2027; Schools Forum meeting 14 January 2027
findings.quote: The deadline for submitting the final schools budget allocation via the authority proforma tool (APT) to the DfE is in January 2027 which, is before the formal ratification of our budget takes place.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 General Fund draft budget is balanced, with a forecast base budget gap of £5.547m by 2030/31.
findings.detail: Table 1 shows a nil cumulative gap for 2027/28, a surplus of £3.392m in 2028/29, a gap of £0.066m in 2029/30 and a gap of £5.547m in 2030/31.
findings.matters: The gap is shown to grow to 2030/31 even with 2027/28 balanced, which lenders and finance directors will weigh against the medium-term plan.
findings.quote: The 2027/28 Draft General Fund budget is currently balanced, with a forecast base budget gap of £5.547m by 2030/31.

findings.headline: The schools block growth fund is expected to face a pressure again, and the council has consulted all schools on options to manage the shortfall.
findings.detail: The paper says the pressure on the growth fund is expected as in previous years. It does not give a £ value for the shortfall.
findings.matters: Growth fund shortfalls are a recurring DSG pressure at councils with expanding school places, and the consultation options show how one authority is responding.
findings.figures: No £ value for the growth fund shortfall is stated in this annex
findings.quote: it is expected that there will be a pressure on the growth fund (as in previous years)

findings.headline: Indicative DSG funding for 2027/28 has not yet been announced, the third consecutive year of delay.
findings.detail: The paper notes that indicative funding, previously shared in July before budget setting, is late again. The final budget in February 2027 will include a full DSG update.
findings.matters: Repeated delay to DSG allocations limits how far finance officers can plan High Needs spending ahead of budget setting.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: This is the third year that there has been a delay in receiving our indicative funding

findings.headline: Schools Forum members did not approve a proposed 0.5% transfer from the schools block to the high needs block, so a disapplication request has been sent to the DfE.
findings.detail: A transfer request was put to a vote in November 2026 after a consultation with schools. The DfE is expected to confirm the outcome of the disapplication request before the APT is submitted in January.
findings.matters: Councils facing the same high needs pressure may consider a schools block transfer, and the outcome of a disapplication request shows how the DfE handles one that Schools Forum has rejected.
findings.figures: 0.5% of the schools block proposed for transfer to the high needs block
findings.quote: but this was not approved by forum members.

findings.headline: Council was not eligible for the High Needs Stability Grant, as it held an overall DSG surplus balance at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says local authorities with an overall DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 received grant equal to 90% of their deficit balance, with a national total of £5.812bn. Milton Keynes had no overall deficit and so received nothing.
findings.matters: Councils with DSG deficits at the same date received grant, so the eligibility test is directly relevant to any council weighing its own DSG position.
findings.figures: 90% of deficit balance; national grant total £5.812bn
findings.quote: Milton Keynes City Council was not eligible for funding as it held an overall DSG surplus balance at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Council has submitted a disapplication request to transfer 0.5% of the Schools Block (approximately £1.515m) to the High Needs Block, after Schools Forum did not support the proposal.
findings.detail: The transfer requires DfE approval through a disapplication request. The final High Needs position, including the outcome of the request, is to be reported in the Final Budget report.
findings.matters: Schools Forum declining a transfer and the council going to DfE over its head is a governance position other councils facing the same pressure will need to understand.
findings.figures: 0.5% of Schools Block allocation; approximately £1.515m
findings.quote: the Council has submitted a disapplication request to the DfE seeking approval to transfer 0.5% of the Schools Block allocation (approximately £1.515m) to the High Needs Block, following Schools Forum’s decision not to support the proposal.

findings.headline: The High Needs Block Action Plan has delivered "substantial savings" to date, according to the paper.
findings.detail: The action plan was put in place to manage sustained increases in high needs demand and expenditure. The paper does not give a £ figure for the savings delivered.
findings.matters: A finance officer at another council can compare the type of high needs action plan and the savings reported against their own demand-management work.
findings.figures: No £ value for savings is stated in this annex
findings.quote: this has delivered substantial savings to date

findings.matters: A savings programme that replaces completed projects with new ones to close a stated gap is a mechanism peer finance teams and lenders will want to see evidenced in figures.
findings.figures: None given in this paper
findings.quote: As projects are completed or closed, additional projects are added to ensure that sufficient savings can be achieved to address the budget gap.

findings.matters: Section 151 formal action is one of the markers that signals financial governance stress, so its absence is a reference point for peers and lenders.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know how a chain of disclaimed and modified opinions traces back to a predecessor auditor's incomplete 2022/23 work.

KPMG says its conclusions will be discussed with the Council before the audit report is signed.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: Total audit fees for 2025/26 are £515,028, down from £525,182 in 2024/25, as the 2024/25 build back assurance variation of £35,185 does not recur.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: Two misstatements were corrected in the 2025/26 accounts: a £871k year-end accrual and a £1.678m uplift to the Waste Recovery Plant valuation.
findings.detail: The £871k relates to expenditure incurred before 31 March 2026 that was not accrued, which management corrected by recognising the expenditure and creditor. The £1.678m reflects capital works on the Waste Recovery Plant, including boiler and furnace works, that had not been fully reflected in the original DRC valuation. The paper says the adjustments have no impact on general fund balances.
findings.matters: A finance director can see how a cut-off error and a valuation omission were caught and corrected before sign-off, and a lender can see that these corrections did not change the general fund position.
findings.figures: Cut-off accrual: £871k; Waste Recovery Plant revaluation: £1.678m
findings.quote: resulting in an understatement of expenditure and creditors by £871k.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: KPMG reports one uncorrected misstatement: the Linford Wood investment property is overstated by £1.965m, against a total investment property fair value of £187.4m.
findings.detail: The overstatement arises from the net initial yield assumption used in the valuation. KPMG’s valuation specialists considered a higher yield appropriate, which gives a lower fair value, and the difference has been left uncorrected. The paper says the misstatement affects the deficit for the year by 1.9m (3%) and total assets by (1.9)m (0.08%) on its materiality table. Almost all of the investment property portfolio is farmland held for development.
findings.matters: A finance director at a council holding development land as investment property can see how a yield assumption affected fair value, and a lender can see that the auditor’s own valuation view differs from management’s on a single asset.
findings.figures: Uncorrected overstatement: £1.965m; investment property fair value: £187.4m; deficit for the year effect: £1.9m (3%); total assets effect: £(1.9)m (0.08%)
findings.quote: The misstatement relates to the overstatement of the Linford Wood investment property by £1.965m

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: KPMG did not identify any risk of significant weakness in the Council’s value for money arrangements, and found no significant weaknesses in any of the three domains.
findings.detail: The paper sets out the value for money outcome for financial sustainability, governance, and improving economy, efficiency and effectiveness. Each domain is recorded as having no significant risks identified and no significant weaknesses identified. Full detail is in the Auditor’s Annual Report.
findings.matters: A finance director at a council with comparable pressures can see how the auditor assessed financial sustainability in the same three domains, and a lender can see the auditor reported no significant weakness.
findings.figures: Value for money domains with no significant risks: 3 of 3; no significant weaknesses: 3 of 3
findings.quote: As noted on the right, we did not identify any risks of a significant weakness in the Council’s arrangements to secure value for money.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: No control deficiencies are outstanding, and the one prior-year recommendation, on identifying related parties, has been implemented.
findings.detail: KPMG identified a related-party control deficiency in 2024/25, where Companies House searches found directorships not captured through the declarations of interest process. In 2025/26 KPMG followed up and is satisfied the recommendation has been completed. The paper records zero significant control deficiencies for the year.
findings.matters: A finance director can point to a closed control recommendation from the prior audit, and a lender can see that no control deficiencies are carried into this year.
findings.figures: Significant control deficiencies: 0; prior-year recommendations: 1 total, 1 implemented, 0 outstanding
findings.quote: There are therefore no control deficiencies outstanding to report.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex B - Milton Keynes City Council - ISA260 report 2025-26
findings.headline: KPMG expects to issue an unmodified auditor’s report on the 2025/26 accounts, after a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 and a qualified opinion for 2024/25.
findings.detail: The paper says the rebuilding-assurance work and a further year of audit work allowed KPMG to conclude on the accounts. It records a disclaimer for 2023/24 issued to meet the statutory backstop, and a qualified opinion for 2024/25 over grants received in advance and opening net assets. The report is still subject to outstanding matters before signature.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with a backlog of disclaimed or qualified years can compare how the rebuilding-assurance process concluded here, and a lender can see the audit opinion history move from disclaimer to qualified to unmodified.
findings.figures: 2023/24: disclaimer of opinion; 2024/25: qualified opinion; 2025/26: unmodified opinion expected
findings.quote: We expect to issue an unmodified Auditor’s Report.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quality Assurance Action Plan Annex B - Quality Assurance Improvement Plan (002)
findings.headline: Milton Keynes internal audit strategy, with a 30/09/2026 action date, is recorded as "InProgress" and not yet complete.
findings.detail: The plan found the Service had no strategy setting out its vision and objectives. The update states a strategy is being developed, and the timetable for reviewing it is to follow once the strategy is produced.
findings.matters: A council's internal audit strategy sets how its audit coverage is directed, so a finance director comparing audit arrangements would see that this one is still in development at the 30/09/2026 date.

findings.quote: InProgress- a Strategy is being developed

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quality Assurance Action Plan Annex B - Quality Assurance Improvement Plan (002)
findings.headline: Chief Internal Auditor's private meetings with the Audit Committee chair and vice chairs, due 28/02/2026, are now "Agreed and to be introduced during 2027-28 meetings."
findings.detail: The finding was that meetings between the Chief Internal Auditor and External Auditor and the Audit Committee chair and vice chairs, without senior management present, had not been maintained. The action was to reinstate them, with a 28/02/2026 date, and the update now places their introduction in 2027-28.
findings.matters: The date for restoring direct access between internal audit and the Audit Committee chair has moved by more than a year, which a finance director elsewhere could look at when judging independence arrangements.

findings.quote: Agreed and to be introduced during 2027-28 meetings.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quality Assurance Action Plan Annex B - Quality Assurance Improvement Plan (002)
findings.headline: Milton Keynes internal audit records trainee auditors recruited and an external contract for specialist audits, marked complete against a 28/02/26 action date.
findings.detail: The plan's finding on internal audit resourcing was raised at several Audit Committee meetings, with the Committee challenging the tight resourcing position. The progress update records trainee recruitment, a training programme and an external provider contract for specialist audits.
findings.matters: A finance director at Milton Keynes or a peer council can compare how an internal audit team with limited staffing has addressed capacity, and whether external providers are used to cover specialist work.

findings.quote: COMPLETE -Trainee auditors have been recruited and a training programme and other support put in place to expedite their experience and audit skills.

findings.detail: KPMG is required to perform procedures on the Council's consolidation return for WGA, but is unable to confirm it has concluded its work in this area because the NAO has not finished its own WGA audit.
