findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: KPMG issued an unmodified opinion on the financial statements and identified no significant weaknesses in value for money arrangements
findings.detail: The auditor found no significant issues in the three key financial statement risks it reported (investment property valuation, management override, and post-retirement benefit obligations). No Public Interest Report, advisory notice, judicial review or Schedule 7 recommendation was made.
findings.matters: A clean opinion with no value for money weaknesses and no statutory recommendations is the position a lender or peer finance team checks first.
findings.figures: Three key financial statement risks with no significant issues; no Schedule 7 recommendations
findings.quote: We identified no significant weaknesses in respect of the arrangements the Council has put in place to secure economy, efficiency, and effectiveness in the use of its resources.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The MTFP identifies a £14.139m cumulative funding gap by 2029/30, and the Council has set a balanced 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The Council says it is responding through savings, income generation and its 'Changing Because We Have To' programme, and that further action is required for the remaining medium-term gap. The auditor's September 2025 forecast showed a £23.623m base budget gap by 2029/30, with £4.558m arising in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council with a balanced year-one budget and a stated medium-term gap of £14.139m is a position peers and lenders compare against their own multi-year plans.
findings.figures: £14.139m cumulative funding gap by 2029/30; £23.623m base budget gap forecast in September 2025; £4.558m in 2026/27
findings.quote: the MTFP identifies a £14.139m cumulative funding gap by 2029/30, reflecting continued demand-led, inflationary and service pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The Council retained a £6.7m DSG surplus, with pressures still within the High Needs block
findings.detail: The paper notes that the Council has operated a DSG surplus in both the current and prior year, unlike many peers, though it reports that high needs costs were expected to exceed government funding.
findings.matters: A council with a DSG surplus while peers carry deficits is a comparison a finance director at another council will want to understand, and the High Needs pressure is the risk that could reverse it.
findings.figures: £6.7m DSG surplus
findings.quote: The Council also retained a £6.7m DSG surplus, although pressures remain within the High Needs block.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Overall reserves rose from £247.608m to £258.238m during 2025/26, with the General Fund working balance at £34.678m
findings.detail: Of the £2.994m General Fund underspend, £2.000m went to the Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve, £0.900m was approved for refurbishment works, and £0.094m went to the General Fund balance. The paper states the working balance is above the Council's minimum recommended level.
findings.matters: The split of the underspend between reserves and refurbishment shows how a council used a year-end surplus, and the reserves rise is a figure lenders and peers track.
findings.figures: £247.608m to £258.238m total reserves; £34.678m General Fund working balance; £2.000m to Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve; £0.900m refurbishment; £0.094m to General Fund
findings.quote: Overall reserves increased from £247.608m to £258.238m during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure was £90.1m below the £233.4m programme for 2025/26, with £70.3m slipped into 2026/27
findings.detail: The auditor identifies the capital underspend as a factor relevant to the value for money assessment of planned investment delivery.
findings.matters: A slippage of £70.3m out of a £233.4m programme is a measure a finance director can compare against their own capital delivery rate.
findings.figures: £90.1m below £233.4m programme; £70.3m slippage into 2026/27
findings.quote: Capital expenditure was £90.1m below the £233.4m programme, including £70.3m of slippage into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: The General Fund closed 2025/26 with a £2.994m underspend against a £283.800m budget requirement
findings.detail: Children's Services overspent by £6.299m, largely from high-cost external residential placements, and this was offset by a £6.261m underspend in Adult Social Care plus underspends elsewhere. The HRA separately reported a £7.655m underspend.
findings.matters: The gap between a children's overspend and an adult social care underspend of similar size shows how the General Fund outturn depended on offsetting service variances.
findings.figures: £2.994m General Fund underspend; £283.800m budget requirement; £6.299m Children's Services overspend; £6.261m Adult Social Care underspend; £7.655m HRA underspend

findings.paper_title: 2025-26 Statement of Accounts Annex A - Milton Keynes City Council - Auditors Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Milton Keynes City Council delivered £8.629m (86%) of its £10.071m savings target in 2025/26, with £1.120m expected in 2026/27 and £0.322m assessed as undeliverable
findings.detail: The savings target included £0.573m carried forward from 2024/25 alongside £9.498m approved for 2025/26. The undeliverable portion was amended through the 2026/27 budget rather than left as an unfunded gap.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the 86% delivery rate and the way unachieved savings were carried forward or written out of the budget.

findings.quote: Of this, £8.629m (86%) was delivered during 2025/26, £1.120m is expected to be delivered in 2026/27 and £0.322m was assessed as undeliverable and amended through the 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Quality Assurance Action Plan Annex A - IA Self Assessment Summary Report
findings.headline: Standard 13.6 Work Program is rated 'Does Not Conform' in the self-assessment, the only standard in the paper with that rating for an engagement-level process.
findings.detail: Standard 13.6 sits under Principle 13 (planning engagements systematically), which is rated partially conforming overall. Other Principle 13 standards are rated generally conforming or partially conforming. The paper refers to separate appendices for the detailed findings and action plans.
findings.matters: A non-conforming engagement work programme standard affects how individual audits are planned, which is the work a finance director relies on when reading audit opinions on council spending and controls.

findings.matters: An internal audit function without a conforming strategy is a concrete gap that a finance director, here or elsewhere, could ask to see closed in the next audit plan cycle.

findings.headline: Principle 8, on the board overseeing the internal audit function, is assessed as 'Partially Conforms', with Standard 8.2 Resources and Standard 8.3 Quality both partially conforming.
findings.detail: The Principle 8 rating sits alongside Standard 8.1 (Board Interaction) and Standard 8.4 (External Quality Assessment), both generally conforming. The partial ratings concern resources and quality, which are the board's oversight responsibilities under the Standards.
findings.matters: Resourcing and quality of internal audit are board-level oversight matters, so a finance director at this or another council will see where the self-assessment places responsibility on the audit committee.
findings.figures: Standard 8.1 Generally Conforms; Standard 8.2 Partially Conforms; Standard 8.3 Partially Conforms; Standard 8.4 Generally conforms

findings.detail: The self-assessment covers Domains II to V of the 2024 Standards. Three principles are rated partially conforming: Principle 8 (board oversight), Principle 9 (strategic planning) and Principle 13 (planning engagements). The paper states that 'Assessor judgement will be needed' on how Standard-level results aggregate.

findings.paper_title: Annex A Calculation of Council Tax Base 2027_28
findings.headline: Milton Keynes' 2027/28 council tax base is 103,062.64 Band D equivalent properties, up from 101,826.87 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper sets out the 2027/28 base after a provision for valuation change and non-collection, then deducts the impact of council tax reductions. The impact of reductions is (8,106.76) in 2027/28 against (8,202.35) in 2026/27.
findings.matters: The tax base multiplied by the Band D charge sets the council tax income the council can budget for, so a larger base in 2027/28 changes the income assumption in its budget.
findings.figures: Tax base 2027/28: 103,062.64 Band D equivalent properties; 2026/27: 101,826.87 Band D equivalent properties. Impact of Council Tax Reductions 2027/28: (8,106.76) Band D equivalent properties; 2026/27: (8,202.35) Band D equivalent properties. Total properties 2027/28: 128,723.00; 2026/27: 127,272.00.
findings.quote: Impact of Council Tax Reductions (8,106.76)

findings.headline: Council Tax income for 2027/28 is set at £199.913m, an increase of £11.785m on 2026/27 precept income, of which £9.502m relates to the proposed 4.99% Band D increase.
findings.detail: The paper converts the tax base into an income figure for Milton Keynes City Council. It also sets the provision for non-collection at 0.80%, giving an expected collection rate of 99.20%, and notes that an overly high collection rate could create a collection fund deficit affecting future budgets.
findings.matters: The income figure and the assumed collection rate are the basis of the council's council tax line in its budget, and a collection rate set too high is the risk the paper itself names.
findings.figures: £199.913m Council Tax income (2027/28); £11.785m increase on 2026/27 precept income; £9.502m of increase relating to 4.99% Band D increase; 0.80% provision for non-collection; 99.20% expected collection rate
findings.quote: This would result in Council Tax income of £199.913m for Milton Keynes City Council

findings.headline: Milton Keynes expects its Council Tax Base to grow by 1,146.34 Band D equivalent properties in 2027/28, against 1,170.04 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the growth to Milton Keynes being a high growth area and gives it as a figure based on future estimates. It also states that the proposed tax base of 103,062.64 Band D equivalents is an increase of 1,235.77 on 2026/27.
findings.matters: The tax base sets the council tax income the council can raise from growth in properties, so a finance director here or at a peer council would compare the forecast growth rate with their own.
findings.figures: 1,146.34 Band D equivalent properties (2027/28); 1,170.04 Band D equivalent properties (26/27); 103,062.64 Band D equivalent properties total; 1,235.77 Band D equivalent properties increase on 2026/27
findings.quote: expected to grow by a total of 1,146.34 Band D equivalent properties (1,170.04 in 26/27)

findings.headline: Quarter 1 2026/27 General Fund underspend of £4.832m forecast, of which £1.3m is one-off and approximately £3.5m is ongoing
findings.detail: The Quarter 1 2026/27 Budget Monitoring Report forecasts a General Fund underspend of £4.832m against the 2026/27 approved budget. Of this, £1.3m relates to one-off items, meaning the ongoing position shows an underspend of approximately £3.5m. The council states it has reflected the ongoing impact of this favourable position within the MTFO where appropriate, suggesting it has been cautious about assuming in-year savings are available to support the medium-term outlook.
findings.matters: Shows whether budget assumptions are realistic and whether the council is generating in-year savings that can support forward planning; indicates budget setting may be prudent but also questions whether forecast is still valid
findings.figures: £4.832m total underspend Quarter 1 2026/27; £1.3m one-off items; approximately £3.5m ongoing
findings.quote: The Quarter 1 2026/27 Budget Monitoring Report currently forecasts a General Fund underspend of (£4.832m), of which £1.3m relates to one-off items.

findings.headline: High Needs Block (dedicated schools grant) expected to go into deficit in 2026/27; impact on General Fund unclear pending government announcements
findings.detail: The council expects the High Needs Block (funding for special educational provision) to move into deficit in 2026/27. The impact on the General Fund is currently unquantified and depends on government policy. The council is awaiting announcements on whether there will be any financial support or whether councils will be required to absorb such deficits from their main budgets. This represents a known but unquantified financial risk to the General Fund in 2026/27 and potentially beyond.
findings.matters: A known emerging deficit in the education budget that could require General Fund support; outcome depends on government announcements, creating uncertainty for medium-term planning
findings.figures: High Needs Block expected into deficit 2026/27; impact on General Fund currently unquantified
findings.quote: High Needs Block - is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27 - Impact on GF Budget is currently unclear as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support.

findings.headline: Savings programme expanded to £12.572m over four years (increase of £9.679m from February) but £3.840m further savings still unidentified
findings.detail: Milton Keynes has identified £9.679m of additional savings since February 2026, bringing total planned savings to £12.572m over the four-year period. The main vehicle is the 'Changing Because We Have To' (CBWHT) programme focused on productivity improvements and ensuring work is undertaken in-house only where appropriate. However, the updated forecast shows that even with these savings identified, a further £3.840m in savings must be found by 31 March 2031. Directors are currently developing detailed business cases for these additional measures.
findings.matters: Shows significant savings programme delivery but also that material unidentified savings are still required; raises questions about remaining deliverability and how the final gap will be closed
findings.figures: £12.572m total savings 2027/28-2030/31; £9.679m increase since February 2026; £3.840m further savings needed by 31/3/2031
findings.quote: The MTFO currently includes savings totalling £12.572m between 2027/28 and 2030/31. Based on the updated financial projection further savings of £3.840m are needed by 31/3/2031.

findings.headline: Utility cost inflation forecast at 15.1% for 2027/28, versus 5% annual increase assumed in February 2026
findings.detail: The February 2026 MTFP assumed utility costs would rise 5% annually from 2027/28 onwards. Updated forecasts from treasury advisors now indicate 15.1% inflation for 2027/28, before returning to 5% in subsequent years. This adds £0.317m to the 2027/28 base budget and reflects current energy market conditions. The large variance from assumption suggests exposure to external cost pressures and raises questions about other inflation forecasts used in the plan.
findings.matters: Reveals how external market factors can significantly shift budget assumptions mid-planning cycle; suggests inflation forecasts carry material downside risk and other assumptions may also miss
findings.figures: 15.1% utility inflation assumed 2027/28 vs 5% in February forecast; adds £0.317m to 2027/28
findings.quote: The February 2026 MTFP assumed a 5% annual increase in gas and electricity prices from 2027/28 onwards. Updated forecasts now indicate a 15.1% increase in 2027/28

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract with new operator from October 2026 adds £2.4m annual base budget pressure from 2027/28
findings.detail: The procurement for the waste recovery park has concluded with a new contractor commencing October 2026. Following tender conclusion, projected operational costs now exceed the previous £1.9m allowance by £0.5m, resulting in a £2.4m annual base budget pressure from 2027/28 onwards. The council notes actual net costs will depend on tonnages, recyclate prices, energy market prices, and plant running costs, creating exposure to external market factors and operator performance.
findings.matters: A new fixed annual cost commitment that persists through the planning period, with performance and market exposure; shows how major infrastructure contracts create structural budget dependencies
findings.figures: £2.4m annual pressure from 2027/28; £0.5m higher than previously estimated; contract commences October 2026
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of the tender and extension of the current contractor we now expect costs to be about £0.500m higher than previously projected and we have included this £2.400m as a base budget pressure from 2027/28.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements at 16% of looked-after children, targeting 12% through lower-cost commissioning to deliver £4.272m saving
findings.detail: Milton Keynes places 16% of looked-after children in external residential settings, significantly above the local authority average of 12%. The MTFO includes a saving of £4.272m dependent on successfully reducing this to 14% by 2027/28 and 12% by 2028/29, through sourcing lower-cost placements and placing children nearer to the city. The council is managing this through in-house recruitment and commissioning, but notes the difficulty in recruiting carers and the execution risk if demand assumptions do not hold.
findings.matters: A specific £4.272m saving whose failure would leave a material unfunded pressure; demonstrates both the structural challenge of high-cost placements and the council's service redesign strategy
findings.figures: 16% external residential placement rate vs 12% LA average; £4.272m projected saving from reduction to 12% by 2028/29
findings.quote: Currently 16% of LAC are placed in external residential settings. The MTFP assumes that MKCC will reduce this in line with the LA average of 12%.

findings.headline: Demand pressure forecasting reduced by £10.619m from February 2026 position, but £24.967m in new pressures still built into four-year plan
findings.detail: Pressures have been remodelled using latest data and now show a reduction of £10.619m compared to February 2026, reflecting better understanding of service-user populations and improved commissioning. However, the MTFO still includes £24.967m of new demand pressures over the four years, with Adult Services alone at £5.787m in 2027/28. The reduction demonstrates improved forecasting but the remaining scale shows social care continues to be the structural budget driver.
findings.matters: Successful demand management is critical to preventing structural budget growth outpacing resources; the large reduction shows progress but remaining material pressures indicate the challenge is far from closed
findings.figures: £10.619m reduction vs February 2026; £24.967m new pressures over four years; Adult Services £5.787m in 2027/28
findings.quote: Across the MTFO period, pressures have reduced by (£10.619m) compared with the February 2026 position, with a further £7.281m pressure included for the additional year added to the MTFO, 2030/31.

findings.headline: 2027/28 forecast shows £0.117m surplus but £3.840m cumulative gap remains over four years
findings.detail: The forecast for 2027/28 has improved to a small surplus, a change from the February 2026 forecast which showed a £1.631m gap. However, the cumulative position through 2030/31 remains a £3.840m gap. The council has updated its assumptions on demand, inflation and funding, and identified additional savings, but the medium-term challenge persists despite near-term improvement.
findings.matters: Determines whether the council has genuinely improved its financial position or has deferred rather than solved its budget challenge
findings.figures: £0.117m surplus 2027/28; £3.840m cumulative gap over four years; £1.631m gap in February 2026 forecast
findings.quote: Over the four years we currently have a forecast base budget funding gap of £3.840m, with a surplus (£0.117m) arising in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Indicative Dedicated Schools Grant funding for 2027/28 will not be announced until December 2026, marking the third consecutive year of delay from historical July notification
findings.detail: The council will not receive its indicative 2027/28 DSG funding and operational guidance until December 2026, pushing full budget update to that month. This represents a repeated break from historical practice where 'Draft allocations used to be published in July of the previous financial year.' This is now 'the third year that there has been a delay in receiving our indicative funding.' The repeated delays compress the council's budget finalization schedule and create uncertainty about the timing and quantum of the schools funding block.
findings.matters: Repeated delays in schools funding notification create planning uncertainty for councils dependent on this material funding stream. December-only notification compresses budget processes into a tight timescale. This affects the council's ability to finalize its overall budget position with certainty.
findings.figures: December 2026 notification vs. historical July timing; three consecutive years of delays
findings.quote: Draft allocations used to be published in July of the previous financial year however this is the third year that there has been a delay in receiving our indicative funding.

findings.headline: All current available capital resources committed to existing programmes; council faces potential funding gap and must make investment prioritization choices through 2031/32
findings.detail: The council has committed all currently available capital resources to financing the existing capital programme, leaving no spare capacity. A capital programme refresh underway will rephase existing projects to align with cashflow and propose extending the programme by one additional year based on government ring-fenced funding. The refresh will include 'an updated view on the potential funding gap and the choices that will need to be made between 2027/28 and 2031/32.' The council is working with directors to review existing and additional requirements.
findings.matters: With no spare capital capacity, the council faces difficult trade-offs between competing investment priorities. This signals to lenders and partners that new initiatives may be difficult to accommodate and constrains ability to respond to emerging investment needs or opportunities.
findings.figures: Capital programme pipeline extending to 2031/32 with potential funding gap under review
findings.quote: The Council has committed all currently available resources to finance the existing capital programme.

findings.headline: HRA currently balanced but exposed to interest rate risk on borrowing, with material additional capital investment needs from housing stock surveys still to be assessed
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account Business Plan is currently balanced over the medium term with borrowing within target Interest Cover Ratio thresholds. However, the council notes 'several material changes still to be incorporated which may significantly alter the outlook.' Ongoing stock condition surveys may identify additional capital investment requirements across the housing stock, which would increase capital expenditure needs. The HRA faces interest rate exposure due to the level of borrowing required to refinance existing schemes, which 'could place additional pressure on the HRA Business Plan.' A draft HRA budget will be presented in December 2026.
findings.matters: Rising or volatile interest rates could significantly impact HRA viability if substantial refinancing is required. Unknown additional capital needs would increase borrowing pressure. This represents a key contingent risk to HRA sustainability for lenders and affects the council's overall debt servicing position.
findings.figures: No specific borrowing quantum disclosed; outcome of stock condition surveys pending
findings.quote: The HRA remains exposed to interest rate risk due to the level of borrowing required to finance existing schemes and refinance existing borrowing. This could place additional pressure on the HRA Business Plan.

findings.headline: Council likely to start 2027/28 with High Needs block deficit after using all brought-forward reserves to balance 2026/27
findings.detail: The council's High Needs Budget faces material pressure with costs exceeding government funding. The 2026/27 budget was balanced entirely through consumption of remaining brought-forward surplus, leaving no buffer. The paper states the council will likely enter 2027/28 in deficit on the High Needs block. A review with the High Needs School reference group is underway to identify savings. While the Statutory Override allows High Needs deficits to be carried forward until 2028 without triggering s114, there remains a risk to the General Fund if the block cannot be managed within DSG allocations. This reflects a national picture: the vast majority of councils with schools responsibility carry High Needs deficits totalling an estimated £5 billion by end 2025/26.
findings.matters: High Needs deficits represent an emerging solvency risk even with the override protection. The exhaustion of reserves removes any cushion against in-year overspend. Lenders and peer councils need to understand how councils are managing this structural funding crisis in school SEND provision.
findings.figures: All remaining brought-forward surplus consumed in 2026/27; £5 billion cumulative national High Needs deficit estimated at end 2025/26
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all the remaining brought forward surplus therefore there is a chance that the block will go into a deficit during the 2026/27 if there were to be any in year overspend. It is therefore likely we may start the 2027/28 financial year in a deficit.

findings.headline: Medium Term Financial Plan gap revised to £3.840m by 2030/31 from £14.139m forecast in February 2026; 2027/28 shows small surplus
findings.detail: The council's budget forecast has been refreshed following Q1 2026/27 results, incorporating updated demand and inflation assumptions and revised funding projections from the three-year local government settlement. The cumulative funding gap by end-forecast has improved substantially: from £14.139m forecast in February 2026 to £3.840m by 2030/31. 2027/28 is forecast to have a surplus of £0.117m. The improvement includes savings proposals discussed with directors, though detailed proposals are still under development.
findings.matters: Shows the council is materially reducing its deficit gap, important for lenders assessing repayment capacity and for peer councils learning how others close budget shortfalls. Remaining gap still requires savings delivery and careful management.
findings.quote: The latest forecast shows a base budget funding gap of £3.840m by 2030/31, with a surplus of (£0.117m) in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: CCLA property fund showing unrealised loss of £1.181m against £15m principal invested
findings.detail: Milton Keynes holds £13.819m in CCLA Local Authorities Property Fund, with fair value loss in Q1 of £0.167m. Overall unrealised loss totals £1.181m (7.9% decline) since initial investment. Fund yielded 4.65% gross return in Q1; council reports no immediate plans to liquidate.
findings.matters: Policy investments in illiquid assets carry valuation risk; unrealised losses on long-term strategic holdings are relevant to balance sheet risk profile and treasury asset management.
findings.figures: £13.819m current holding vs £15.0m invested; unrealised loss £1.181m (7.9%); Q1 fair value loss £0.167m; yield 4.65%
findings.quote: On 30th June 2026, our holdings stood at £13.819m against opening balance of £13.986m on 1st April 2026, representing a fair value loss so far this year of £0.167m and an overall unrealised loss of £1.181m against the £15.0m total cash deposited.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: CIPFA proposes most significant review of Prudential and Treasury Management Codes since Liability Benchmark introduction
findings.detail: CIPFA's second consultation proposes enhanced group structure risk review, embedding Liability Benchmark as central treasury tool, clarification of affordability requirements, and removal of non-treasury investments from TMC scope. MHCLG separately consulting on new Capital Risk Metrics framework. Milton Keynes preparing responses citing concerns about unintended consequences and practical implementation challenges.
findings.matters: New regulatory framework will alter how councils manage treasury operations and report risk; group structure scrutiny affects multi-purpose authorities; changes to investment governance scope require practice restructuring.
findings.figures: MHCLG consultation closing 6 August 2026; CIPFA consultation closing 12 August 2026
findings.quote: These proposals represent the most significant review of the Prudential and Treasury Management Codes since the introduction of the Liability Benchmark

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: HRA forecast to require £70m new external borrowing as capital programme progresses
findings.detail: Officer commentary notes the HRA is approaching the point of requiring additional external funding to meet capital objectives. Currently £80m internal lending from General Fund is outstanding; forecast assumes £70m new external loans, though further internal loans may be considered as alternative, marking a shift toward external debt.
findings.matters: Material increase in HRA external debt extends refinancing obligations, changes the debt maturity profile, and affects interest rate exposure; relevant to long-term affordability of housing services.
findings.figures: £70m forecast new external borrowing; £80m internal loans outstanding (up from £50m in 2022); HRA external debt forecast £260.86m
findings.quote: The HRA is approaching a point of requiring additional funding to meet its business plan capital objectives (subject to slippage).

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: General Fund financing cost ratio forecast 3.91% against budgeted 4.43%; HRA forecast 36.25% against budgeted 40.64%
findings.detail: Both funds show financing costs tracking significantly below the February 2026 budget forecasts. General Fund improvement reflects outperforming investment income; HRA improvement reflects delayed new borrowing and reduced voluntary MRP due to capital programme slippage from 2025/26.
findings.matters: Lower financing ratios improve revenue headroom for services; better budget tracking than forecast reduces financial pressure and demonstrates improved cash management.
findings.figures: GF 3.91% vs 4.43% budgeted (0.52 percentage point improvement); HRA 36.25% vs 40.64% budgeted (4.39 percentage point improvement)
findings.quote: The GF ratio has decreased which reflects the positive impact upon net revenue of expecting to outperform our budget for investment income. The HRA ratio has decreased due to delaying new borrowing (saving in interest costs)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: Investment portfolio returned 4.31%, outperforming the 3.75% SONIA benchmark by 0.56 percentage points
findings.detail: Milton Keynes achieved average returns of 4.31% on £320.2m of investments, exceeding the SONIA 3-month backward-looking benchmark by 0.56 percentage points. The portfolio increased from £285.7m opening balance following net cash inflows of £34.5m. No counterparty credit losses occurred during the quarter.
findings.matters: Strong cash management and returns above market benchmark generate additional revenue to offset financing costs and support service funding.
findings.figures: 4.31% return vs 3.75% benchmark (+0.56%); investment holdings £320.199m (up from £285.735m opening)
findings.quote: the average rate of investment return was 4.31%, which was 0.56% above benchmark

findings.headline: Milton Keynes identifies inflationary pressure as its most substantial financial challenge in the 2027/28 MTFO period
findings.detail: Against a backdrop of subdued national economic growth (0.7% GDP), inflation forecast to rise to 3.2% by end 2026/27, and National Living Wage increases of 4.1% from April 2026, the council has explicitly identified inflation as its principal financial risk for the medium-term outlook.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders assess councils by how clearly they have identified principal risks; this shows Milton Keynes has recognized inflation as the key planning pressure for 2027/28 and that this is the focus of medium-term financial planning.
findings.figures: 0.7% GDP growth, 2.6% CPI June 2026, forecast 3.2% end 2026/27, 4.1% National Living Wage increase
findings.quote: For MKCC, this risk, particularly in relation to inflationary pressure, represents the most substantial financial challenge in the 2027/28 MTFO period.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex F - Tariff Monitoring
findings.headline: Multiple capital schemes delayed by prerequisite project completions and internal resource constraints: Broughton Brook crossing (£200k) and Fairfields meeting place (£100k)
findings.detail: Two delivery risk patterns emerge: scheme interdependencies and internal resource constraints. Broughton Brook Fen Street crossing (£200k slipped) awaits surrounding road network completion. Brooklands connections depend on Linear Park adoption process completion. Fairfields Community Meeting Place (£100k slipped) was delayed by changes in project resourcing at the meeting place. These delays extend into 2027/28 for some schemes.
findings.matters: Interdependent capital schemes create cascade delay risk; internal resource constraints on capital delivery may indicate systemic capacity issues that undermine programme forecasting and delivery reliability.
findings.figures: Broughton Brook slippage £200k, Fairfields Meeting Place slippage £100k, Fairfields Playing Fields slippage £82k
findings.quote: Delivery of the crossing is dependent on completion of the surrounding road network. As a result, this element of the programme is expected to slip into a future financial year.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex F - Tariff Monitoring
findings.headline: Tattenhoe Park local play areas (£450k budget) slipped by up to two years due to planning permission delays, with staggered delivery March 2027 to 2027/28
findings.detail: The £450k Tattenhoe Park Local Play Areas scheme shows outturn of £150k with £300k slipped to future years. Cause is ongoing planning permission for three sites. Tender documents are expected autumn 2026. One play area is scheduled for completion by March 2027, with the other two expected in the following financial year.
findings.matters: A major leisure capital scheme slipped by up to two financial years indicates planning and regulatory delays that signal risks to other council development projects and timelines for deploying developer contributions.
findings.figures: Budget £450k, outturn £150k, slippage £300k
findings.quote: Planning permission for the three local play area sites is ongoing. Tender documents are expected to be published in autumn 2026. One play area is scheduled for completion by March 2027, with the remaining two expected to be completed in the following financial year.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex F - Tariff Monitoring
findings.headline: Tariff capital programme slipped £1.1m (3.7%) in Q1 2026-27, entirely attributable to timing delays rather than overspend or savings
findings.detail: The £29.4m tariff-funded capital programme achieved £28.3m outturn with £1.1m deferred to future financial years. All variance is explained by programme slippage (timing) rather than cost changes. The paper identifies specific causes for each delay: planning approvals pending, internal resource availability, and prerequisite scheme completion.
findings.matters: A council finance director must track capital delivery against developer contribution funding obligations; a lender monitors how efficiently capital is deployed and the council's developer relationships; peers managing similar tariff programmes want visibility of common delivery challenges.
findings.figures: Revised budget £29,397k, outturn £28,295k, variance (£1,102k), entirely due to slippage of £1,102k
findings.quote: Total Tariff Programme    29,397    28,295    (1,102)    1,102    0

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: Passenger Transport programme showing significant current-year underspend; delivery deferred to second priority
findings.detail: Passenger Transport (upgraded bus stops and multi-modal hubs) is showing a current-year underspend of £765,423 against a budget of £840,511. Delivery has been deprioritised in favour of completing LA Bus Grant schemes, resulting in forecast slippage.
findings.matters: Significant underspend signals competing priorities; deferral may signal external grant conditions or capacity constraints.
findings.figures: Current Year Capital Budget £840,511; Current Year Actuals £75,088; Under/Over on Current Year Project Outturn -£765,423
findings.quote: Priority of delivery to LA Bus Grant funded projects below, hence partial project slippage.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: Civic Offices Balcony Solution project delivered early with anticipated underspend
findings.detail: Main works at Civic Offices were completed in December 2025, with additional specialist protection work finished by May 2026. Final costs are awaited but an underspend is anticipated.
findings.matters: Early delivery and under-budget performance demonstrates project management capability and suggests headroom in this programme.
findings.figures: Total Scheme Forecast £475,486 with Forecast Variance -£10,000
findings.quote: Main works completed Dec 25 and additional specialist protection works completed April thru May 26. Awaiting final costs but anticipate small underspend.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: £1.333m capital slippage deferred to 2027/28, including £504k health facility and £429k bus grant funding
findings.detail: Two significant programme slippages are forecast: Lakes Estate Health Facility (£504k) now expected to complete in spring 2027 rather than this financial year due to design and tendering timescales, and LA Bus Grant 2026/27 programme (£429k) continuing into 2027/28 as delivery is at planning stage and priority is completing the prior-year programme.
findings.matters: Slippage defers investment benefits and may signal tighter delivery timescales ahead; both projects affect external stakeholders — tenants for the health facility and DfT for bus grant funding.
findings.figures: Forecast Slippage to Future Years: £1,333,000. Lakes Estate Health Facility: £2,504,000 budget split £2,000,000 (2026/27) and £504,000 slippage. LA Bus Grant 2026/27: £1,729,000 budget, £1,300,000 forecast for current year, £429,000 slippage
findings.quote: Tendering in process and plan to award summer 26 and delivery estimated January 27 and complete Spring 27, hence partial slippage

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: Bradwell Windmill cultural project paused; tender costs exceed budget, timeline extension required
findings.detail: Bradwell Windmill project has been paused after tender returns came in above current budget. The council is reviewing options and next steps. Project timeline will require extension. The scheme remains in amber status.
findings.matters: Project pauses signal either poor scoping or cost inflation in the market; a postponed cultural commitment may affect the council's regeneration narrative.
findings.figures: Total Scheme Forecast £304,350 with Forecast Variance 0, but project paused
findings.quote: Tenders to deliver required work received, however cost in excess of current budget, project paused as options and next steps reviewed, project timeline will require extension, to be confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: MK East HIF social infrastructure scheme reporting £400,000 overspend recoverable from tariff funding
findings.detail: The £29.6m MK East HIF project is forecasting a £400,000 overspend due to extensive measures required for power, water and drainage connections. The council has identified tariff funding to recover this cost. Recommissioning work is part-complete, with forecast figures based on assumed final account contract costs.
findings.matters: A material overspend on a major infrastructure project signals either underestimated scope or cost inflation; the requirement to draw on tariff funding to offset it shows how later projects may be squeezed.
findings.figures: Total Scheme Forecast £29,604,298; Forecast Variance to Capital Budget £400,000
findings.quote: Overspend due to lengthy measures to provide power/water/drainage in lieu of permanent connections. Recommissioning partly completed; forecast includes assumed final account contract costs, Tariff funding identified for overspend.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Schools reserves improving by £2.211m, counter to sector-wide financial pressures
findings.detail: Schools balances moved from (10.455)m to (8.243)m, a positive movement of £2.211m. This is notable given schools across England face significant budget pressures and are typically drawing on reserves.
findings.matters: Suggests Milton Keynes schools may be managing finances more effectively than peers, or benefiting from favourable local funding; relevant to other councils assessing school financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £2.211m positive movement in schools reserves

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Collection fund reserve built up by £5.848m, reflecting cash management focus
findings.detail: The council has increased its collection fund cashflow reserve from (19.201)m to (13.352)m through a positive movement of £5.848m, indicating deliberate action to manage collection fund timing and volatility.
findings.matters: Active collection fund reserve management is typical of councils managing collection pressures or seeking to build cash resilience; shows financial management response to income volatility.
findings.figures: £5.848m positive movement
findings.quote: Collection Fund Cashflow Reserve (19.201) 0.000 5.848 (13.352)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Waste asset renewal reserve drawn down £3.571m in Q1
findings.detail: The waste service has drawn £3.571m from its dedicated asset renewal reserve to cover service costs, leaving it at (14.977)m negative. This indicates waste service costs are not fully absorbed by revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Using renewal reserves to fund revenue operations erodes future asset replacement capacity; shows waste service cost management is constrained and peers may face similar pressures.
findings.figures: £3.571m drawn, closing (14.977)m
findings.quote: Waste Asset Renewals Reserve (11.406) 0.000 (3.571) (14.977)

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Tariff risk reserve drawn down £4.156m in Q1, balance now £19.596m negative
findings.detail: The tariff risk reserve has been drawn by £4.156m in the quarter to absorb cost pressures, leaving the balance substantially negative. This signals tariff-related cost pressures are materializing rather than being contained in revenue.
findings.matters: Indicates the council is using reserves rather than revenue solutions to absorb tariff costs; a large negative balance provides minimal buffer for further tariff shocks or volatility.
findings.figures: £4.156m drawn, closing (19.596)m

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Capital reserve stands at £47.999m negative, the largest single component of the reserves deficit
findings.detail: The general fund capital reserve is substantially negative at (47.999)m, accounting for approximately 20% of the total reserves deficit. This indicates the capital spending programme is not fully funded from available resources.
findings.matters: A negative capital reserve indicates the council's infrastructure investment depends on external financing, grants, or deferral; lenders and peers need to understand the sustainability of this funding model.
findings.figures: (47.999)m represents 20% of total (236.672)m deficit

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Council reserves deficit narrowing by £21.566m in Q1 2026-27, from £258.238m to £236.672m negative
findings.detail: Milton Keynes' accumulated reserves deficit is reducing in-year through positive movements across multiple categories including schools, political priorities, collection fund, and capital funding, partially offset by draws on waste and tariff reserves. The trajectory shows improvement but from a very large deficit position.
findings.matters: A £236m+ negative reserve position is a fundamental financial stress indicator to lenders and peer councils; whether this improvement trajectory is sustainable is critical to assessing long-term financial viability.
findings.figures: Opening (258.238)m, closing (236.672)m, positive movement 21.566m

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: New Bradwell Household Waste Recycling Centre requires £0.544m capital remediation to address contamination risks
findings.detail: The council is seeking approval for £0.544m targeted remediation works at the New Bradwell HWRC to address contamination risks and maintain safe operation. The council frames this as avoiding the higher costs of full site remediation, closure or mothballing, and as helping to retain a strategic waste asset and associated lease income. Funding will come from revenue contributions.
findings.matters: Unplanned capital costs on operational assets indicate emerging environmental and operational liabilities; the council is managing the risk proactively rather than deferring, but the issue was not anticipated in the original programme
findings.quote: The project seeks approval for targeted remediation works at the New Bradwell Household Waste Recycling Centre to address contamination risks and support the site's continued safe operation.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: Homes England awarded additional £50m Housing Infrastructure Fund grant for Milton Keynes East highways, citing construction cost inflation impacts
findings.detail: The council originally received £94.6m HIF funding in July 2020, with Phase 1 infrastructure now complete. Homes England has committed an additional £50m for Phase 2 and later highway works to March 2028, explicitly recognising that construction cost inflation has impacted the programme's delivery. The council has arranged back-to-back agreements with developer Berkeley to manage risk of further cost escalation.
findings.matters: Construction inflation is a systemic issue affecting capital delivery across councils; this shows how a grant-funder is accommodating cost increases and that the council has negotiated developer risk-sharing to protect its position
findings.figures: £50m additional HIF; original HIF £94.6m; Phase 2 completion target March 2028
findings.quote: Homes England have now offered to provide a further £50m of funding for the next phases of highway works to March 2028, recognising the construction cost inflation which has impacted the construction works programme to date, and allowing the acceleration of housing delivery on the wider site.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand risks from Section 21 court backlogs and Renters Rights Act implementation
findings.detail: Currently supporting 1,011 households in temporary accommodation (including those in HRA properties), with £0.740m forecast underspend. Forecast assumes continued management through lower-cost Harben House placements and successful move-ons to private rental. Explicit risks flagged: Section 21 court backlogs slowing eviction proceedings and Renters Rights Act implementation that could increase household demand.
findings.matters: Housing/homelessness pressure is structural; regulatory changes could materially increase service costs and eliminate forecast saving.
findings.figures: 1,011 households in temporary accommodation; £0.740m forecast underspend
findings.quote: There are a number of risks associated with temporary accommodation, including the potential impact of court backlogs affecting Section 21 cases and the implementation of the Renters' Right Act.

findings.headline: General Fund working balance £34.677m provides only £3.707m buffer above minimum recommended level
findings.detail: General Fund working balance stands at £34.677m with £3.707m headroom above minimum recommended level. Paper describes this as 'small buffer for unplanned expenditure'. Against backdrop of multiple identified risks (MKWRP overspend, remaining savings delivery, DSG deficit, children's placement volatility, temporary accommodation demand), limited reserve flexibility to absorb adverse movements.
findings.matters: Constrained reserve position reduces resilience to downside scenarios; material risk crystallisation could force difficult service trade-offs.
findings.figures: £34.677m General Fund balance; £3.707m headroom above minimum
findings.quote: The current General Fund working balance is £34.677m, which provides headroom of £3.707m above than the minimum recommended level, providing a small buffer for unplanned expenditure.

findings.headline: Capital programme in-year overspend of £0.410m after £1.333m slippage to future years
findings.detail: Capital budget of £239.153m with £1.333m planned slippage to 2027/28. After slippage, forecast in-year overspend of £0.410m. Driven primarily by MK East HIF Social Infrastructure overspend of £0.400m, caused by prolonged temporary power, water and drainage arrangements while permanent infrastructure connections installed. Paper states funding shortfall to be met from future tariff receipts.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivering over budget; dependent on future developer contributions (tariff income) to cover spending gaps.
findings.figures: £0.410m capital overspend in-year; £1.333m slippage; £0.400m MK East HIF overspend; £239.153m capital budget
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is forecasting underspend of (£0.923m), of which £1.333m is planned to slip to later years, leaving an in-year forecast overspend of £0.410m.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block forecast into £0.146m deficit by year-end
findings.detail: Overall DSG position improved significantly to £5.004m surplus (from £2.514m budgeted) through Early Years uptake increase of £2.395m. However High Needs Block faces 'significant pressure' from independent school placements and education packages costing £0.622m. Despite vacancy savings of £0.230m and additional grant of £0.160m, block forecast to move into deficit. Ring-fenced blocks mean deficit cannot be offset by other surpluses and carries forward as obligation.
findings.matters: Structural pressure on SEND provision; ring-fenced deficit creates ongoing negative carry-forward and signals insufficient funding for rising demand.
findings.figures: £0.146m High Needs year-end deficit; £0.622m cost of independent placements; £0.230m vacancy savings; £0.160m additional grant
findings.quote: The High Needs block is under significant pressure and based on forecast demand it is expected that the block will go into deficit in 2026/27. At Period 3, this forecast deficit is expected to be £0.146m.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste and Recycling Park costs exceed budget from April 2026 operational takeover
findings.detail: Council assumed responsibility for all running costs and repairs at MKWRP from April 2026. Costs in April and May already tracking above budget. Council provisioned £2m from contingency but paper explicitly identifies facility as 'significant risk to the general fund budget' with no stated mitigation if overspend continues through remainder of year.
findings.matters: New operational cost burden starting at year-start with immediate overspend; could eliminate claimed year-end underspend if adverse trend continues.
findings.figures: £2m contingency provision made; costs from April 2026 running above budget
findings.quote: Since April 2026 MKCC is responsible for all running costs and repairs at MKWRP. Initial estimates based on April and May, are reporting costs higher than budget, and whilst we have made a provision of £2m to be met from contingency, MKWRP remains a significant risk to the general fund budget.

findings.headline: General Fund forecast underspend of £4.832m at quarter one
findings.detail: Adult Social Care placements managed within budget despite material cost overspend offset by higher client contributions and external delivery transition savings. Temporary accommodation demand held at 1,011 households with cost control through lower-cost placements. Children's services benefiting from reduced legal proceedings and provider contract savings. Full-year position assumes delivery of £9.356m (94%) of £9.982m approved savings target, with £4.184m delivered by Q1 and remainder dependent on continued delivery through Q2-Q4.
findings.matters: Interim position shows budget management working, but year-end outcome dependent on undelivered savings and containment of identified risks.
findings.figures: £4.832m underspend; £9.356m of £9.982m savings forecast to land; £4.184m delivered by Q1
findings.quote: The General Fund Services are currently forecasting an underspend of (£4.832m).

findings.headline: Internal audit resource constraints escalated in September have been addressed by filling three vacancies
findings.detail: The committee discussed in September that internal audit could not fully deliver its plan due to stretched resources. By February 2026, three positions had been filled and a framework for specialist audits put in place. The committee had sought assurance that resource levels would improve in the near term, which appears to have been achieved.
findings.matters: Internal audit capacity is essential to detect control breakdowns and financial irregularities early — resource gaps create audit blind spots that increase financial and operational risk
findings.figures: three positions had been filled
findings.quote: At the September meeting, the challenges to delivery of the Audit Plan due to stretched resources was discussed with Committee seeking assurance that levels of resource available will be improved in the very near future. At the February 2026 meeting it was noted that three positions had been filled, and a framework arrangement put in place for delivery of specialist Internal audits.

findings.headline: Two internal audits issued limited assurance opinions, indicating significant control issues
findings.detail: During 2025-26, internal audit issued two reports with limited assurance opinions. The committee defines limited assurance as meaning auditors identified significant control issues presenting high risk to the control environment, or the control environment had not operated as intended. Full reports were circulated to committee members but this summary does not specify which areas were affected.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses affect the reliability of financial reporting and the council's ability to safeguard assets — a lender needs to know whether these issues affect financial controls, expenditure, or income
findings.figures: Two limited assurance audit opinion reports
findings.quote: Two limited assurance opinion reports were issued during the year and circulated to Committee members.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: Landlord Incentive Scheme: deposit recovery process in progress via new bond scheme; rent guarantee payment recovery unresolved with no income recovery officers assigned
findings.detail: Two financial recovery gaps in the Landlord Incentive Scheme. Deposits: A new Deposit Bond Scheme is being drawn to replace direct cash deposits held by the council to 'greatly reduce MKCC losses', suggesting prior losses from the cash deposit approach. Rent guarantees: No process exists to recover rent guarantee payments made on behalf of tenants who default. The council lacks dedicated income recovery officers in the service; as of July 2026, discussion is ongoing about whether recovery should transfer to the council's debt recovery team.
findings.matters: Both create direct financial risk to the council. Deposits and guarantees represent cash exposures; lack of recovery process means losses are deferred or unrecorded. The move to a bond scheme acknowledges prior losses.
findings.figures: Deposit Bond Scheme being drawn to replace cash deposits. Rent guarantee recovery: no income recovery officers assigned. Due date 30/09/27.
findings.quote: A new Deposit Bond Scheme is currently being drawn to replace the current cash deposits that are paid, and this should ensure that MKCC losses are greatly reduced.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: Structures inspection compliance improvements in progress since October 2024; original target now 18 months overdue
findings.detail: A significant audit finding on delays in structures inspection completion and approval remains in progress with an original target of 31 October 2024 revised to 12 December 2025, and still not closed as of July 2026. Successive updates through 2025–26 report incremental improvements in compliance rates and process adjustments (e.g. extending planning/inspection cycle from 30 days to 2 months from February 2026), indicating the council is still working to implement resolution.
findings.matters: Inspection compliance directly affects asset safety and risk management. Sustained delays in achieving basic compliance, with multiple missed targets and continued remediation, suggest resource constraints or process challenges that have persisted for over 18 months.
findings.figures: Original target 31/10/24. Revised to 12/12/25. Still in progress July 2026. Planning/inspection cycle extended 30 days to 2 months February 2026.
findings.quote: The monitoring that has occurred since the last update has shown that the 30 day target for inspectors to plan & inspect has proved to be too inflexible and a 2 month planning and inspection target will be introduced from February 2026

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care Plans not issued within statutory 20-week timescale; backlog project extended from January to October 2026 now dependent on agency support
findings.detail: The council is not meeting the statutory 20-week timescale for issuing EHCPs. A backlog clearance project originally targeted for 30 January 2026 has been extended to 31 October 2026. As of July 2026, Educational Psychologists' assessment work is completed on time, but plan-writing is the bottleneck. Agency workers were approved to start 10 August 2026 to write plans, with progress review at end October.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory timescales in SEND support creates legal and reputational risk for the council and indicates demand-capacity mismatch. Extended backlog management requiring agency spend demonstrates sustained pressure on permanent resources.
findings.figures: Original backlog target 30/01/26. Revised to 31/10/26. Agency workers approved start date 10/08/26. Review end October 2026.
findings.quote: The writing of the plans is the part of the assessement process we now need to address. A plan is being progressed to utilise agency workers to write the plans to clear the final backlog.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: NEC Housing System user access monitoring control essential action delayed to October 2026 pending supplier delivery with no fixed date confirmed
findings.detail: An essential control for monitoring user activity within the NEC Housing System remains in progress. A licence was purchased and installed in July 2026, but implementation depends on the supplier (NEC) configuring a data warehouse. The supplier has committed resource but delivery is later than expected, promised for October 2026 with 'no fixed date in the month as of yet.' The tracker notes 'This could mean slippage of the target date.'
findings.matters: User access monitoring is a foundational control for system integrity, data security and fraud prevention. Dependency on third-party supplier delivery and lack of a fixed date creates implementation risk. Slippage would leave an essential control gap in housing system access.
findings.figures: Licence installed July 2026. Supplier commitment October 2026, no fixed date within month. Original target 31/10/26.
findings.quote: This is later than we had hoped and pushed for but is now promised for October 2026. No fixed date in the month as of yet. This could mean slippage of the target date.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: Fishermead Rough Sleeping contract awarded at higher price post-award based on updated TUPE and pension costs; variation approval from Director still being pursued
findings.detail: The Fishermead Rough Sleeping facility contract was awarded at a higher price than initially budgeted. The increase was agreed post-award following updated TUPE and pension information. As of July 2026, authorisation for the contract variation remains outstanding and is 'being requested from Director of Adult Services.' A Contract Management Oversight Group has since been established for oversight; KPI data reporting issues are being resolved with the provider.
findings.matters: Post-award price increases indicate cost control and procurement governance gaps. Extended timescale to obtain Director approval for a variation raises questions about approval processes. The establishment of new oversight governance suggests prior control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Quantified price increase not stated in tracker. Variation approval status as at July 2026: pending Director approval.
findings.quote: A higher price was agreed post-award based on updated TUPE and pension information. The authorisation for the variation is being requested from Director of Adult Services

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: IT patch management policy missed December 2025 and May 2026 targets; now due October 2026 with security team vacancies and recruitment underway
findings.detail: The council's IT patch management policy, first targeted for 31 December 2025, was revised to 31 May 2026. A June 2026 update reported slippage due to other work commitments with an estimated three-month window. By July 2026, further delays were reported due to vacancies in the security team with recruitment in progress. New target is October 2026.
findings.matters: Patch management is foundational to IT security and system resilience. Unpatched systems create material vulnerability to cyber attack. Repeated missed deadlines coupled with staffing gaps suggest security resources are constrained and cyber resilience may be at risk.
findings.figures: Original target 31/12/25. Revised to 31/05/26. Further slipped June 2026. Now October 2026. Security team has vacancies with recruitment in progress.
findings.quote: July 2026 - we have vacanies in this team and currently out to recruit, also other work committments. This should be complete by Oct 2026

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: Children's external placement commissioning lacks documented governance, audit trails, rationale and value-for-money evidence across multiple placements
findings.detail: Seven audit findings in external placement commissioning remain open with December 2026 targets. Governance gaps include: placement referral forms not consistently authorised; placement rationale not documented; procurement activity not evidenced or auditable; spot purchase process not defined; delegation and approval arrangements not formally documented; procurement documentation fragmented across systems; and value-for-money assessment absent, with the audit finding that placements lacked 'consistent or structured approach to documenting cost comparisons, benchmarking, cost negotiations, or the rationale for selecting higher-cost placements.' Two findings are essential priority.
findings.matters: Placement spending is typically high-value per case; governance gaps in procurement, cost justification and audit trails expose the council to overspending, unauthorised commitments and inability to demonstrate value-for-money. This affects both revenue and compliance.
findings.figures: Seven findings. Two marked essential priority. Most due 31/12/26. One (value-for-money) had a revised target of 31/07/26 and remains in progress, indicating potential overdue status.
findings.quote: There was limited evidence to demonstrate that external placements represented value for money. While decisions were primarily needs-led, there was no consistent or structured approach to documenting cost comparisons, benchmarking, cost negotiations, or the rationale for selecting higher-cost placements.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex C - Actions Tracker
findings.headline: IT business continuity plan not tested since November 2023; training, dependencies and testing schedule all still in progress against October 2026 deadlines
findings.detail: The council's IT Business Continuity Plan has not been formally tested or exercised since November 2023. Three linked audit findings remain in progress as of July 2026: dependencies from other council departments on IT remain undefined; no training timetable has been established for staff to execute the plan; and no regular testing schedule has been implemented. All three are due by 31 October 2026.
findings.matters: An untested BCP with undefined dependencies and staff untrained in their roles creates material risk to business continuity. A lender depends on councils' ability to maintain financial operations and service delivery through disruptions; this paper shows a significant gap.
findings.figures: BCP last tested November 2023. Three related actions due 31/10/26, all marked in progress as of July 2026.
findings.quote: At the time of audit, it was noted that the Council's IT BCP had not been tested to ensure continued adequacy, since November 2023.

findings.headline: Information Governance risk above management target
findings.detail: Information Governance (SR9) has residual 12 against target 9. The council has not reduced information governance risk to its planned level.
findings.matters: Information governance failures affect data security and operational compliance. The residual-to-target gap indicates risk mitigation has underperformed.

findings.headline: Fraud Prevention risk above management target
findings.detail: Fraud Prevention (SR17) is at residual 12 versus a target of 8. The council's fraud risk remains above its intended reduction level.
findings.matters: Fraud risk directly affects financial control and stewardship of public resources. The gap between residual and target indicates fraud prevention measures have not achieved planned improvements.
findings.figures: SR17: Residual 12, Target 8
findings.quote: SR17 Fraud Prevention Dir. Finance & Resources 12 8

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept AC - RM Update -Annex C Risk Scorecard
findings.headline: Cybersecurity risk remains at very high level above management target
findings.detail: Cybersecurity (SR10) has a residual score of 15 against a management target of 10. Current cyber risk exposure exceeds the level the council has set as its reduction target.
findings.matters: Cybersecurity affects the council's operational resilience and integrity of financial systems. The persistent gap between residual and target indicates planned risk reduction has not been achieved.
findings.figures: SR10: Residual 15, Target 10
findings.quote: SR10 Cybersecurity Dir. Finance & Resources 15 10

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept AC - RM Update -Annex C Risk Scorecard
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability identified as strategic risk at maximum acceptable level
findings.detail: Financial Sustainability (SR1) is the council's top strategic risk, scored at residual 15 matching its target of 15. This represents an accepted position at the upper boundary of the council's risk tolerance, with no planned reduction.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council recognizes financial sustainability as its primary strategic risk and regards the current risk level as acceptable.
findings.figures: SR1: Residual 15, Target 15
findings.quote: SR1 Financial sustainability Dir. Finance & Resources 15 15

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept AC - RM Update Annex B Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Children's social care placement sufficiency risk at maximum, with cost consequences explicitly noted and controls partially inadequate.
findings.detail: The risk of failing to secure sufficient high-quality placements for children in care is scored at 15 (maximum likelihood), with a target of 10. The register identifies placement cost pressures as a direct consequence: 'Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements'. Triggers include rising LAC numbers and 'National decrease in placement sufficiency across external market'. Several mitigation controls are rated only as 'Reasonable' rather than 'Good', including external provider quality reviews and commissioning arrangements, indicating acknowledged gaps in risk management.
findings.matters: Placement costs represent a large discretionary spending area vulnerable to demand spikes; uncontrolled placement sufficiency can rapidly create budget overruns where the council has limited ability to constrain numbers.
findings.figures: Current Score 15, Target Score 10, Previous Score 15. Last review 17/06/2026, next review 15/09/2026.
findings.quote: Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept AC - RM Update Annex B Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk remains at maximum score with no planned improvement despite controls assessed as adequate.
findings.detail: The council's strategic financial sustainability risk is scored at 15 (the maximum), unchanged from its previous assessment and with a target score identical to the current score, indicating no planned reduction. This occurs despite controls for this risk being rated as adequate. The risk register notes as potential consequences: failure to manage resources to achieve a balanced budget, loss of government funding, economic decline, section 114 notice, and government intervention. The unchanged target suggests the council considers this risk unremediable within existing governance.
findings.matters: A lender must understand why the council believes financial sustainability risk cannot be materially reduced, and whether this reflects structural external pressures or budget imbalance without remediation path.
findings.figures: Current Score 15, Target Score 15, Previous Score 15. Risk likelihood 5, consequence 4.
findings.quote: Failure to manage resources to achieve a balanced budget; loss of Government funding, decline in economic climate; s114 Notice and government intervention

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept AC - RM Update Annex B Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Waste recovery plant transitions to new commercial contract in October 2026 with final costs not yet settled.
findings.detail: The council's waste recovery plant has operated under a support contract worth approximately £700k/month in revenue costs, expiring in October 2026. The plant has experienced catastrophic boiler failures in October 2022 and October 2025, each rendering it unavailable for four months. A new commercial contract commences 01/10/2026 with a new cost structure being negotiated; the council notes that market volatility and engineering challenges are still driving cost estimates. The transition includes a stoploss mechanism on revenue spend after 24 months, but the pre-stoploss cost envelope remains uncertain.
findings.matters: A major operational asset with £7.8m annual disposal costs is undergoing contract renewal within five weeks of committee date, with final monthly costs unknown and binding the council to new financial commitments.
findings.figures: £700k/month revenue support (expires October 2026); disposal £7.8M pa; total monthly contingency cost £840k; capital investment £17M until 2033
findings.quote: c£700k revenue support (expires October 2026 when new contract commences). Market volatility and engineering challenges still driving risk costing.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex A- Audit Progress
findings.headline: Two primary schools audited and both received Limited assurance for compliance, indicating that control environment did not operate as intended and significant errors were detected
findings.detail: Two primary school audits from 2025-26 both received Limited assurance opinion on compliance with controls, defined as meaning the control environment has not operated as intended with significant errors detected. The full audit reports will be shared with the Audit Committee after September 2026 when schools resume. Limited compliance assurance is a material control rating reserved for significant control weaknesses.
findings.matters: Limited compliance assurance in schools indicates financial controls are failing; if this spans multiple schools it suggests a systemic issue in how the council oversees school financial management.
findings.figures: Two schools with Limited compliance assurance rating
findings.quote: The schools' reports will be shared with committee members after September 2026 when schools resume following the summer break and can provide feedback.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex A- Audit Progress
findings.headline: School finance team member identified as having breached key financial controls; school management raised concern and audit is supporting investigation
findings.detail: A school's senior management identified a breach of key financial controls by a member of the finance team. This indicates either a system breakdown in controls or potential misconduct by a staff member. Internal Audit is providing support as the school and management work through the investigation.
findings.matters: Financial control breaches in schools indicate either that the control system failed or there has been fraud or misappropriation by a staff member.
findings.figures: One school; one staff member
findings.quote: Concerns from a school, where Senior management identified breach of key financial controls by a member of the school finance team.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex A- Audit Progress
findings.headline: Whistleblowing allegation council incorrectly assessed client social care contribution, resulting in overpayment not recovered; audit reviewing
findings.detail: An allegation was received from a care provider that the council incorrectly assessed a client's contribution toward care costs, resulting in the council overpaying for care. The allegation states the council has failed to recover the overpayment. Internal Audit is undertaking preliminary review. If substantiated, this represents direct financial loss that has not been recovered.
findings.matters: This is direct financial loss; incorrect contribution assessment processes could affect multiple clients, meaning the loss could scale.
findings.figures: One client; amount not stated
findings.quote: allegation from a Care provider that MKCC incorrectly assessed a client contribution towards their care costs, resulting in overpayment by the Council and that the Council has failed to recover the alleged overpayment.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex A- Audit Progress
findings.headline: Children's external placements audited and found spot purchases not consistently authorised and cost variations not properly documented or approved
findings.detail: High-cost individual placements (spot purchases) for children in external care were not consistently approved in line with Contract Procedure Rules. Cost variations were not documented or approved. Placement decisions and rationale were inconsistently recorded in the Liquidlogic system. This absence of authorization trail and audit evidence for high-cost placements undermines budget control on what are typically expensive placements.
findings.matters: Children's social care placement costs are major budget drivers, particularly spot purchases which are procured outside planned contracts; lack of authorization and documentation creates risk of uncontrolled spending.
findings.figures: Spot purchases of unquantified value
findings.quote: There was limited assurance that higher-cost and spot purchase placements were consistently authorised in line with Contract Procedure Rules requirements due to inconsistent documentation of approval arrangements.

findings.paper_title: 22 Sept 26 AC - IA Progress Update Annex A- Audit Progress
findings.headline: Landlord Incentive Scheme has multiple critical control gaps including lack of separation of duties and no process to recover rent guarantees paid to landlords
