findings.quote: These adjustments will affect our Business Rates charges for our properties, creating a financial pressure of £0.250m.

findings.headline: Capital programme has no unallocated funding; all £56.473m of resource surplus is ring-fenced to education and transport
findings.detail: Although the capital programme appears to have a surplus of resources over expenditure, the council states all of this is 'either Education or Local Transport specific, meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects within the current Programme'. Several unquantified projects (leisure centre dilapidations, pipeline schemes) are not yet included and 'will require funding in the future, therefore increasing the overall funding shortfall'.
findings.matters: The council has no discretionary capital capacity for new projects. Any unforeseen capital need (asset failure, compliance issue) cannot be funded from the planned programme and would require either reserves, prudential borrowing, or reallocation from existing schemes.
findings.figures: £56.473m of cumulative surplus entirely ring-fenced; £44.172m surplus in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: Whilst Table 5 shows an excess of resources over planned expenditure, all £56.473m of this funding is either Education or Local Transport specific, meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects within the current Programme.

findings.headline: 2023/24 accounts disclaimed by auditors; 2024/25 audit expected to receive modified opinion
findings.detail: The council's external auditors disclaimed the 2023/24 accounts due to the previous auditor being unable to resource the 2022/23 audit. While 'significant progress' has been made on the 2024/25 audit, the council 'anticipates that a modified opinion will be issued for 2024/25, due to the issues with the non-completion of the 2022/23 audit'.
findings.matters: Audit disclaimers and modified opinions indicate control or evidence weaknesses. Consecutive years of audit qualification suggests the council may have underlying accounting or control issues that could mask other problems.
findings.figures: 2023/24: disclaimed opinion; 2024/25: modified opinion expected
findings.quote: The Council's 2023/24 Statement of Accounts were disclaimed by our external auditors, as a result of our previous auditors being unable to resource the 2022/23 audit. Whilst significant progress has been made with the 2024/25 audit and review of critical balances from 2022/23 as part of the national building back assurance work, we are anticipating that a modified opinion will be issued for 2024/25

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows cumulative funding gap of £14.139m by 2029/30, growing from zero in 2026/27 to £7.212m
findings.detail: The council has balanced 2026/27 through a £5m savings programme, but the MTFP shows a growing structural deficit. The annual gap grows from £1.632m in 2027/28 to £7.212m in 2029/30. The council will need to identify further significant savings in the medium term, with no savings plan yet published.
findings.matters: A growing MTFP gap suggests sustained budget pressure. The council's ability to deliver £5m savings in 2026/27 and then find additional savings of £7.2m by 2029/30 demonstrates repeated reliance on savings to balance, which may constrain discretionary spending and reserves rebuilding.
findings.quote: The overall financial position is summarised in the table below, showing a current gap of £14.139m over the medium term.

findings.headline: SEND reform timing and funding remain uncertain, with White Paper expected early 2026 and statutory override extension beyond March 2028 unconfirmed
findings.detail: The council acknowledges 'significant uncertainties on what these reforms could entail as well as future funding'. A SEND White Paper is expected early 2026, and the government has extended the statutory override allowing schools deficits to sit outside the general fund, but only to 31 March 2028. The council is 'expecting the government to confirm specific financial support for existing deficits and deficits accruing up until the 31 March 2028', but states 'no details of the level of support have been published'.
findings.matters: SEND is the council's largest demand risk. Without clarity on reform scope, funding, and the statutory override extension, the council cannot forecast the true cost of high-needs education beyond 2028.
findings.figures: No figures on SEND reform impact; statutory override expires 31 March 2028; current deficits expected to grow significantly in future years
findings.quote: The SEND white paper is expected to be published by the Government in early 2026 outlining reforms to the service. There are currently therefore significant uncertainties on what these reforms could entail as well as future funding.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park operating at a loss; council now covers losses from 2026/27 following October 2025 unplanned shutdown
findings.detail: The MKWRP is a critical asset for processing waste but the council states it 'currently operates at a loss'. From 2026/27 the council will cover these operating losses in the revenue budget. An unplanned shutdown occurred in October 2025, and the council expects 'significant costs' from this to be met from the corporate contingency. Additionally, an Emissions Trading Scheme charge on the gasification element of the plant begins January 2028, creating further unquantified pressure. A new operating contract begins October 2026.
findings.matters: A material operating loss on a critical asset, combined with recent operational failure and unquantified future ETS liability, presents significant cost exposure. Lenders would need visibility on the new contract terms and mitigation plans for ETS costs.
findings.figures: Plant operates at loss (amount not specified); October 2025 shutdown costs to be funded from contingency; ETS impact from January 2028 (no provision yet made)
findings.quote: From 2026/27 the operating losses will be met by the Council. A provision has been made in the budget for the projected losses based on the current operating position.

findings.headline: High Needs Block running a £1.930m in-year deficit with statutory override extending only to March 2028
findings.detail: The council expected 3% funding growth for schools but received 0% (cash-flat funding). They will offset part of this with a £1.173m carry-forward surplus from 2025/26, leaving a £1.930m shortfall. The statutory override that allows this deficit to sit outside the general fund expires 31 March 2028, and council projections show the deficit growing significantly thereafter. They are awaiting a SEND White Paper to determine whether government will provide additional support.
findings.matters: If the statutory override is not extended beyond 2028, a growing schools deficit would have to be funded from the general fund or reserves, materially constraining the council's finances. This is a material contingent liability.
findings.figures: £1.930m in-year deficit 2026/27; £1.173m carry-forward used to offset; statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The draft high needs budget was modelled on a 3% funding increase as advised by the DfE, the final budget is a 0% increase in funding which means that there is now a deficit for 2026/27 in year of £1.930m.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: £182k commercial property income increase is amber-rated and depends on successful rent increases across the portfolio
findings.detail: Commercial property income of £182k in 2026/27 is rated amber and rests on a recent review that aims to ensure 'all rents are updated and appropriately set' and to add new income streams. No detail is provided on whether tenants have accepted increases or what the new streams are.
findings.matters: Amber-rated income assumptions based on subjective rent-setting judgements are higher risk; vacant units, tenant resistance, or economic downturn could prevent realisation.
findings.figures: £182k income assumed for 2026/27
findings.quote: A review has been undertaken to ensure that all rents are updated and appropriately set. Additional income streams have also been added. As a result, there is expected to be an increase in the base line rental income of the portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: New leisure contract income assumptions are highly variable: £212k in 2026/27 escalates to £638k in 2027/28, then falls to £315k
findings.detail: Income from the new leisure contract is budgeted at £212k in 2026/27 but triples to £638k in 2027/28, then drops sharply to £315k in 2028/29 and £103k in 2029/30. The large and unexplained swings suggest the underlying assumptions—possibly participation rates or tariff changes—are unstable.
findings.matters: Highly volatile income savings from a single contract-dependent source can mask unrealistic assumptions; if the 2027/28 assumption does not hold, the budget has a material gap.
findings.quote: New leisure contract - to reflect increased income as a result of the new leisure contract

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: £0.86m Household Waste Recycling Centres capital project is amber-rated; involves land purchase and site disposal
findings.detail: A three-year capital project to move to two 'Recycling and Reuse' sites is expected to save £215k (2026/27), £345k (2027/28), and £300k (2028/29), totalling £0.86m. The amber rating indicates the council has not fully de-risked delivery of the land purchase and site disposals.
findings.matters: Amber-rated capital savings that fail would leave a £860k budget gap across the MTFP; lenders need confidence that land acquisitions and property transactions are proceeding to plan.
findings.figures: £0.860m total; £215k, £345k, £300k across three years
findings.quote: A Delegated Decision was taken in January 2025, which detailed the move to two new 'Recycling and Reuse' sites. This involved purchasing new land and disposing of existing sites. There will be a saving in management and transportation costs of the new planned arrangements. The saving being included over a 3 year period is £0.860M.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Property Asset Rationalisation savings have been re-profiled and delayed due to dependencies on other council projects
findings.detail: Property asset sales and building mergers were originally expected to deliver capital receipts and running cost savings. The paper now states the saving has been 're-profiled to allow more time to continue to review property related savings' and acknowledges 'dependencies on other wider projects'—signalling slippage.
findings.matters: Re-profiled capital projects signal either earlier over-optimism or emerging blockages; lenders assess whether the council's capital and property strategy is realistic and executable.
findings.figures: 2026/27: £50k; 2027/28 and 2028/29: negative (£150k, £173k) indicating revised assumptions
findings.quote: There is a programme of property mergers that is being implemented but it has dependencies on other wider projects. The saving has been re-profiled to allow more time to continue to review property related savings.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: £185k income assumption for 2027/28 from EV chargers has not yet been procured and rests on unverified market feedback
findings.detail: Concessionary EV charger income of £185k in 2027/28 is rated amber. The proposal states the procurement 'has not been undertaken yet but is due to commence in phases from 2026 onwards' and is 'a prudent view based on initial feedback from market engagement'—speculative at this stage.
findings.matters: Unproven income assumptions are a leading risk in local authority budget plans; if this does not materialise, the 2027/28 budget has an unmitigated £185k gap.
findings.figures: £185k income budgeted for 2027/28
findings.quote: The procurement has not been undertaken yet but is due to commence in phases from 2026 onwards. The income stream is a prudent view based on initial feedback from market engagement.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: Amber-rated staffing reduction at Linford Wood Place (12.6 FTE) carries delivery risk to Adult Services savings
findings.detail: The Adult Services Linford Wood Place proposal to save £299k in 2026/27 and 2027/28 is marked amber—the council's own risk rating for uncertain delivery. It relies on a 12.6 FTE reduction and consolidation to one site delivering efficiency gains.
findings.matters: Staffing reductions marked as amber-risk signal the council is uncertain whether the headcount cuts will deliver the planned saving without service quality loss that could undermine financial stability.
findings.figures: £299k in 2026/27 and 2027/28; 12.6 FTE reduction
findings.quote: Linford Wood Place - saving is due to a reduction of 12.6 FTE within the establishment, teams will be able to deliver efficiencies by being based on one site

findings.headline: Adult Services Learning Disability population forecast to grow 4% (32 new users at £0.050m each); autism diagnoses growing 34 additional users annually through MTFP
findings.detail: LD population pressures driven by demography and reaching adulthood. Service growth expected 4% (32 new users). Autism pressures reflect rising diagnoses due to increased public awareness; 34 additional service users budgeted annually continuing through MTFP. Both drive supported living and day care costs.
findings.matters: Structural demographic and health-related demand growth in adult social care is the largest long-term financial challenge for councils. Sustained 4%+ growth (above inflation) in multiple cohorts compounds year-on-year and strains long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: LD: 4% growth, 32 service users @ £0.050m each; Autism: 34 additional users per year
findings.quote: Population statistics suggest a 4% growth for LD...For 2026/27 there is anticipated net growth of 32 service users costing an average £0.050m per annum. [Autism:] there has been a significant increase in adults receiving a diagnosis of autism...The pressure assumes an additional 34 service users each year.

findings.headline: Election reserves depleted; base budget now carries election costs, creating £368k pressure in 2029/30 full Council election year
findings.detail: Reserves previously funding election costs alongside base budget have been exhausted. From 2029/30, base budget incorporates average election costs. Annual reserve contributions will begin in 2029/30 fallow year to fund subsequent elections. This restructuring eliminates prior flexibility.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates prior elections exceeded budget or reserves were drawn for other purposes. Moving to base budget reduces financial flexibility and increases budget volatility tied to four-year election cycles.
findings.figures: £368k pressure in 2029/30
findings.quote: In the past, reserves were used alongside the base budget to cover these expenses, but those reserves have now been depleted. Starting from the 2029/20, a budget has been incorporated into the base budget to cover the average cost of elections.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract re-procurement creates £5.9m 2026/27 pressure, offset by £1.9m saving in 2027/28
findings.detail: Council is re-procuring the MKWRP contract with October 2026 start date. Current operating costs underpin the £5.9m 2026/27 pressure. New contract includes incentives for cost reduction, with £1.9m savings projected for 2027/28 once confirmed.
findings.matters: Major contract renewal creates significant one-year cash pressure before savings materialise. The lag between cost increase and savings realisation affects borrowing requirements and cashflow planning.
findings.quote: The Council is currently re-procuring the contract to operate and maintain the MKWRP. The new contract anticipated start date is Oct 2026...The new contract will include incentives for the provider to reduce this cost pressure.

findings.headline: Children with Disabilities packages growing 11% with per-child costs rising faster than volume; 19% package growth and 22% cost inflation since 2023/24
findings.detail: Since 2023/24, the number of children in CWD packages has increased 19% while package costs rose 22%. The 2026/27 projection shows 11% growth (378 to 419 packages). Growth is attributed to increased diagnoses of Autism Spectrum Disorder and ADHD requiring higher support ratios (duty of care constraint).
findings.matters: Dual pressures of rising diagnoses and higher per-child support costs are both challenging. Support ratios are non-negotiable under safeguarding; this creates a hard cost floor that cannot be compressed without reducing service to existing children.
findings.figures: 19% package increase + 22% cost inflation 2023/24-2026/27; 11% growth 2026/27 (378→419); £300k pressure
findings.quote: Since 2023/24 the number of children receiving a package has increased by 19% whilst the cost of a package has increased by 22%. The number of CWD packages in 2026/27 is expected grow by 11%, from 378 to 419.

findings.headline: Looked After Children population projected to reach 526 by end 2026/27, up 37 from September 2025, driving external fostering to 160 placements
findings.detail: LAC population is expected to rise from 489 in September 2025 to 526 by end of 2026/27. External independent fostering placements budgeted at 160 for 2026/27 (up from 146), because in-house fostering capacity remains full. Roughly 69% of the LAC cohort is expected to require fostering.
findings.matters: Rising LAC numbers are leading indicators of social need and capacity constraints. When councils cannot place children internally, they move to expensive external markets. This 7.6% growth trajectory compounds and signals either demographic shift or policy/threshold changes.
findings.figures: LAC population 489→526 (37 increase, 7.6%); external IFA placements 146→160 (14 increase); £1,099k pressure
findings.quote: In September 2025 we had 489 LAC and our projections anticipate this number will reach 526 by the end of 2026/27. [...] The pressure for 2026/27 is based on 160 full year IFA placements (the 2025/26 budgeted number of placements was 146).

findings.headline: Children's residential placements rising 31% to 63 full-year equivalents in 2026/27, costing £7.65m
findings.detail: The council is budgeting 63 full-year high-cost residential placements in 2026/27, up from 48 in 2025/26. The paper notes there were 69 actual placements in September 2025 and step-down plans exist for some children, but projections indicate the level will remain persistently high. This is marked as HIGH DEMAND: EXCEPTIONAL risk.
findings.matters: Rising looked-after children and higher placement costs reflect service demand that in-house capacity cannot meet. Residential placements are high-cost and sticky; the trajectory compounds year-on-year and creates structural financial exposure.
findings.figures: 63 full-year placements vs 48 budgeted in 2025/26 (31% increase); £7,650k pressure for 2026/27
findings.quote: there has been an increase in the number of high cost residential placements, there were 69 placements at September 2025...The pressure for 2026/27 is based on the equivalent of 63 full year high cost placements (the 2025/26 budgeted placements was 48).

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: Total minimum working balance requirement is £30.97m after applying 25% reduction for multiple-event probability
findings.detail: After detailed risk assessment across eight risk categories (service costs, income, commercial, performance, residents support, government funding, balance sheet, and major events), the council determines it requires £30.97m in reserves. This reflects a 25% reduction from the gross £41.3m assessed risk to account for the low probability that all risks would crystallise simultaneously.
findings.matters: This is the council's own assessment of the reserve buffer needed to absorb foreseeable shocks without requiring emergency borrowing or service cuts.
findings.figures: Gross minimum working balance £41,293,942; after 25% probability reduction: £30,970,456
findings.quote: TOTAL ASSESSED MINIMUM WORKING BALANCE 41,293,942 [with] Percentage Reduction (25%) for Probability of Multiple Events (10,323,485) [resulting in] Total Minimum Working Balance Required 30,970,456

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: Adult social care placements demand remains unpredictable despite aging population being a known structural driver
findings.detail: The council flags adult social care placements as high-risk and demand-unpredictable, driven by an aging population and increasing care needs. Despite these being predictable structural factors, the council cannot forecast with confidence.
findings.matters: ASC is typically the largest budget area; inability to predict demand within acceptable margins indicates forecast weakness.
findings.figures: £5,904,565 minimum prudent reserve on £118,091,305 budget (5% risk factor, rated high)
findings.quote: With an ageing population and increased care needs across adult services the level of demand remains unpredictable.

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: MKWRP operator contract tender carries material commercial risk if procurement unsuccessful
findings.detail: The council is tendering a new operator contract for Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park from October 2026. The paper flags material commercial risks if the procurement does not deliver a successful outcome, which could result in additional unbudgeted costs.
findings.matters: Major procurement failure on a critical service would force the council into emergency contracting and additional cost exposure.
findings.figures: £500,000 risk provision
findings.quote: The Council is tendering the operator contract for Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park (MKWRP). There are material commercial risks associated with this procurement which if unsuccessful could lead to additional costs for the authority if a successful procurement outcome is not achieved.

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: Housing Benefit uncapped cost liability: council must fund full cost of supported housing and temporary accommodation after government subsidy cap
findings.detail: Milton Keynes is required by regulation to fund the full cost of eligible expenditure for supported housing and temporary accommodation provision, but the DWP subsidy is capped. The council must make up the difference, and this gap is expected to widen as demand rises.
findings.matters: This is a hard unfunded mandate with no ceiling on council liability, and demand is forecast to increase, making it a structural budget pressure.
findings.figures: £300,000 risk provision in reserves
findings.quote: MKCC is required under regulation to fund the full cost of eligible expenditure for the provision of supported housing as well as Temporary Accommodation, whilst the subsidy that can be claimed from DWP is capped, leaving the authority to fund the difference.

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: Homelessness demand rising due to cost-of-living crisis compressing rental supply, driving up temporary accommodation and prevention service costs
findings.detail: The council flags homelessness as a high-risk, unpredictable demand driver, with dual pressures: more people presenting as homeless, and landlords exiting the rental market due to rising mortgage costs, both reducing available affordable housing and pushing up costs for the council's temporary accommodation and prevention services.
findings.matters: This combines rising service demand with tightening supply, creating a cost squeeze that generic budget flexibility cannot address.
findings.figures: £2,283,319 minimum prudent reserve on £22,833,193 budget (10% risk factor, rated high)
findings.quote: Due to an increasing number of people presenting as homeless the level of demand is unpredictable. Furthermore the cost of living crisis is impacting on landlords who are then increasing rents above what tenants can afford or opting to sell the property due to increasing mortgage rates resulting in fewer rental properties within the market.

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: High Needs Block ring-fenced surplus expected to be fully consumed in 2026/27 with no funding uplift
findings.detail: The council notes that the ring-fenced surplus in the High Needs Block (£69.7m exposure) is expected to be completely used up in 2026/27. This occurs because there is no increase in the funding allocation between 2025/26 and 2026/27, despite continued demand growth in EHCP provision and increased complexity of need. A full government review of SEND is pending but changes and future funding remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Loss of this buffer means the council will face immediate DSG deficit pressure in 2027/28 unless demand moderates or government funding increases.
findings.figures: £69,700,347 High Needs Block exposure; £700,000 risk provision; ring-fenced surplus expected fully utilised in 26/27
findings.quote: There is currently a ring-fenced surplus in the high needs block but this is expected to be fully utilised in 26/27 due to there being no increase in the funding allocation between 25/26 and 26/27.

findings.paper_title: Annex R - Reserves Risk Assessment 26-7 Final Budget
findings.headline: Children's social care placements driving 10% reserve requirement on £52m budget due to external market cost inflation
findings.detail: The council holds £5.2m in reserves against £52.4m controllable budget for children's placements. The paper attributes this pressure to increasing complexity of needs, growth in numbers entering care, and lack of in-house capacity causing external market costs to rise. This is flagged as a high-risk, demand-driven cost driver.
findings.matters: Structural cost pressures in a statutory service that the council cannot decline to provide shape the baseline cost trajectory and reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: £5,238,984 minimum prudent reserve on £52,389,842 controllable budget at 10% assessed risk factor
findings.quote: Increasing demand for specialist placements due to complex needs of children coming into care and increasing number of children coming in to care. Lack of in-house capacity across Local Authorities is causing a pressure in the external market which is seeing costs increase significantly to meet demand and needs.

findings.headline: Sheltered housing service transfer from Adults Social Care adding £0.163m net cost with integration complexity
findings.detail: The council is transferring sheltered housing service from Adults Social Care (General Fund) to the Housing Neighbourhood Team (HRA), adding £0.163m in costs in 2026-27. Sheltered housing also saw increased intensive management charges (£0.538m) from a consultation. This integration adds complexity and cost to HRA operations.
findings.matters: Service transfer adds costs and operational complexity; could indicate future integration issues or cost control challenges; sheltered housing charges increasing significantly.
findings.figures: £0.163m net increase from service transfer; £0.538m intensive housing management charge increase
findings.quote: £0.163m net increase in costs associated with the transfer of the Sheltered Housing Service from Adults Social Care (GF) to Housing Neighbourhood Team (HRA).

findings.headline: Available new borrowing headroom reduced and highly constrained by debt cap; headroom fell £28.651m from draft budget
findings.detail: Table 4 shows available new borrowing capacity for 2026-27 is £69.54m, but this declined by £28.651m from the draft budget position. The council is operating close to its maximum borrowing limit (£421.11m cap vs £351.57m actual), leaving limited capacity to fund unexpected capital needs or cost pressures without breaching the debt cap.
findings.matters: Declining headroom constrains financial flexibility; council already using 83% of debt cap; any deterioration in financial position leaves limited borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Available new borrowing 2026/27: £69.54m (down £28.651m from draft); Actual borrowing £351.57m vs cap £421.11m

findings.headline: Rent increases already at maximum allowed (4.8%), limiting ability to offset cost pressures
findings.detail: Government rent policy allows a maximum increase of CPI + 1%, which for 2026-27 is 4.8%. The council is already at this maximum, proposing £5.22 per week average increase for tenants. No additional income can be raised through rents unless government policy changes (rent convergence is being awaited but not factored into the plan).
findings.matters: At maximum rent policy limit; any further cost increases cannot be covered by rent rises; limits financial flexibility and headroom.
findings.figures: 4.8% maximum rent increase (CPI 3.8% + 1%); average £5.22/week increase
findings.quote: Rent setting for social landlords is determined by Government policy under The Rent Standard. This allows for a maximum annual increase in rents of September CPI (3.8%) + 1%, therefore for 2026/27 the maximum increase is 4.8%.

findings.headline: 30-year business plan assumes interest rates fall to 4.50% from 2028-29 onwards, creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: The business plan plans for borrowing 2025/26-2027/28 at 5.00% but assumes subsequent borrowing from 2028-29 onwards at 4.50%. This embeds a bet that interest rates will fall 50 basis points and remain lower for the remainder of the 30-year period. If rates remain above 4.50%, the plan's financial headroom erodes.
findings.matters: Refinancing assumptions critical to 30-year plan viability; current market conditions suggest rates may not fall to assumed levels, risking plan sufficiency.
findings.figures: 5.00% borrowing cost 2025/26-2027/28; 4.50% from 2028/29 onwards
findings.quote: The business plan makes cost provision for the borrowing requirements from 2025/26 to 2027/28 to be funded at an interest rate of 5.00% over 30 years, with subsequent borrowing required from 2028/29 onwards at an interest rate of 4.50% across the remaining plan period.

findings.headline: Interest cover ratio weak at 1.50 in 2026-27 and declining from draft budget assumptions
findings.detail: Table 4 shows interest cover ratio of only 1.50 in 2026-27 (down 0.17 from draft), indicating tight debt service coverage. This means gross rental income covers interest costs by only 1.5x, leaving limited buffer for adverse changes. The ratio improves to 1.87 by 2030-31 but only if assumptions hold.
findings.matters: Low interest cover ratio indicates limited cushion against income shocks or rate rises; any deterioration in rental income or further rate increases creates debt service risk.
findings.figures: Interest Cover Ratio 2026/27: 1.50 (down 0.17 from draft)
findings.quote: Interest Cover Ratio 1.50

findings.headline: Major decanting programme at Serpentine Court and Reema Blocks creating £0.751m Council Tax billing cost burden
findings.detail: The council is actively decanting residents from Serpentine Court and Reema Blocks while managing properties classed as 'out of management'. Council Tax billing processes have become more complex (now requiring gov.uk submission with photographs) and slower at the Valuation Office, creating a one-off £0.751m cost in 2026-27. This indicates significant remediation or demolition work underway.
findings.matters: Major decanting programmes indicate asset disposal or major remediation underway; administrative cost suggests scale of work; indicates use of reserves to fund operational costs during transformation.
findings.figures: £0.751m one-off Council Tax cost in 2026/27
findings.quote: With decants actively happening in Serpentine Court and the Reema Blocks along with the properties that are classed as 'out of management' this is a considerable cost.

findings.headline: Void rates increasing as stock is identified for removal from management due to condition surveys
findings.detail: Dwelling rent income is down £0.135m in 2026-27 due to a 0.2% increase in void rates. The council attributes this to 'a more prudent approach as stock continues to be identified for out of management and the outcome of the stock condition surveys are unknown.' This suggests worsening stock condition is driving properties out of lettable stock.
findings.matters: Rising voids reduce rental income and indicate asset utilization deterioration; suggests condition survey results may reveal further stock quality issues affecting income.
findings.figures: £0.135m rent reduction; 0.2% void rate increase; void rate moving to 1.2% until 2030/31 then 1.0%
findings.quote: Dwelling Rent - £0.135m reduction from 2026/27 represents an increase in the voids rate of 0.2%, this reflects a more prudent approach as stock continues to be identified for out of management and the outcome of the stock condition surveys are unknown.

findings.headline: £2.7m Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund grant being returned due to delivery complexities
findings.detail: The council held £2.7m of SHDF Wave 2 grant to fund a capital decarbonisation scheme. Due to delivery complexities, this grant is 'now likely to be returned'. This removes £2.7m of grant funding from the capital programme in 2026-27, creating a funding gap that must be addressed through reserves or borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital funding gap of £2.7m requires replacement funding; indicates delivery risk on decarbonisation commitments and tighter capital resources.
findings.figures: £2.700m grant removed from 2026/27 capital funding
findings.quote: With the complexities of delivering the Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) Wave 2, the £2.700m of grant we are holding to fund the scheme is now likely to be returned.

findings.headline: PWLB concessionary HRA borrowing rate (40 basis points discount) expires 31 March 2026, forcing higher-cost external borrowing
findings.detail: The council currently borrows HRA funds at 40 basis points below General Fund rates under a government scheme ending March 2026. Thereafter, external borrowing will cost 40bp more than planned. The council plans to draw down borrowing before March 2026 as cash position weakens, locking in current rates on some debt but leaving refinancing risk thereafter.
findings.matters: Material increase in borrowing costs from April 2026 will erode debt service coverage and tighten the 30-year plan; timing and quantum of pre-March drawdown affects cost profile.
findings.figures: 40 basis points discount ending 31 March 2026; business plan assumes 5.00% from 2025/26-2027/28, then 4.50% thereafter
findings.quote: The HRA is currently able to borrow from the PWLB at 40 basis points less than the GF, but this ends in March 2026.

findings.headline: HRA financial position has declined with structural asset challenges from non-traditional construction and aging stock
findings.detail: The council reports sustained financial decline driven by inflation, government rent caps, higher borrowing rates, and asset-related challenges. As a new town, Milton Keynes has aging housing stock with substantial non-traditional construction materials requiring significant remediation. The council is accelerating condition surveys over three years to better understand the asset liabilities.
findings.matters: Major structural asset liabilities indicate long-term capital funding pressures that could affect debt service capacity; lenders need clarity on stock condition and remediation timelines.
findings.figures: HRA position 'declined in recent years'; 'substantial proportion of our stock being built from non-traditional construction materials'
findings.quote: The financial position of the HRA has declined in recent years, for several reasons including the recent economic challenges where we have seen record and sustained levels of inflation, previous government policy decision on rent setting (caps and reductions), higher borrowing rates and additional regulatory requirements. As a new town and now a city, we grew quickly and that gives us further challenges with our stock, with similar ageing profiles and a substantial proportion of our stock being built from non-traditional construction materials, so we face several significant asset related challenges at the same time.

findings.headline: Sensitivity analysis shows pessimistic scenario reaches a £65.9m budget gap (vs £14.1m base case)
findings.detail: Table 13 presents three scenarios: Optimistic shows a (£30.365m) surplus; base case (MTFP) shows £14.139m gap; pessimistic shows £65.884m gap. The pessimistic scenario (table 14b) assumes only modest adverse changes: 250 fewer council tax properties, 2% higher national living wage, 5% higher children/adult placement demand, 10% higher homelessness, and 5% loss of parking/planning income. This wide range (£45.7m between pessimistic and optimistic) signals high financial vulnerability.
findings.matters: A £51.7m swing to the pessimistic case (from £14.1m gap to £65.9m) driven by modest demand and income variations demonstrates that the council's finances are fragile and dependent on assumptions holding. Actual performance could easily exceed the MTFP gap.
findings.figures: Pessimistic scenario total: £65.884m; base case: £14.139m; optimistic: (£30.365m) surplus; total sensitivity range £96.2m
findings.quote: Table 13 Budget Scenario's... Pessimistic 10.017 14.497 19.199 22.171 65.884

findings.headline: Homelessness is 50% above the England average and driving capital and revenue investment with ongoing demand uncertainty
findings.detail: Section 13 (benchmarking) shows 'In 2025/26 Q1, DLUHC assessed the number of households as homeless per thousand in Milton Keynes was 2.77, which was greater than All English unitary authorities' average number of households assessed as homeless per thousand of 1.84.' The council has invested in accommodation, and while section 9.21 states 'no additional pressures have been put in the MTFP' because it is 'being well managed,' the high baseline and continued population growth create ongoing volatility.
findings.matters: Homelessness 50% above national average indicates a structural demand challenge in the council's area (driven by housing affordability and population growth) that may require sustained above-average investment.
findings.figures: 2.77 households assessed as homeless per 1,000 vs England average of 1.84 (2025/26 Q1); 863 households in temporary accommodation vs England average of 316
findings.quote: In 2025/26 Q1, DLUHC assessed the number of households as homeless per thousand in Milton Keynes was 2.77, which was greater than All English unitary authorities' average number of households assessed as homeless per thousand of 1.84.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) waste funding is declining and uncertain beyond 2026/27
findings.detail: Section 6.4 states 'The funding level beyond 2026/27 is not clear as this will be dependent upon actual EPR collected by the government, behaviour changes by the sector and how government may choose to allocate funding to authorities.' The council has assumed £4.819m in 2026/27 but table 4 shows it declining to £4.219m (2027/28), £3.519m (2028/29), £2.819m (2029/30). This is a new grant introduced in the Autumn Budget 2024 with no clarity on multi-year funding.
findings.matters: A declining and uncertain income stream (£2m reduction over three years) from a brand-new source means the council cannot assume it as permanent baseline funding and will need to find alternative savings.
findings.figures: £4.819m 2026/27, declining to £2.819m by 2029/30 (total MTFP decline of £2.0m)
findings.quote: The funding level beyond 2026/27 is not clear as this will be dependent upon actual EPR collected by the government, behaviour changes by the sector and how government may choose to allocate funding to authorities.

findings.headline: Business Rates Retention Scheme entirely reset in 2026/27, removing all business growth income and introducing valuation appeal risk
findings.detail: Section 8.3 states 'the Business Rates Retention Scheme (BRRS) has been entirely reset in 2026/27, starting on April 1, 2026. All business rates growth has been removed and redistributed using new funding formulas from that date.' Section 8.7 identifies significant collection risks: 'Ratepayers are able to raise challenges to their rating valuations and where successful the rateable value is reduced... we have assumed in the 2026/27 budget that appeals losses will result in the loss of 1.5% of the net rates payable.' The council expects to collect net rates of £249.185m but retains only £67.701m baseline.
findings.matters: Removal of all business growth income and a 1.5% loss assumption on valuation appeals (with scope for 'significant variations') means the retained business rates income is now entirely baseline and more volatile, without the benefit of economic growth in Milton Keynes (which has strong GVA growth of £16.7bn).
findings.figures: Net rates collected £249.185m; council retains £67.701m baseline (50% of net rates less fire authority share and tariff/levy); 1.5% appeal loss assumption
findings.quote: the Business Rates Retention Scheme (BRRS) has been entirely reset in 2026/27... All business rates growth has been removed and redistributed using new funding formulas from that date.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes waste recovery contract is being re-procured mid-cycle with current operating costs of £5.9m pressure in 2026/27
findings.detail: Section 9.23 states 'The Council is currently re-procuring the contract to operate and maintain the MKWRP. The new contract anticipated start date is Oct 2026. Whilst the commissioning is still ongoing, current operating costs have been used as the basis of the pressure of £5.9m in 2026/27. The new contract will include incentives for the provider to reduce this cost pressure and when savings are confirmed, they will be incorporated into future MTFP workings.' This is a major commercial contract with uncertain outcomes.
findings.matters: A £5.9m cost pressure from a waste contract re-procurement with savings incentives 'to be confirmed' means the full year impact is contingent on commercial negotiation outcomes, introducing upside/downside risk to the baseline.
findings.figures: £5.9m contractual change pressure in 2026/27 (section 9.23); section 10.3 identifies £6.762m total savings/income 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: The Council is currently re-procuring the contract to operate and maintain the MKWRP. The new contract anticipated start date is Oct 2026... current operating costs have been used as the basis of the pressure of £5.9m in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Agora regeneration scheme costs and revenues remain unquantified and a Cabinet decision is pending
findings.detail: Section 4.3 notes that the MTFP 'includes the costs of interest and minimum revenue provision relating to the financing of the Agora project within the capital programme. No assumptions have yet been included in the MTFP for the income anticipated from this scheme. This will be updated once build costs are more certain and decisions are finalised on how this asset will be held.' Section 1.19 records 'The regeneration of the former Agora shopping centre and the adjoining car park has been a Council priority for over two decades' and that 'a separate Cabinet Decision is planned to be taken on 3 February 2026 to further update on this regeneration, as well as set out future decision making to deliver it.'
findings.matters: A major capital scheme with decades of difficulty, unresolved build costs, and unmodelled income makes the council's financial projections incomplete. Any increase in borrowing costs or delay in income crystallisation will worsen the MTFP gap.
findings.figures: Agora interest and MRP costs embedded in capital financing costs (£1.692m total over MTFP) but income from the scheme not yet assumed
findings.quote: The reported gap includes the costs of interest and minimum revenue provision relating to the financing of the Agora project within the capital programme. No assumptions have yet been included in the MTFP for the income anticipated from this scheme. This will be updated once build costs are more certain and decisions are finalised on how this asset will be held.

findings.headline: Contractual inflation in social care has spiked 28% in one year and now projects £37.593m pressure over the MTFP
findings.detail: Section 9.9 states 'Contractual Inflation for 2026/27 has risen by £2.202m since February 2025... Over the medium term it is estimated that contractual inflation will rise to a budget pressure of £37.593m, an increase of 28% from February 2025, which is a significant risk to the Councils financial position.' The main driver is National Living Wage inflation (section 9.10): the Foundation Living Wage is forecast to increase 5.58% for 2026/27, then 3.54% in 2027/28. Adult services alone carry £5.802m of contractual inflation in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A 28% year-on-year increase in contractual inflation projections (driven by care worker wages) is well ahead of core inflation and signals that care placement costs and staffing costs are accelerating, likely exceeding the council's savings and income plans.
findings.figures: £2.202m increase since February 2025; £37.593m total MTFP pressure (28% increase from prior forecast); £5.802m adult services inflation in 2026/27; 5.58% Foundation Living Wage increase 2026/27
findings.quote: Contractual Inflation for 2026/27 has risen by £2.202m since February 2025... Over the medium term it is estimated that contractual inflation will rise to a budget pressure of £37.593m, an increase of 28% from February 2025, which is a significant risk to the Councils financial position.

findings.headline: Looked after children have surged 26% in three years with uncertain peak and £17.125m pressure built in
findings.detail: Section 9.16 records LAC numbers rising 'from an average of 379 in 2023/24 to 477 in 2024/25 (26% increase)' and in December 2025 standing at 481. Section 9.18 explicitly states 'There remains a lot of uncertainty in the MTFP regarding the longer-term forecasts for Children's Placements. Of the £17.615m budget pressure in the medium term, £7.639m has been built into the 26/27 budget. This is because future demands at this point are difficult to predict.' The service believes the peak has been reached but acknowledges uncertainty and risk to budget projections.
findings.matters: A 26% surge in the most expensive placements (high-cost residential care) with acknowledged forecasting uncertainty means actual outturn could significantly exceed budget if the peak has not been reached or if placement numbers plateau at elevated levels.
findings.figures: LAC increased from 379 (2023/24) to 477 (2024/25) to 481 (December 2025); £17.125m MTFP pressure (£7.639m in 2026/27); additional staff costs £0.140m
findings.quote: Looked after Children (LAC) numbers over the last 3 years from an average of 379 in 2023/24 to 477 in 2024/25 (26% increase)... There remains a lot of uncertainty in the MTFP regarding the longer-term forecasts for Children's Placements... there is still some uncertainty and therefore a risk to the budget projection included in the MTFP.

findings.headline: High Needs Block (special education) will have zero reserves by March 2027 with no in-year contingency
findings.detail: Section 11.3 states the surplus will reduce from £3.103m to £1.173m in 2025/26 due to demand and inflation, and then 'the HNB 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all of this remaining surplus. There will therefore be no surplus by the end of March 2027 and there is no contingency in year to allow for any volatility.' The statutory override protecting councils with deficits expires March 2027 (extended to end 2027/28), creating a cliff edge. Nationally, 2 in 3 councils carry HNB deficits forecast to reach £5bn by March 2026.
findings.matters: A zero-contingency ring-fenced budget block with a track record of overspend (currently in-year overspend in 2025/26) is a immediate budget risk that will force the general fund to absorb any overspend once the statutory override expires.
findings.figures: Surplus reduces from £3.103m budgeted to £1.173m forecast in 2025/26; used entirely in 2026/27 leaving £0m; £4.023m high needs block allocation increase for 2026/27 but insufficient to cover demand
findings.quote: the HNB 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all of this remaining surplus. There will therefore be no surplus by the end of March 2027 and there is no contingency in year to allow for any volatility.

findings.headline: The council has a £14.139m cumulative funding gap across the MTFP period with no identified solution
findings.detail: The budget is balanced in 2026/27 but the gap grows to £1.632m in 2027/28, £6.927m cumulatively by 2028/29, reaching £14.139m by 2029/30. The council has put in place a 'Change Because We Have To' programme but no specific savings are attached to these future years. Section 10.5 states the council 'will need to take further difficult decisions' but these have not been identified.
findings.matters: A £14m unfunded gap over three years signals the council cannot deliver a balanced budget without major service reductions or further borrowing, which directly affects financial sustainability and borrowing costs.
findings.figures: £14.139m cumulative gap (£0m, £1.632m, £6.927m cumulative, £14.139m by 2029/30)
findings.quote: Looking beyond 2026/27, the funding gap is currently £14.139m. The Council will need to take further difficult decisions to address these challenges over this period.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Placement costs for children in care are rising, with no cap on demand.
findings.detail: Risk SR15 flags 'Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements' and lists as a trigger 'Change in demand for children (e.g. increase in LAC numbers, child protection referrals)'. The risk score is 15 (target 10), with no recent improvement. The council is attempting to grow in-house foster carer recruitment and adoption services, but the triggers suggest external market forces and demand are outpacing supply.
findings.matters: Placement costs (especially residential and external foster care) are a volatile line item that grows with demand and market prices. A council unable to forecast or limit this spend faces in-year budget pressure.
findings.figures: Current risk score 15, target 10. No specific cost figures disclosed.
findings.quote: Increased costs due to failure to properly plan to ensure sufficient access to high quality placements

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Milton Keynes has aging assets of similar vintage requiring more maintenance spend than budgeted.
findings.detail: Risk SR16 identifies that 'the assets are of a similar age which can lead to large numbers of defects/interventions being required. this leads to insufficient budget or budget exceeded for works required to appropriately maintain the assets.' This means the council faces a cohort risk: many assets reaching end-of-life at once, creating uneven demand spikes that current budgets cannot absorb.
findings.matters: A council with assets of similar age faces unpredictable lumpy maintenance demands and may need to borrow or defer maintenance. This is a precursor to service deterioration or unexpected capital pressure.
findings.figures: No specific budget figures disclosed, but the risk is identified as recurring and structural.
findings.quote: the age and quality of MK assets – the assets are of a similar age which can lead to large numbers of defects/interventions being required. this leads to insufficient budget or budget exceeded for works required to appropriately maintain the assets.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Housing landlord acknowledges insufficient budget for repairs due to rent cost cap and inflation.
findings.detail: Risk SR04 identifies the core problem: 'insufficient budget to deliver works to standard required, including external factors such as imposed rent cost cap, inflation and interest rates.' The risk is currently scored 9 (target 6), meaning it remains elevated. The council is taking action (condition surveys due 01/11/2025, NEC procurement by 01/04/2026) but acknowledges the gap between what it needs to spend and what it can spend.
findings.matters: Housing Revenue Account is a material asset and income stream. A council unable to maintain its housing stock to standard faces compliance failures, tenant claims, and regulator intervention. The rent cap + inflation squeeze is a known structural problem.
findings.figures: Current risk score 9, target score 6. Risk score higher than target indicates mitigation is incomplete.
findings.quote: Budget – insufficient budget to deliver works to standard required, including external factors such as imposed rent cost cap, inflation and interest rates.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: Waste Recovery Plant carries up to £6.5M exposure from a single unplanned outage.
findings.detail: Risk SR13 details exposure from the Waste Recovery Plant's poor availability. The council is liable for up to £500k property damage plus up to 90 days of direct losses (less first 5 days) if the plant fails. The catastrophic boiler failure in October 2022 left the facility unavailable for 4 months and cost the contractors £2M per month, so maximum exposure could reach £6.5M. The plant has a history of only 60% availability. The council has now discovered a £4M annual cost delta in the income/expenditure model, equivalent to a gate fee of £60 per tonne.
findings.matters: The plant is critical waste infrastructure with severe financial consequences if it fails. The discovery of a £4M annual cost gap in the operating model suggests the council may have mispriced this service for years.
findings.figures: Maximum exposure £6.5M from a single failure; £500k property damage + 90 days direct losses; catastrophic boiler failure in Oct 2022 cost contractors £2M per month; new cost model reveals £4M annual delta; monthly cost approximately £840k (staff £300k pa, disposal £7.8M pa, insurances £1.1M pa, NNDR £800k pa).
findings.quote: The contractors losses owing to the catastrophic boiler failure equated to around £2M per month (including lost revenue, haulage and disposal and staff costs) so maximum exposure could be around £6.5M.

findings.paper_title: Annex A - Strategic Risk Register Aug 2025
findings.headline: The council faces unprecedented savings requirements and exceptional financial challenges.
findings.detail: Risk SR07 explicitly identifies 'Exceptional Financial Challenges requiring unprecedented savings' as a trigger and consequence. This language signals the council believes it faces budget pressures beyond the norm, with triggers including failure to manage large increases in demand and failure to put in place business continuity plans for service provider failure.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council has identified the scale of its own challenge. This language—'unprecedented'—suggests the finance team believes standard solutions are insufficient.
findings.figures: No specific savings target or amount disclosed, but categorised as 'unprecedented'.
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Challenges requiring unprecedented savings

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes forecasts £0.376m high needs deficit for 2026/27, rising to £2.473m in 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes City Council forecasts a year-end deficit of £0.376m for 2026/27 on high needs, the part of schools funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Its period 6 forecast shows an in-year deficit of £1.615m, partly offset by a £1.239m surplus brought forward from 2025/26. For 2027/28 the draft budget forecasts a year-end deficit of £2.473m. The Department for Education (DfE) has not yet confirmed allocations of the dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, and the draft assumes no increase in high needs funding.

The council's quarter 2 outturn report puts the overall DSG surplus carried forward at £1.623m, against £2.514m budgeted, a movement of £0.891m that it says is driven mainly by the early years block. It gives independent placements as 87 against a budget of 80. The council has applied to DfE to move 0.5% of the schools block, about £1.515m, to high needs. Its reform plan for special educational needs awaits DfE approval, expected in November. The final high needs position goes to Cabinet with the final budget in February 2027.

The council did not receive the High Needs Stability Grant, which covered 90% of the overall DSG deficit at 31 March 2026 for councils in deficit, because it held an overall surplus. The national total was £5.812bn. Its reserves risk assessment sets the maximum high needs shortfall it is liable for at £64.7m, with a £1m risk provision. The effect on the General Fund is described as unclear until government announces whether support will be provided.

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes forecasts £0.376m high needs deficit for 2026/27, and £2.473m schools grant deficit for 2027/28
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes City Council forecasts a deficit of £0.376m on high needs, the part of schools funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, at the end of 2026/27. Its draft 2027/28 budget, before Cabinet on 1 December, forecasts a year-end deficit of £2.473m on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. The Department for Education (DfE) has not yet confirmed allocations for 2027/28.

The 2026/27 figure comes from the period 6 forecast: an in-year high needs deficit of £1.615m, partly offset by a £1.239m surplus brought forward. The papers say high needs funding rose by 0% in 2026/27, which created pressure on the budget. The council received nothing from the High Needs Stability Grant, which paid £5.812bn nationally in October at 90% of each authority's deficit at 31 March 2026, because it held a surplus then. The quarter 2 report forecasts the grant's carry-forward at £1.623m against £2.514m budgeted, mainly from an Early Years DfE adjustment and additional provider payments.

The council's High Needs Block Action Plan "has delivered substantial savings to date", the paper says, with no figure given. Schools Forum did not approve moving 0.5% of the schools block, about £1.515m, to high needs, so the council has asked the DfE to approve the transfer. The outcome will be reported in the Final Budget report.

news_drafts.headline: Milton Keynes used all its remaining schools surplus to balance 2026/27, and expects a high needs deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Milton Keynes City Council used all of its remaining brought-forward surplus on special educational needs funding to balance the 2026/27 budget, and expects to start 2027/28 in deficit on that spending, papers for the Budget and Resources Scrutiny Committee on 6 October show. The money is in the "high needs" block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities, paid for from the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools).

The council's medium-term financial outlook says costs on high needs are running ahead of government funding. It says "there is a chance that the block will go into a deficit during the 2026/27 if there were to be any in year overspend", so "it is therefore likely we may start the 2027/28 financial year in a deficit." A separate General Fund annex, covering the council's main day-to-day budget, says the block "is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27". It says the effect on that budget is unclear "as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support." The paper gives no figure for the deficit. A review with the high needs school reference group is under way to find savings.

A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such deficits off a council's main balance sheet, lets them be carried forward until 2028. The paper estimates councils with schools responsibilities hold about £5 billion of high needs deficits between them by the end of 2025/26. The council also says it will not receive its indicative 2027/28 schools funding until December 2026. Draft allocations "used to be published in July", it says, and this is the third year of delay. The full budget update will wait until then.
